# ANSI Escape Sequences

An ANSI escape sequence is a short byte pattern that tells a terminal to do something other than print a character: move the cursor, erase part of the screen, switch to bold, or set a window title. Every terminal program—a shell prompt, `git`, `vim`, a compiler's colored diagnostics—speaks this protocol, and a terminal emulator is mostly the machinery that interprets it.

## What it is

A terminal receives a stream of bytes over a pseudo-terminal and decides, byte by byte, whether each one is text to place in the next cell or the start of a command. The commands all begin with the escape byte, `0x1B` (written `ESC`, `\033`, or `\x1b`). Three families cover almost everything a user will meet:

| Form | Name | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `ESC [` … final byte | CSI, control sequence | Cursor movement, erase, modes, scrolling |
| `ESC ]` … `BEL`/`ST` | OSC, operating system command | Titles, hyperlinks, application-defined notices |
| `ESC [` … `m` | SGR, select graphic rendition | Color and text attributes |

CSI sequences carry numeric parameters separated by semicolons and end in a letter. `ESC[2J` erases the display, `ESC[3;5H` puts the cursor at row 3, column 5, and `ESC[1m` turns on bold. The parameters are optional and have defaults, which is why `ESC[H` and `ESC[1;1H` mean the same thing. SGR is a CSI sequence whose final byte is `m`; it sets the attributes that apply to everything printed afterwards, until another SGR changes them.

```text
\x1b[2J        erase the whole display
\x1b[H         move the cursor home
\x1b[3;5H      move to row 3, column 5
\x1b[K         erase from the cursor to the end of the line
\x1b[1;31m     bold, red foreground
\x1b[0m        reset all attributes
\x1b[?1049h    switch to the alternate screen
\x1b]0;title\x07   set the window title
```

A useful way to read this is as a tiny painting language. The terminal has a cursor; printing a character writes it at the cursor and advances one cell. Nothing in the stream says "this word is red"—the sequence says "the foreground is now red", and the color stays in effect until reset. Erasing is equally literal: it blanks cells, it does not delete text from a document. The terminal keeps no document at all, only the current state of the grid.

Cursor movement is what makes interactive output possible. Instead of appending lines, a program can jump back to a known position and overwrite what it drew before. A scrolling region (set with `ESC[<top>;<bottom>r`) narrows the part of the screen that scrolls, which is how a full-screen application keeps a status bar fixed while its content moves. Erase and scroll-region commands together are the whole basis of screen-oriented programs; there is no separate drawing API.

## How gPTY uses it

gPTY has two parsers over the same bytes, for two different jobs. The concept matcher uses a deliberately small line parser in `crates/gpty-core/src/parser.rs` that walks the stream with the Rust `vte` crate and keeps only printable text, discarding colors, cursor moves, and erase operations. That is what lets a regex trigger match a command's output without being confused by formatting.

The display path is different. `crates/gpty-core/src/term.rs` wraps `alacritty_terminal`, feeds the same bytes through `vte::ansi::Processor`, and maintains full grid state: cursor position, SGR attributes, scrolling regions, alternate-screen mode, and mouse modes. It is the grid that knows a cell is bold or red, and it hands the Godot renderer a resolved picture of the screen.

One detail shows why "just strip the escapes" is not enough. On Windows, ConPTY renders line breaks by moving the cursor to the next row rather than emitting a newline byte. The line parser therefore interprets cursor moves that advance the row, committing the pending line, while ignoring same-row moves—those are prompt redraws and progress-bar updates that must not be split into separate lines.

## Why bytes and not markup

It is tempting to think of terminal output as styled text, like HTML. It is not. The stream is imperative: it mutates cursor and attribute state, and the visible result depends on the order of every instruction before it. That is why the same byte stream can render differently at a different window width, and why scrollback is a record of lines rather than a record of commands.

It also means terminal output is untrusted display data. A program can paint anything it likes on the grid—including escape sequences that look like prompts—but those bytes are interpreted by the emulator as drawing instructions, never executed. gPTY's concept engine is built around that rule: a concept can capture output and route it to another pane, but it can never write to a PTY or run a command. The effects gPTY honors beyond the grid are deliberately few: OSC title updates, emulator replies such as cursor-position reports that are written back to the child, and the display-only `gpty_state=` declaration used for agent state.

## Limits and edge cases

Unknown or malformed sequences are ignored rather than treated as text. A sequence that is never terminated is different: the parser stays inside it, so every byte after it is swallowed and the string's payload accumulates until a terminator arrives. Both halves matter — output stops being interpreted *and* memory grows — so a terminal has to bound it, and what needs bounding depends on which sequences its parser actually buffers.

gPTY closes an unterminated OSC after 64 KiB with a `BEL` and resumes normal parsing, from one shared guard (`crates/gpty-core/src/escstring.rs`) placed in front of both parsers: the display grid and the plain-text line parser. A truncated title or hyperlink can therefore neither hold text extraction hostage nor grow the process. DCS, APC, PM and SOS payloads are read and discarded by `alacritty_terminal` instead of buffered, so they are not counted — measuring that is what decides the guard's scope rather than assuming every string behaves alike.

Finally, escape sequences do not compose into a reliable "screenshot" format. If you need the screen as text, ask the terminal for its resolved cells, not for the bytes that produced them—which is exactly what `paneRead` does.

# ConPTY

ConPTY is Windows' pseudo console: the mechanism that gives a Windows program the same
"you are attached to a terminal" illusion a Unix PTY gives. It is why a gPTY pane on
Windows can run an interactive shell, a full-screen editor or a colorized build without
the app needing a second terminal implementation.

## What it is

Unix has `/dev/ptmx`: the kernel allocates a master and a slave device and puts a line
discipline between them. Windows has no such device. Historically, console programs
talked to `conhost.exe` through the Win32 console API — a rich set of calls for writing
characters, setting colors and moving the cursor — and there was no supported way for an
unrelated application to host that console inside its own window.

ConPTY closes that gap with a *pseudo console*: a console host process plus a pair of
pipes. The application creates the pseudo console, gets a handle for the "master" side,
and starts the child attached to it. Everything the child does through the console API is
executed against a real console buffer and then **re-rendered** by the console host into
a stream of VT-style bytes, which the application reads from the pipe. Input travels the
other way: the application writes bytes, the console host turns them into console input
records for the child.

Two consequences follow from "there is a process in the middle", and they matter:
the output gPTY receives is a rendering of console state rather than the child's raw
writes, and input goes through a translation step instead of a kernel line discipline.

## The familiar example

A Windows program that prints in color and draws a progress bar with cursor movement is
usually calling console APIs, not writing escape sequences. Under a ConPTY, the console
host observes those calls and emits the equivalent VT sequences for the hosting
application. That is why a pane can display such a program correctly even though the
program never produced a byte of ANSI text itself. On Unix the same program would be
writing the escape sequences directly to the slave device.

## Why `portable-pty` exists

gPTY's engine asks for a PTY once, through `portable-pty` 0.9, using a single set of
types: a native PTY system handle, a command builder, a master handle, and a size. The
allocation itself — `/dev/ptmx` on Unix, a pseudo console on Windows — happens inside
the crate, so the pane's spawn, read loop and resize logic are written once.

The platform branches that remain are small but informative — executable lookup honors
Windows' `PATHEXT` extensions, and foreground-job detection returns "unknown" on Windows
because a pseudo console has no foreground-process-group equivalent to compare against.
That last one is the clearest statement of what ConPTY does not model: there is no
process-group notion to ask about.

## What actually differs

| Question | Unix PTY | ConPTY |
|---|---|---|
| What the pair is | Kernel device pair (`/dev/ptmx`, `/dev/pts/N`) | A console host process plus pipes |
| Line discipline | In the kernel | Not present; the console host handles input |
| Where output comes from | The child's own writes | The console host's re-rendering of console state |
| Interrupt | `Ctrl+C` becomes `SIGINT` via the line discipline | A console control event delivered by the console host |
| Window size | `ioctl` plus `SIGWINCH` to the child | A resize request to the pseudo console |

The practical reading of that table: the *contract* is the same — a program that asks
"am I on a terminal?" hears yes, and an application can read a VT-style byte stream and
drive a grid — while the *mechanism* differs enough that timing and some edge cases are
not identical.

## Limits and edge cases

- Latency is one process deeper. Output passes through the console host before gPTY sees
  it, so a burst of writes can arrive in slightly different chunks than on Unix. The
  parser does not care: the byte stream is still a byte stream.
- Re-rendering can normalize. Because the console host converts console state into
  sequences, some details of *how* a program drew something may not survive byte-for-byte.
  In practice this is invisible for normal interactive use, and it is the reason
  terminal-compatibility edge cases are often platform-specific.
- Resize is a request, not a signal. A program that ignores the new size will keep
  drawing at the old dimensions, exactly as on Unix.
- Text selection and copy in the pane are gPTY's own (the grid is gPTY's state); they do
  not depend on the Windows console's selection mode.
- Closing the pane tears down the pseudo console, and the child is expected to notice.
  A detached helper process can keep running, the same as a Unix equivalent.

# Full-Screen TUI

A full-screen TUI is an interactive program that owns the whole terminal screen and repaints it, the way `vim`, `htop`, and `lazygit` do. It is not a different protocol from ordinary terminal output—it is the same escape sequences used with cursor addressing and a second screen buffer.

## What it is

A shell prompt writes append-only output: print a line, newline, print the next. A full-screen program cannot work that way. Its cursor sits wherever it is needed—the middle of the screen, the end of the status bar—and the content changes in place, so it must be able to say "put the cursor here and overwrite these cells."

Three mechanisms make that practical:

- **Cursor addressing.** `ESC[row;colH` places the cursor at an absolute position. Erase commands (`ESC[2J` for the display, `ESC[K` for the rest of a line) clear cells before the program writes new content.
- **The alternate screen.** `ESC[?1049h` switches to a second buffer, and `ESC[?1049l` switches back. The application gets a clean screen without destroying the shell's scrollback, and on exit the original screen reappears exactly as it was.
- **Terminal modes.** The program hides the cursor while repainting (`ESC[?25l`), can capture mouse events, and can ask for bracketed paste so pasted text is distinguishable from typed keys. All of these are set with sequences and are part of the same stream.

The consequence is a repaint model rather than an append model. The program keeps its own model of what the screen should show and emits the minimum sequences—or a full frame—to make the terminal match. Nothing about the screen is retained by the terminal as a document; the program is responsible for redrawing after a resize, a scroll, or a redraw request.

## How gPTY uses it

The pane does not need a special TUI mode. The same grid wraps `alacritty_terminal`, so alternate-screen switching, cursor addressing, and mode changes are already part of the emulator state. gPTY reads that state in a few places where a full-screen program must be treated differently from a shell.

The grid can report whether the alternate screen is active. That answer keeps the emulator's resize surgery off full-screen apps: when a pane grows and the grid has scrollback, gPTY normally issues a sequence that deletes the rows revealed from history, so a resize does not pull old output into view. For an alternate-screen application that would corrupt the app's own layout, so the check is skipped. The same check gates concept matching: redraw output from a TUI is not a command's output and must not trigger captures.

Mode state also reaches the UI. Mouse reporting is exposed as a bitmask of click, drag, motion, and SGR encoding; when the application has enabled reporting the pane forwards mouse events to it, and when the mask is zero the pane keeps the mouse for selection and scrollback. Bracketed paste is exposed so a paste is wrapped in `ESC[200~`/`ESC[201~` instead of being fed line by line. If the application hides the cursor, the pane paints no cursor at all rather than drawing one at a stale position.

What the user sees is the application filling the pane, with gPTY's own chrome around it: the tile border, the pane title (often set by an OSC title sequence), and the pane's search bar if opened. Resizing the tile sends the application a resize notification; well-behaved TUIs redraw, and the alternate screen returns when they exit.

## Why it is not a separate protocol

There is no "TUI escape sequence". A full-screen program is a program that uses the same vocabulary more aggressively: absolute addressing instead of newlines, erase instead of overwrite-by-printing, mode switches instead of a plain byte stream. This matters when something goes wrong. A TUI that crashes without leaving the alternate screen leaves the terminal in that buffer; a TUI that dies mid-repaint leaves a half-drawn frame. Both are fixed by the sequences the program failed to send, not by a terminal-specific reset.

It also means the terminal cannot tell a "TUI" from a shell by looking at the bytes. gPTY's alternate-screen check is a signal, not a definition: a program may paint the primary screen with the same addressing, and the OMP TUI does exactly that. The terminal's job is to keep the grid honest either way; the program's job is to redraw.

## Limits and edge cases

Because the alternate screen keeps no scrollback, you cannot scroll up inside a full-screen app to see earlier frames—the app's own paging is the only history. Mouse-wheel scrolling in such a pane depends on whether the app asked for mouse reporting: when it did, the wheel is forwarded as events, not used for gPTY's history.

Selection and copy still work on the visible grid, but they read cells as currently drawn. A selection made while an app is repainting captures whatever was on screen at that moment. Resizing a tile is a real event for the application, not a scale operation, so an app that ignores the notification can leave artifacts until it is redrawn or restarted.

# Pseudo-Terminal (PTY)

A pseudo-terminal is a pair of virtual devices that makes an ordinary program believe
it is talking to a real terminal. One end, the *master*, is held by the application that
owns the window; the other end, the *slave*, is handed to the program. Everything gPTY
does with a terminal pane starts here.

## What it is

The pair behaves like a very short cable with a peculiar middle. Write to the master and
the bytes come out of the slave, exactly as if a user had typed them on a keyboard; write
to the slave and the bytes appear on the master, exactly as if the terminal were printing
them. On Linux the master is opened through `/dev/ptmx`, which allocates a new pair and
returns a file descriptor for the master plus a name for the slave (`/dev/pts/N`).

The middle of that cable is the part a pipe does not have: the **line discipline**. It is
a small kernel state machine that implements the behaviors every shell assumes exist:

| Behavior | What it means | Typical bytes |
|---|---|---|
| Echo | Typed characters are echoed back by the kernel, not by the program | everything |
| Canonical mode | Input is delivered line-by-line, and backspace edits before delivery | `Enter`, `Backspace` |
| Signal characters | A keystroke becomes a signal to the foreground process | `Ctrl+C`, `Ctrl+Z`, `Ctrl+\` |
| Terminal size | The pair carries rows and columns | — |
| Job control | One process group is *foreground*; background readers get stopped | `Ctrl+Z` then `fg` |

That last row is why a PTY is not optional. Job control, `Ctrl+C`, prompts, progress
bars and full-screen editors all depend on the program being able to ask the kernel
"am I attached to a terminal?" — the `isatty()` call — and getting a yes.

## A pipe is not a terminal

A pipe also carries bytes in both directions, so it is tempting to think a pipe would do.
It will not, for three concrete reasons that a newcomer can observe:

- `isatty()` returns false, so programs change behavior. `ls` stops coloring, `git` drops
  its pager, Python prints no prompt, and many tools switch to block-buffered output, so
  lines arrive late or in a burst.
- There is no line discipline: no echo, no line editing, no `Ctrl+C` translation, no
  terminal size.
- There is no foreground process group, so job control does not exist at all.

So `ls --color=auto | cat` prints plain names, while the same command in a terminal
prints colors. Nothing is broken — the program correctly noticed it was not talking to a
terminal.

## How gPTY uses it

gPTY does not touch `/dev/ptmx` directly. It uses `portable-pty` 0.9 through
`crates/gpty-core/src/pty.rs`, which asks the platform for a native PTY pair and
presents one cross-platform interface. Each terminal pane owns exactly one PTY.

The lifecycle is short and worth knowing because it explains most of the app's timing:

1. A pane is created and a PTY pair is allocated.
2. A `CommandBuilder` is filled with the pane's program (a shell by default), its
   arguments, its working directory and its environment. `TERM` is set to
   `xterm-256color` so programs emit a modern, predictable dialect of escape sequences.
3. The program is spawned on the **slave** side and immediately believes it is
   interactive.
4. A dedicated OS thread per PTY reads the master and forwards output to the pane's
   terminal task, which folds the bytes into the screen grid.
5. Typing in the pane writes to the master; resizing the tile sends the new rows and
   columns, which the kernel turns into a `SIGWINCH` for the child.

Output backpressure is deliberate. The reader may queue 256 unread chunks — about 1 MiB
per pane — and then it stops reading. When the kernel's buffer fills, the child's write
blocks. That is correct behavior for a terminal: dropping chunks would corrupt the byte
stream, because escape sequences span chunk boundaries and are not self-contained
records.

## Limits and edge cases

- A flooding command (`yes`, `cat /dev/urandom`) does not grow gPTY's memory without
  bound; it slows down instead, because the pane stops draining.
- Closing a pane closes the master and, on Unix, kills the child's whole process group,
  so a `sleep`, a build or a `yes` started from that shell does not linger after the
  pane is gone. A process that escaped the group (by calling `setsid`, say) is beyond
  that reach and can hold the slave open after the pane has closed.
- Resizing is not a redraw request. The child gets `SIGWINCH` and decides what to do; a
  program that ignores it will draw at the old width inside a narrower pane.
- Every pane costs one OS thread for its I/O, independent of how many panes exist.

# Scrollback

Scrollback is the history of lines that have scrolled off the top of a terminal's visible screen. It is what lets you scroll up to read a build log that has already passed, and in gPTY it is also written to disk so the output is still there after a restart.

## What it is

A terminal grid has a fixed number of rows and columns—24×80 by default in gPTY. Output does not make the grid taller. When the cursor is on the bottom row and the program prints a newline, the whole grid shifts up by one row, the top row falls out of the viewport, and a blank row appears at the bottom. That top row is not necessarily lost: the emulator can retain it in a scrollback buffer.

It helps to separate three things:

- The **grid** is the rows × columns of cells that the application is actively drawing into.
- The **viewport** is the window onto the grid that the user currently sees.
- The **scrollback** is the retained history above the viewport.

Scrolling does not move the cursor or change what the application believes is on screen. It only changes which rows the viewport shows. When the view is scrolled back, new output keeps arriving at the bottom of the grid; the user is simply looking elsewhere. Scrolling back to the bottom resumes following live output.

## How gPTY uses it

The in-memory terminal is an `alacritty_terminal` grid configured with a bounded scrollback. gPTY's default is 10,000 retained lines per pane, and the "History lines" control in the Terminal settings tab accepts 100 to 100,000. This number caps how many scrolled-off rows the grid keeps in memory, so it bounds memory use per pane as well as how far back the display can scroll.

Persistence is separate. Each pane can own a SQLite store holding its output lines, with an FTS5 full-text index over them. Lines are queued and committed by a per-pane writer thread rather than inserted on the terminal path, because an insert costs roughly 30 µs and holding the grid lock for that long would stall rendering. The store survives restart: on the next launch, the pane's saved rows are fed back into the grid's scrollback so scrolling up shows the previous session.

Two bounds apply to what a pane retains on disk: a row cap (the same history-lines setting) and a derived byte cap of about 1 KiB per retained row. The byte cap exists because one output line can be up to 16 KiB; without it, 10,000 pathological lines could mean hundreds of megabytes. Consequently the store's size is not derivable from the settings alone, which is why the Terminal tab shows an "On disk:" row that sums the database and its `-wal`/`-shm` siblings.

Navigation is deliberately simple. `PageUp` and `PageDown` scroll the viewport through history; the mouse wheel scrolls three lines per notch by default. `Ctrl+Shift+F` opens the pane's search bar. Its scope toggle switches between the live grid and the persisted history: the live search is a regex over the in-memory scrollback plus screen, while the persisted search is free text against SQLite. Persisted terms are sanitized into quoted, ANDed FTS5 terms, so punctuation such as `main.rs` is searchable instead of being a syntax error, and results come back newest-first with a limit clamped to 1–500 (the pane asks for 100).

## The alternate screen

Full-screen applications such as `vim`, `less`, and `btop` switch to the alternate screen buffer. In gPTY, that buffer keeps no scrollback: the app's constant repainting does not fill the normal history, and switching back restores the primary screen as it was. This is also why the concept engine skips matching while the alternate screen is active—redraw output is not shell output, and capturing it would produce garbage.

The distinction is per buffer, not per program. An application can paint the primary screen without entering the alternate screen; gPTY's grid notes the OMP TUI as an example. Such a program can therefore add lines to history as it repaints.

## Limits and edge cases

Persistence is write-behind, so the most recent output may not yet be searchable if it was printed since the last flush; the pane flushes the queue when it closes. A pane restored under a different identity has no matching store, and history search reports that as "no history stored" rather than an empty result—the pane distinguishes the two.

Scrolling back does not stop output, but new lines can push old ones out of the in-memory buffer while you are reading, and the oldest lines are also the first the row and byte caps delete. The store file is restricted to the owner on Unix, because every line a pane prints—including anything secret that passed through it—is written there.

# Shell

A shell is an ordinary program that reads commands and runs other programs. It is not
part of the terminal, not part of the PTY, and not part of gPTY — it is simply the
program a pane usually starts, and understanding which mode it is in explains most
"why does this behave differently" moments.

## What it is

When a pane starts, PTY slave in hand, it executes one program: by default an
interactive shell such as `bash`, `zsh` or `fish`. On Windows it might be PowerShell or
`cmd`. The shell then does three jobs in a loop: print a prompt, read a line of text,
and act on it — run a program, run a *builtin*, expand a variable, or report an error.

Some commands are builtins rather than executables, and the reason is structural:
`cd` cannot be a separate program, because a child process cannot change its parent's
working directory. The same is true of `export` and `alias`. So the shell grows a small
vocabulary of its own (variables, quoting, pipelines, redirections, exit codes) and
executes everything else as a child process, which inherits the PTY.

## Interactive versus non-interactive

The same binary behaves very differently depending on how it was started, and this is
the single most useful thing to know about shells.

| | Interactive | Non-interactive |
|---|---|---|
| Reads from | The terminal | A script, `-c` string, or stdin |
| Prints a prompt | Yes | No |
| Line editing, history, completion | Yes (usually) | No |
| Job control | Yes | Usually off |
| Startup files | Interactive ones are read | A much smaller set, if any |
| Errors | Reported at the prompt, shell continues | May exit with a status |

Whether a shell considers itself interactive depends on whether its input is a terminal
— which loops straight back to the [[pty|PTY]]. Remove the PTY and `bash` quietly
becomes a script interpreter: no prompt, no `Ctrl+C` handling at the shell level, no
history.

## `-c` and startup files in general terms

Shells accept a command string instead of a session: `sh -c 'make test'` runs `make test`
in a fresh shell, then exits with the command's status code. This is the standard way to
run "one command through a shell" from another program, because it is the only way to get
shell features — pipes, globs, `&&`, variable expansion — without writing a script file.

Startup files are the shell's configuration hooks. In general terms: a *login* shell
reads profile files, an *interactive* shell reads a per-shell rc file (`.bashrc`,
`.zshrc` and so on), and a non-interactive shell may read almost nothing — or, for some
shells, one "environment file" named by an environment variable. That asymmetry is why a
command can work interactively and fail under `-c`: your `PATH` tweak lives in a file
that only interactive shells read.

There is a security-shaped corner here. Because some of those variables name a file the
shell will *execute* at startup, setting them from a saved layout or a profile is
equivalent to injecting code. gPTY drops variables like `BASH_ENV`, `ENV`,
`PROMPT_COMMAND` and `ZDOTDIR` when they come from pane settings, layouts or profiles;
you can still set them yourself inside a shell, where the value comes from you and not
from a file someone sent you.

## How gPTY uses it

A terminal pane's program is configurable, but not from the Pane Settings popup. The
program and its arguments come from the tile that created the pane — a profile, a saved
layout tile, or the creation call (`gpty new-pane -c ...`) — while the working directory
comes from the workspace's default directory. The pane settings popup does own the
environment override. Together those values are what is started on the PTY slave; left
alone, the program is a shell, so the pane looks and feels like a terminal.

Two gPTY features deliberately take different paths, and the difference is worth
memorizing:

- `gpty pane-run --command "cargo test"` opens a **new terminal pane** and runs the
  command **through the configured shell**. Shell syntax works, so pipes and `&&` are
  fine, and the pane keeps the shell's environment and startup files.
- The CLI View pane runs an **argv array directly**: no shell, no PTY, no expansion.
  `cargo test` is a program and an argument, not a line to interpret. That is also why
  it strips workspace credentials from the child's environment — there is no shell in
  between to sanitize anything for it.

A third path exists for the same reason: gPTY's concept captures and control-API
injections send bytes or text to a pane, and those arrive at the shell as input, not as
commands executed by gPTY. The shell decides what they mean.

## Limits and edge cases

- The shell is a child of the GUI process. If it exits, the pane's foreground program is
  gone; the pane reports the exit rather than respawning silently.
- `Ctrl+V` is passed through to the shell as a literal `^V`, which readline uses for
  quoted insert. Paste is `Ctrl+Shift+V`; see [[keyboard-shortcuts|the shortcut list]].
- A program launched from the shell inherits the PTY, so it can take over the whole
  screen; that is normal and is the subject of [[full-screen-tui]].
- Output the shell writes is not privileged in any way. Anything a program prints is
  untrusted text that the [[terminal-emulator]] interprets, which is why concepts may
  capture it but never act on it.

# Terminal Colors

Terminal colors are attributes attached to cells by SGR escape sequences. A program does not send pixels; it names a color—one of sixteen, an index into 256, or an explicit RGB triplet—and the terminal resolves that name to a color when it paints the cell.

## What it is

Three generations of color coexist in the same escape syntax, and every modern terminal understands all three.

**The sixteen ANSI colors.** Eight base colors and eight bright variants, each with a fixed index. SGR 30–37 select the foreground and 40–47 the background; 90–97 and 100–107 select the bright foreground and background. SGR 0 resets everything, 1 turns on bold, and 7 reverses foreground and background.

**256 colors.** `ESC[38;5;n` sets the foreground and `ESC[48;5;n` the background, where `n` runs from 0 to 255. Indices 0–15 are the ANSI colors, 16–231 are a 6×6×6 RGB cube, and 232–255 are a grayscale ramp. This is the palette a `256color` `TERM` describes.

**Truecolor.** `ESC[38;2;r;g;bm` and `ESC[48;2;r;g;bm` carry 8-bit red, green, and blue components directly, so the program picks the exact color rather than an index. This is what modern tools use for syntax highlighting and gradients.

```bash
printf '\033[31mred text\033[0m\n'
printf '\033[38;5;208morange from the 256-color cube\033[0m\n'
printf '\033[38;2;120;180;255mexact blue\033[0m\n'
printf '\033[7minverse video\033[27m back to normal\n'
```

SGR is stateful: a color set now applies to every character printed after it, until another SGR changes it. That is why output is often wrapped in a color/reset pair, and why a program that crashes mid-line can leave the rest of the screen in an unintended attribute.

## How gPTY uses it

The engine stores the sixteen system colors as an array of RGB triplets in `crates/gpty-core/src/color.rs`. That array is the default palette, and it is what the ANSI indices resolve to unless a pane supplies its own.

Resolution happens in one place. `color_to_rgb` maps a named color through the palette, expands indexed colors using the ANSI table for 0–15, the 6×6×6 cube for 16–231, and the grayscale ramp for 232–255, and passes truecolor components through unchanged. The grid asks that function for every cell it exports, so the UI never interprets SGR itself.

Each pane can replace the base sixteen colors with a scheme file. The pane's settings popup has a "Color scheme:" picker; the file is read as text, newlines become separators, spaces are removed, and up to sixteen `#rrggbb` values are applied in order. An empty scheme resets to the built-in palette. This is a palette substitution, not a filter: truecolor output is unaffected, while ANSI colors change everywhere at once.

## Paint-ready cells

A cell carries its resolved foreground and background as RGB, plus attribute flags. SGR 7 (inverse) is stored as its own bit rather than applied at parse time. Before the grid is packed for rendering, the inverse swap is applied once, so the foreground the renderer receives is always the glyph color and the background is always the background. The inverse bit also travels to Godot, but as cell data—not as an instruction to swap again.

That distinction is not academic. A shell's readline wraps the echo of a bracketed paste in `ESC[7m`/`ESC[27m`; a renderer that swapped only the text color and not the background painted the pasted line in its own background color and made it invisible. Resolving both colors before drawing removes the possibility.

Default colors are part of the theme too: cells that never received an SGR use a light gray foreground and a dark gray background, and the Appearance settings tab controls chrome colors such as selection and focus borders separately from the terminal palette.

## Limits and edge cases

Indexed colors 0–15 are only as accurate as the palette in effect; a scheme that omits entries leaves the existing values in place, and a value that is not a valid `#rrggbb` string is ignored rather than guessed. The 6×6×6 cube is a standard approximation, so a 256-color program and a truecolor program asking for the same visual color may end up slightly different.

Bold is an attribute, not a color—gPTY does not automatically brighten bold text—so programs that relied on that old terminal behavior may look flatter. And because color is per cell, changing the scheme affects what is already on screen as well as new output: the palette is the interpretation of the stored indices, not a property of the text.

# Terminal Emulator

A terminal emulator is the program that reads the byte stream a program writes and
maintains the screen you see. The program on the other side never draws anything; it
emits a description of the screen, and the emulator interprets it.

## What it is

In 1978 a terminal was a physical device with a serial cable, and its manual defined a
set of escape sequences: `ESC [ 2 J` cleared the screen, `ESC [ 1 ; 3 1 m` set a color.
Programs were written against that manual. The devices are gone, but the sequences
remain, so a modern emulator is a compatibility interpreter for decades of accumulated
convention — VT100, VT220, xterm and their many extensions.

The important consequence is a separation of responsibilities that newcomers often miss:

| The program | The emulator |
|---|---|
| Writes bytes | Reads bytes |
| Knows a rectangle of rows and columns | Maintains that rectangle |
| Sends "move cursor to row 3, clear to end of line" | Performs the move and clears |
| Sends "set foreground to color 4" | Records the color on subsequent cells |
| Never knows what is actually visible | Owns the visible state |

So `top` does not paint your screen. It emits a sequence of cursor moves and text, and
whatever emulator is listening decides how that looks. This is why the same program looks
different in two terminals, and why a terminal can support features the program has never
heard of — a searchable scrollback, for instance, is invisible to the program.

## The concrete version

Run `printf '\033[2J\033[H\033[1;31mhello\033[0m\n'`. The bytes mean: erase the display,
home the cursor, switch to bold red, print `hello`, reset attributes. Nothing about that
output says "red text in the top-left corner" — it says "apply these operations in
order". A program that prints a progress bar takes this further: it emits carriage
returns and erase-line sequences many times per second, rewriting one line in place.

## How gPTY uses it

gPTY separates the interpretation from the drawing, in two Rust crates with a narrow seam:

- **`vte` 0.15** is the ANSI parser. It is a state machine over bytes, not over screens;
  it recognizes control characters, printable runs and CSI/OSC/DCS sequences and reports
  them as calls.
- **`alacritty_terminal` 0.26** is the terminal state machine. It applies those calls to
  a grid, a cursor, scroll regions and attribute state, and records which cells changed.
- **`TermGrid`** in `crates/gpty-core/src/term.rs` wraps the two and exports the result to
  the UI as plain structs: character, foreground, background, bold, italic, underline.
  The Godot pane draws those cells; it is a renderer, not a terminal.

gPTY reads the same PTY output three ways, which is worth knowing because it explains
features that seem unrelated:

- Through the full emulator, to produce the visible screen and the [[terminal-grid|grid]].
- Through a plain-text line parser that strips escape sequences, to feed concept
  triggers and the plain-text scrollback index. (See [[concepts]] and [[history]].)
- As raw bytes, when a concept capture buffers output to route to another pane.

The emulator also owns the input direction in a limited way: `keymap.rs` converts a
keyboard event into the byte sequence the program expects, and the emulator's mouse
tracking state decides whether the pane sends mouse reports at all or treats a drag as a
text selection. Cursor shape — block, underline or beam — is likewise chosen by the
program's escape sequences, with gPTY's settings providing the default.

## Limits and edge cases

- **Unsupported sequences are ignored, not fatal.** An emulator must never crash on
  arbitrary bytes; the worst case is that a program draws something odd.
- **Attributes are per cell.** A color set mid-line does not retroactively restyle the
  text already printed, so selecting and re-copying text preserves what was on screen at
  the time.
- **The program can change what a keystroke means.** In a full-screen application, arrow
  keys send escape sequences rather than editing a line; in a shell prompt they edit the
  line. That switching is the emulator honoring the application's mode requests.
- **`Ctrl+V` is deliberately passed through** as a literal `^V` rather than being
  captured as paste, because shells and editors use it. Paste is `Ctrl+Shift+V`, and copy
  is `Ctrl+Shift+C`; see [[keyboard-shortcuts]].
- **Not every terminal is equal.** A program probing for capabilities gets gPTY's answer
  via `TERM=xterm-256color`, so features gPTY does not implement are not advertised.
- **Rendering latency is gPTY's own.** Interpretation is fast; the visible step is a
  Godot `_draw()` over the cells flagged as [[terminal-grid|damaged]].

# Terminal Foundations

Every terminal you have ever used is at least two programs wearing one costume: a
program that *produces* text, and a program that *draws* it. This cluster explains the
pieces in between, using gPTY's own implementation as the worked example. Read these
six notes before the project notes and the rest of the wiki will have somewhere to sit.

## Why start here

A newcomer can use gPTY for a week without knowing what a PTY is. Then something
strange happens: a command that works in a normal terminal refuses to print color, a
full-screen program draws garbage, pasting does nothing, resizing a pane leaves stale
text, or a script that works in CI hangs when run by hand. Every one of those is a
consequence of the layers below, not a bug in the app.

The layers are worth separating because each one owns a different question, and each
one fails in its own way:

| Layer | Owns | In gPTY |
|---|---|---|
| PTY | Makes a program believe it talks to a terminal | `portable-pty` 0.9, `crates/gpty-core/src/pty.rs` |
| Emulator | Turns the byte stream into screen state | `vte` 0.15 + `alacritty_terminal` 0.26, `term.rs` |
| Grid | Holds cells, cursor, damage | `TermGrid`, handed to Godot as cell rows |
| Shell | Decides what a typed line means | the program spawned on the PTY's slave side |

The single most useful distinction in this cluster: a **PTY is a kernel interface**,
a **terminal emulator is an interpreter**, a **grid is state**, and a **shell is just a
program**. Four different things that people casually call "the terminal".

## Reading order

1. This hub, for the map.
2. [[pty]] — the kernel object that makes interactive programs work at all.
3. [[terminal-emulator]] — who reads the bytes that come back.
4. [[terminal-grid]] — where the picture actually lives.
5. [[shell]] — the program most panes start, and why `gpty pane-run` behaves the way
   it does.
6. [[conpty]] — the same story on Windows, where the pseudo console is a process, not
   a device.

If you only have five minutes, read [[pty]] and [[terminal-emulator]] and stop.

## The notes

[[pty|Pseudo-Terminal (PTY)]] explains the master/slave pair, why a pipe is not a
terminal (no line discipline, no job control, `isatty` returns false), and why a shell
that sees a pipe stops being interactive. It is the reason a gPTY pane can run `vim`.

[[conpty|ConPTY]] covers Windows, where there is no `/dev/ptmx` and the pseudo console
is a broker process that re-renders output before gPTY sees it. ConPTY is also why
`portable-pty` exists: gPTY asks for one API and the crate picks the platform's
mechanism.

[[shell|Shell]] separates interactive from non-interactive shells, explains `-c`,
prompts, and startup files in general terms, and pins down a distinction that matters
daily: `paneRun` goes through the configured shell, while the CLI View pane runs an
argv array with no shell at all.

[[terminal-emulator|Terminal Emulator]] is the interpreter. The program on the other
side writes bytes — text, plus escape sequences that move the cursor and set colors —
and the emulator turns that stream into a screen. In gPTY that is `vte` feeding
`alacritty_terminal`; the Godot UI is a renderer of the resulting state, not a
terminal itself.

[[terminal-grid|Terminal Grid]] is that state: a rectangle of cells with a character,
a foreground, a background and attribute flags, plus one cursor position. gPTY panes
default to 24 rows by 80 columns, and the UI repaints only cells the emulator marked
as damaged.

# Terminal Grid

The terminal grid is the screen state: a fixed rectangle of character cells plus a
cursor position. Everything a terminal shows lives there, and everything gPTY's UI draws
is read from it.

## What it is

A terminal does not store "a picture". It stores rows and columns of cells, and each cell
holds one character together with how it should look. In gPTY a cell is literally a small
struct: the character, a foreground RGB triple, a background RGB triple, and flags for
bold, italic, underline, inverse and "wide".

That design is old and it is not an accident. Text-based programs are written against a
rectangle: `top` knows it has 24 rows and 80 columns (`24×80` — the shape a terminal
grew up with, inherited from hardware), a text editor knows which line it is on, a
progress bar knows where the current line ends. The rectangle is the contract between the
program and the screen.

Two more pieces complete the state:

- **The cursor.** One cell position, plus a shape (block, underline or beam) and a
  visibility flag. A program moves it; the emulator keeps it.
- **Attributes applied at write time.** When the program writes a character, the current
  color and flags are copied into that cell. Changing the color afterwards does not
  affect cells already written.

## How gPTY uses it

`TermGrid` in `crates/gpty-core/src/term.rs` owns one `alacritty_terminal` terminal and
hands the UI a rectangle of `CellInfo`. The Godot pane's `_draw()` converts those cells
into glyphs and background rectangles; it holds no text of its own.

The interesting part is how it avoids repainting everything, because a terminal redraws
many times per second and the visible change is usually tiny.

1. The [[terminal-emulator|emulator]] records which cells it wrote and which row ranges
   changed. `alacritty_terminal` exposes that as `TermDamage`: either `Full` (everything)
   or `Partial` (a list of row/column bounds).
2. `TermGrid::get_grid_updates(force_full)` converts that into `GridUpdate::Full` — all
   rows — or `GridUpdate::Partial`, a flat list of `CellUpdate { row, col, cell }`.
3. The UI repaints only those cells.

A full update is forced in three situations, and they are worth knowing because they
explain a visible behavior: the first frame after a resize or open, a change to the color
palette (which restyles cells that have not been rewritten), and a change to the
scrollback view offset. Scrolling the view back is not a change to the grid's contents;
it shifts which lines are being displayed, so the whole visible rectangle must be
redrawn.

The grid's dimensions come from the pane's tile. gPTY's default is 24 rows by 80
columns; the same numbers are given to the PTY so the child is told its size, and
resizing the tile updates both together.

## Practical consequences

| Thing you see | What it is |
|---|---|
| Text redrawn in place (`top`, progress bars) | The program moving the cursor and rewriting cells |
| Selection highlighting | Cell ranges in the grid, not text spans |
| A character occupying two columns | A `wide` cell (see [[text-width-and-unicode]]) |
| Scrolling past the top line | [[scrollback]], stored outside the grid |
| A stale fragment after a resize | A program that drew once and ignored the new size |

## Limits and edge cases

- **A cell is not a character position you can reason about casually.** Wide characters
  occupy two columns; that is why [[text-width-and-unicode]] exists as its own note.
- **The grid is not the scrollback.** By default a pane keeps 10,000 lines of history in
  SQLite (clamped between 100 and 100,000), separate from the visible rectangle. Search
  runs over that text, which is plain text extracted from the same byte stream — see
  [[history]].
- **Resizing is not a re-layout of history.** The rectangle changes, the PTY is resized
  and the child receives a signal; programs that redraw will, others will not.
- **"Grid" is an overloaded word in gPTY.** The *terminal* grid is this cell rectangle;
  the *layout* grid is the tiling system measured in 60 abstract units with a minimum
  tile of 6. They are unrelated; see [[layout]].
- **Copy and search read cells, not the original bytes.** What you copy is what is on
  screen, attributes included, not the escape sequences that produced it.
- **Damage is the whole optimization.** If a render is skipped, the next one catches up
  from the same damage list, because the list is cleared only when it is turned into
  updates.

# Text Width and Unicode

A terminal does not lay out text the way a word processor does. It places characters into a fixed grid of cells, and the width of a character in cells—not its length in bytes or codepoints—decides where the next character goes. Getting that width wrong is what makes CJK text, emoji, and accented characters drift out of alignment.

## What it is

There are four different units in play, and confusing them is the root of most terminal text bugs:

| Unit | What it counts | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Byte | UTF-8 encoding units | `é` is 2 bytes; `字` is 3 |
| Codepoint | Unicode scalar values | `é` can be 1 or 2 codepoints |
| Grapheme cluster | What a reader sees as one character | a letter plus a combining accent |
| Display cell | Grid columns the terminal advances | `a` is 1; `字` is 2; a combining accent is 0 |

A cell is the terminal's unit. Most Latin characters occupy one cell. East Asian wide characters—Chinese, Japanese, Korean ideographs and full-width forms—occupy two, because they are drawn at roughly twice the width. Combining marks occupy zero: they attach to the preceding character rather than advancing the cursor. Emoji are the messy case: many are wide, and a family emoji built from several people joined by zero-width joiners is a single grapheme cluster that still occupies two cells.

The important consequence is that a string of N codepoints can occupy more or fewer than N cells, and the terminal has to decide cell by cell. The program and the terminal must agree on the same width table. When they do not, a line that the program counted as 40 columns wide may need 44, and everything after it shifts.

## How gPTY uses it

The grid is rows × columns of cells—24×80 by default—and every cell holds exactly one character plus its attributes. A wide character is stored in two parts: the glyph in its starting cell, and a spacer cell immediately after it. The first cell carries a wide flag; the second exists only to reserve the column.

That flag survives all the way to the renderer. The grid export packs a per-cell `attrs` integer whose bit 16 means "wide character". The Godot pane uses it to draw the glyph once and advance two cell widths, skipping the spacer instead of painting a second character on top. Backgrounds and underlines are painted across both cells, which is why a selected or highlighted wide character forms one continuous block rather than a glyph followed by a gap.

The same cell model governs cursor movement, damage tracking, and text extraction. Damage updates name a row and column and describe changed cells; a wide character changing therefore touches both of its cells. `paneRead` walks the grid column by column and joins one character per cell, trimming trailing spaces, so its lines have the same column structure as the screen.

## Why misalignment is a width bug

If a program believes `字` is one column, it pads a table for one column and the terminal writes two—so the next column of the table appears one cell to the right. If the terminal believes an emoji is one cell but the font draws it two cells wide, the glyph overlaps its neighbor. Neither problem is fixed by changing the font: the layout was computed from the wrong width.

This is why terminal applications use a width function rather than string length. It is also why the width of ambiguous characters—some symbols and emoji that can be narrow or wide depending on context—is a compatibility question. Two programs can both be "correct" Unicode and still disagree about how many columns a character needs.

## Selection, copying, and editing

Selection is a rectangle over cells, not over codepoints. A wide character that straddles a selection edge still occupies two columns, so a selection can cover half of it visually. Copying walks the selected columns and appends the character in each cell; because the spacer after a wide character is a space in the grid, copied text can carry a padding space after each wide glyph. That is a property of copying cells, not of the clipboard.

Editing has the related hazard: when an application erases or overwrites half of a wide character, the other half must go too. A terminal that erases a single cell can leave a stray half-glyph or a spacer with nothing in front of it. gPTY's grid inherits the emulator's handling of wide cells, so erasing and clearing reason about the pair.

## Limits and edge cases

The grid stores one character per cell, not a full grapheme cluster. A base letter and its combining accent are separate codepoints, and a family emoji is a sequence that the terminal places in a cell and its spacer; the grid does not model the sequence as a unit. That is fine for painting and for cursor arithmetic, and it is why the terminal is not a text editor: it never needs to normalize, sort, or reverse a string.

The practical rule for anything reading terminal output is to treat the grid as authoritative. Do not re-measure the text with a different width table, and do not assume a character is one column. Numbers, paths, and ASCII code are safe; anything else should be read cell by cell.

# Getting Started

This is the shortest path from a download to a workspace you understand. It assumes you have used a terminal before, not that you have used gPTY.

If you want the ideas first, read [[gpty]]; if you want to build from source, see [[contributing]].

## Get the app

Release bundles are standalone: they carry the engine and the export, so you do not need Godot installed.

| Platform | Package |
|---|---|
| Linux | `gpty-v<version>-linux-x86_64.tar.gz` — extract; `./gpty-gui.sh` starts the GUI, `./gpty` is the CLI |
| macOS | `gpty-v<version>-macos.zip` — unzip; right-click the `.app` → Open; `gpty` sits beside it |
| Windows | `gpty-v<version>-windows-x86_64.zip` — unzip; `gpty-gui.exe` starts the GUI, `gpty.exe` is the CLI |

Each release publishes `SHA256SUMS`; verify the download before running it. Assets also carry a build-provenance attestation. The binaries are not code-signed, so the checksum and the source are the trust path.

The CLI is the same binary family as the GUI. It talks to a running GUI over a local socket and does not need a toolchain.

## First launch

Start the GUI. On a fresh profile you get **Workspace 1** with one terminal pane, already focused. Type a command; it runs in the shell gPTY started for that pane.

The window has three regions:

- The **sidebar** on the left: window mode, workspaces, profiles, and pane rows. `Ctrl+Shift+B` hides it.
- The **grid** in the middle: every pane is a tile here. Drag a divider to resize.
- The **titlebar** above each pane: the pane name, and its minimize, position, type, settings, and close controls.

The **command palette** (`Ctrl+Shift+P`) is the fastest way to create a pane: type `new` and pick a type. The sidebar's `+` button and the per-type shortcuts do the same thing.

## Learn five shortcuts

| Keys | What it does |
|---|---|
| `Ctrl+Shift+N` | New terminal pane |
| `Ctrl+Shift+P` | Command palette |
| `Ctrl+Shift+W` | Close the focused pane |
| `Ctrl+Shift+B` | Toggle the sidebar |
| `Ctrl+Shift+C` / `Ctrl+Shift+V` | Copy the selection / paste |

`Ctrl+V` on its own is deliberately sent to the shell as `^V`; readline and vim use it. Paste is always `Ctrl+Shift+V`. The full list is in [[keyboard-shortcuts]].

## Make the grid yours

New panes join the tiling grid; there is no separate "split right" mode to learn first. Drag the dividers to trade space. The sidebar's pane rows can minimize a pane, move it, change its type, open its settings, or close it.

Two ideas are worth separating now, because the rest of the app depends on them:

- A **layout** is the arrangement of panes in one workspace. The palette's `save` writes the whole workspace set to disk, and `load` reloads it; the workspace you close is auto-saved too.
- A **profile** is a reusable named set of tiles. Save one from the sidebar's Profiles `+` button, or with `gpty layout save <name>` (the CLI keeps the older "layout" verb; the record is a profile).
- A **workspace** is a tab containing its own layout and its own default directory. Create one from the sidebar; switch with `Ctrl+PageUp` / `Ctrl+PageDown`.

The workspace you close is auto-saved and restored on the next launch. [[layout]], [[workspace]], and [[profile]] explain the differences; [[profile|Profiles]] also lists the shipped **Agent Workspace**.

## Try the non-terminal panes

| Pane | Open it | Try |
|---|---|---|
| [[code-viewer]] | `Ctrl+Shift+D`, then pick a file | Read a source file without leaving the app |
| [[file-tree]] | `Ctrl+Shift+T` | Browse a directory; supported files open in a viewer or media pane |
| [[wiki-pane]] | Palette → `new wiki`, or the sidebar's **Knowledge Base** profile | Read the bundled wiki, or point a pane at any Markdown vault |
| [[media-pane]] | Palette → `new media`, or a media file from the file tree | Play a local audio or video file |
| [[cli-view]] | Palette → `new cli view` | Stream a command's stdout without a PTY |
| [[inspector]] | `Ctrl+Shift+O` | Ask a private, read-only question about what is on screen |
| [[reasoning]] | Palette → `new reasoning` | Watch an agent's lifecycle events (needs the OMP extension) |

The Inspector is a private Q&A session, not a chat with the terminal's agent. Reasoning is passive; it shows events a cooperating agent emits and never drives it.

## Automate something small

The GUI owns the workspace; the CLI is a stateless client. With the GUI running:

```bash
gpty list-panes
gpty new-pane --pane-type terminal --command "cargo test" --title tests
gpty pane-wait T2 --pattern "tests passed" --timeout-ms 30000
gpty pane-read T2 --lines 40
gpty pane-status T2
```

`pane-run` opens a new terminal pane and runs a command through your configured shell. `pane-wait` matches a Rust regex against recent output. `pane-read` is a snapshot of screen plus scrollback, not a stream. [[control-api]] has the whole surface; [[agent-workflow]] has the recipes an agent should follow.

One place for the words this wiki uses without re-defining them. Each entry links to the note that explains it properly; where no note exists, the definition is the whole story.

| Term | What it means here |

| Agent state | A display-only badge (idle, working, needs attention, completed, failed) describing what an agent in a terminal is doing. See [[agent-state]]. |
| ANSI escape sequence | Bytes beginning with ESC that move the cursor, change colors, or switch screens instead of printing. See [[ansi-escape-sequences]]. |
| Attachment ID | The stable per-pane identifier (`T1`, `pane-8f3a1c2d`, or a name you set) that the control API and per-pane environment use. See [[pane]]. |

# gPTY

gPTY is a desktop workspace built on Rust and Godot: a tiling grid of terminal panes and specialty panes, driven by a public control API, with a small engine that routes output between panes. The name is Godot + PTY; the capitals are for reading, the binary is `gpty`.

It is a terminal emulator, but the point is the workspace around it. A terminal is one pane among several, and every pane is addressable from a shell, a script, or an agent over the same API. The grid, the visual panes, and the control surface are the product; the shell inside a terminal is still just a shell.

## Why this exists

Most terminals are a window around one PTY. Multiplexers add sessions and panes inside a character grid. gPTY starts from a different question: what if the panes were real GUI surfaces, and what if the workspace itself were an API?

That choice buys things a terminal multiplexer cannot easily do: a media pane that decodes video, a wiki pane that draws its own link graph, a code viewer, a file tree, a Markdown preview. It also keeps the terminal honest — the grid, scrollback, colors, selection, and full-screen programs behave like a terminal, because the engine is built on `alacritty_terminal` and `portable-pty` rather than a new emulator.

It does not try to be an IDE, a browser, or an agent runtime. The design goal is to be a good host: panes for programs, a public API for orchestrators, and a display layer that never pretends to be in charge of them.

## The layers

gPTY is explicit about where its responsibility ends. The model is a stack from the operating system up to the ecosystem:

| Layer | Owner | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| L4 | Ecosystem | Agent CLIs and apps: Claude Code, codex, opencode, OMP, vim, btop |
| L3 | Ecosystem, open market | Orchestration: agent waits, pane states, plugin workflows |
| L2 | gPTY | Control surface: JSON-RPC socket, CLI, MCP, event socket |
| L1 | gPTY | PTY foundation: lifecycle, grid, capture, history, security |
| L0 | Operating system | `/dev/ptmx`, ConPTY, sockets |

gPTY owns L0–L2 and ships a thin built-in L3 — concept routing, Inspector sessions, profile restore. It does not absorb an orchestrator's state machine into core. A tool like herdr can run inside a pane today and drive the public API as a guest; cloning its session manager is not the plan.

The same boundary shows up in the agent features: gPTY **observes and displays** agent state, it never manages it. There is no agent runtime, no wait/block state machine, and no action taken on your behalf because an agent looked busy. Panes expose primitives (`paneStatus`, `paneWait`, events); an orchestrator builds the policy.

## The feature map

| Area | What you get | Start at |

| Layout | 60-unit tiling grid, splits, drag, named layouts | [[layout]] |
| Workspaces | Tabs of independent pane sets, each with a default directory | [[workspace]] |
| Profiles | Named tile sets, including the shipped Agent Workspace | [[profile]] |
| Other panes | Code viewer, file tree, wiki, media, CLI view, Inspector, Reasoning | [[pane]] |
| Automation | JSON-RPC, CLI, MCP, pane states, tags, broadcast | [[control-api]] |

| Plugins | Manifest-based add-ons, reviewed before install, run as you | [[plugins]] |
| Trust | Consent gates for restored programs and plugin installs | [[workspace-trust]] |

## What it deliberately is not

- **Not an orchestrator.** Concept routing and agent-state badges are display paths. gPTY does not decide when an agent is done or start the next task.
- **Not an IDE.** The code viewer reads; it does not edit. A full editor is a different product.
- **Not a browser host.** There is no webview pane and no general plugin UI runtime; `cli_view` streams a command's stdout and is the v1 plugin surface. Native third-party GDScript/Rust panes are outside the v1 trust model.
- **Not a clone of a terminal multiplexer.** It can run tmux, Zellij, or herdr inside a pane. It is not trying to replace their session model.
- **Not a zero-config promise.** Layouts, profiles, and plugins are files, and files are untrusted; the app asks before it runs something they name.

## Status and licensing

gPTY is a side project in active development; the current release line is 0.7. The core is GPL-3.0-or-later, with a section 7 permission that keeps plugins, extensions, adapters, and data files free of copyleft. Plugins can be MIT or Apache-2.0 and ship alongside the app.

The codebase was built with heavy LLM assistance under human review. That is worth knowing when you read it: the architecture is deliberate, but some corners are less polished than a mature emulator's.

# Agent State

Agent state is a pane-level display of what a terminal-hosted agent appears to be doing: idle, working, waiting for you, finished, or failed. It is a badge and a status field, and it never makes anything happen.

## The five states

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `idle` | No agent activity known |
| `working` | A turn is in flight |
| `needs-attention` | The agent finished and wants the user |
| `completed` | The agent finished successfully |
| `failed` | The agent finished with a failure |

## Three tiers, strongest first

A terminal does not have one source of truth about an agent. It may have an extension reporting through a capability, a program declaring its own state, or nothing but text on screen. gPTY merges these with a strict precedence:

| Tier | Source | Strength | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Capability-authenticated `ompEvent` submissions | Authoritative | Requires the per-PTY event capability injected at spawn; only the pane's own program has it |
| 2 | OSC `gpty_state=<value>` declarations | Declared, spoofable | Whitelisted values, single-shot, at most once per 500 ms per terminal |
| 3 | Conservative failure regexes and decay | Heuristic | Display only; a "failed" observation decays to idle after 60 s |

The merge rule is simple: a stronger tier always wins, a weaker tier is ignored, and within the same tier the newest observation wins. Only Tier 3 decays — a state from an authoritative source persists until that source declares a change, so a completed agent does not quietly turn idle because the screen was quiet.

Tier 2 is deliberately spoofable. Anything that can print can emit an escape sequence, including pasted text and a `cat`-ed log file. That is acceptable because the value only paints a badge: it is whitelisted, rate-limited, ignored while capturing or on the alternate screen, and suppressed for the post-resize window when a TUI repaints. It is never an input to a decision.

Tier 3 exists to catch the obvious signals a terminal can see — `test result: FAILED`, `could not compile`, `assertion failed` — and to get out of the way. A false positive costs a badge flash; a false negative costs nothing, because the real signal is supposed to come from Tier 1.

## Where it shows up

The terminal pane renders a badge from its state, and panes that observe the same terminal receive the same deliveries through a body hook. Programmatically, `paneStatus` reports `agent_state` and `agent_state_tier` alongside liveness and `idle_ms`, which is enough to build a dashboard or an alert without scraping the screen.

Nothing else consumes it. Agent state does not trigger actions, start captures, enable or disable concepts, change layouts, or send IPC. That is a guarantee, not an implementation detail: the tiers exist to answer "what does this look like", and the untrusted tier cannot reach any code path that acts.

## Declaring state from inside a pane

A program can tell the terminal what it is doing:

```bash
gpty state working
gpty state needs-attention
gpty state completed
```

The command declares the state of the pane it runs in, over the event socket, using the credentials the pane injected into its environment. It accepts exactly the five state names. This is not an MCP tool and it does not go through the control socket.

This path matters most on Windows: ConPTY re-renders the terminal, consuming the `gpty_state` OSC before gPTY's parser can see it, so an explicit declaration is the only way a program can set the badge there.

`gpty state` is a declaration with the pane's capability, not a truth claim the app can audit. The capability proves the caller is the program in that pane; it does not prove the claim is honest, and the state still only paints a badge.

## Why exit codes are not used

A pane's exit code describes the process gPTY spawned — usually a shell — not the agent or the command inside it. A foreground command's exit is not reliably attributable in a PTY: the shell keeps running, a wrapper may swallow the status, and a command may finish while a child is still printing. Encoding "the tool finished" from an exit status would produce a state that is confidently wrong, so the model does not try.

# Architecture

gPTY is two runtimes in one process: a Rust engine that owns terminal and workspace state, and a Godot scene tree that draws it. A thin GDExtension layer is the only bridge between them. Understanding that split explains most of the app's behavior — including why the UI polls, why every API call is asynchronous under the hood, and why untrusted input is validated on both sides.

## The pieces

| Piece | Language | Owns |
|---|---|---|
| `gpty-core` | Rust | PTY lifecycle, ANSI parsing, the terminal grid, concepts and capture, scrollback history, the vault index, wikilinks |
| `gpty-ipc` | Rust | JSON-RPC 2.0 types, transport, server, client |
| `gpty-gdext` | Rust | The GDExtension classes (`GptyTerminal`, `GptyAi`, `GptyCliView`, `GptyMedia`, `GptyMarkdown`) and the control/event listeners |
| `gpty-cli` | Rust | The stateless `gpty` client and the MCP server |
| `gpty-ai` | Rust | Inspector backends: a mock and a private OMP RPC process |
| `gpty-media` | Rust | A pinned FFmpeg build, one decode session per file |
| `godot/` | GDScript | The scene tree, tiling grid, pane bodies, settings, dialogs, and all drawing |

The dependency arrows point one way: the engine does not know about Godot. The GDExtension knows both. The UI knows only the GDExtension API.

## Terminal data flow

```text
shell / TUI
   │ bytes
   ▼
PTY master ── dedicated OS thread ──► vte parser ──► alacritty_terminal grid
                                                       │ Arc<Mutex<TermGrid>>
                                                       ▼
                                        GptyTerminal (gdext)
                                                       │ packed updates
                                                       ▼
                                   terminal_pane.gd _draw()
```

Each PTY has its own blocking I/O thread. Output is parsed into the grid under a lock; the UI asks for the cells that changed since the last frame and paints them. A generation counter lets an idle UI skip the poll entirely. The full update shape and the packed arrays are documented in the GDExtension README; the important part is that the UI never owns the terminal state.

## Control data flow

```text
gpty CLI / MCP client
   │ JSON-RPC over a Unix socket or named pipe
   ▼
IpcServer (tokio task, gdext)
   │ queue
   ▼
GDScript drains once per frame ──► workspace / IPC handlers
   │                                      │
   └──────────── oneshot ◄────────────────┘
```

The Godot scene tree is single-threaded, so the socket thread never touches it. Requests are queued, GDScript drains them each frame, and the answer completes a oneshot the socket thread is waiting on. `version` and `shutdown` are answered in Rust; `vaultSearch` and `vaultRead` run natively off the GUI thread because a vault is a directory, not workspace state. Everything else round-trips through the UI.

This is also why the CLI is stateless: one invocation, one connection, one request, one response, exit. There is no persistent client session to lose.

## The other pipelines

```text
OMP extension ──► gpty-events.sock ──► omp_events.rs ──► drain_agent_events()
                                                            │
                                                            ▼
                                                   Reasoning pane + badges
```

```text
Inspector prompt ──► GptyAi ──► private omp --mode rpc --no-tools --no-session
                                      │
                                      ▼
                              session_poll envelopes
```

```text
cli_view config ──► CliProcess (argv child, merged stdout/stderr)
                        │ bounded line queue
                        ▼
                 cli_view_pane.poll_lines()
```

```text
media pane ──► GptyMedia ──► gpty-media worker thread (FFmpeg)
                                  │ bounded RGBA/PCM queues
                                  ▼
                         poll_video / poll_audio
```

These four are deliberately separate from the terminal path. An agent event cannot mutate a grid; a media decoder cannot block the GUI; an Inspector answer cannot reach a shell.

## The FFI contract

Everything crossing from Rust to GDScript is either a string or a packed array:

- Structured answers are JSON strings. The UI parses them and checks the shape before use.
- Grid and media frames are packed arrays with explicit dimensions.
- No Godot object is shared into the engine, and no engine lock is held across a UI call.

Every edge re-validates. A path from a layout, a profile, a vault, or a media file is checked at use, not only at load; an IPC request has a size cap and a handler budget; a captured terminal line is untrusted text. This is not redundancy for its own sake — a file is attacker-controlled input, and the UI and the engine are separate trust surfaces.

## Why Godot

Godot gives the project a real renderer and a scene tree without building either from scratch: custom `_draw()` for the grid, containers for the tiling layout, `RichTextLabel` for Markdown, custom canvases for the link graph and the concept editor, and an export path for three platforms. The cost is a second runtime and an FFI seam; the benefit is that a media pane, a graph canvas, and a settings dialog are ordinary UI work rather than terminal escape sequences.

The engine choice is deliberately boring: `portable-pty` for the PTY, `vte` for parsing, `alacritty_terminal` for grid semantics. The project is not trying to re-derive DEC STD 070; it is trying to build the workspace around a solid one.

# Capture

Capture is the state machine that runs between a concept's trigger and the pane that receives the output. It answers one question at a time: which bytes belong to the terminal grid, and which belong to the block being handed to another pane.

## Starting a capture

A concept triggers on a line. That line has already been consumed by the emulator, so it reaches the grid normally — you still see the command you typed. From the next chunk of output onward the terminal enters capture mode and stops feeding bytes to the grid.

That is why the terminal appears to freeze on the trigger line for the duration of a capture: the output is being held, not lost. A capture is not a filter that copies output; it withholds it.

## Why raw bytes

The buffer holds the raw byte stream, not plain-text lines. Two consumers need different things from it:

- The receiver pane gets plain-text lines, parsed from the buffered bytes with ANSI escape sequences stripped, because it is a viewer for the content.
- The terminal gets the original bytes back if there is no receiver. Replaying text would lose colours, cursor movement, and the exact layout of a diff or a table.

Keeping the bytes is what makes the fallback safe: a capture that cannot be routed can be replayed into the grid exactly as it would have arrived, as if the concept had never fired.

## Stopping

A capture ends at the first of these:

| Stop | Detail |
|---|---|
| Timeout | The concept's `stop_timeout_ms` elapses (300 ms for `cat`, 500 ms for `git diff`, 2,000 ms for `cargo check`) |
| User input | Typing stops the capture when the concept has `stop_on_input`; resizes and internal capture commands never stop it |
| Byte cap | 4 MiB of buffered output |
| Pane teardown | Closing the source pane finalizes what is in flight |

The timeout is the concept's own window and it starts when the trigger matches, which is why a rule for a long build carries a longer value than a rule for `cat`. The byte cap bounds memory when a concept matches a flood.

When a capture finalizes it is assigned an id, its plain-text lines are extracted, and the event is queued for the GUI. Queues hold at most 64 captures and drop the oldest: a stalled GUI must not grow without bound.

## Routing

The GUI drains each pane's capture queue every frame and offers the event to the panes in its workspace. The first pane whose type matches the action's target — and that accepts routed content — receives it.

The Inspector is a receiver only when its `accept_concept_captures` option is on. That pane sends what it is given to its own model backend, so captured terminal output leaving the pane is a deliberate choice the user makes.

Two outcomes follow:

| Outcome | What happens |
|---|---|
| Routed | The sender acknowledges the capture. The buffered bytes are discarded, except the tail after the last newline: the shell prompt was never emitted as a line, so it is replayed after a newline to put it back on the grid. |
| No receiver | The sender flushes the capture. Every raw byte is replayed into the grid and the parsed lines are stored to scrollback and history, exactly as if no concept had matched. A toast names the target pane type that was missing. |

A capture still in flight when its pane is torn down is finalized into a workspace-level orphan queue. Routing from there works the same way, with one difference: the source grid is gone, so a miss can only be reported, not replayed.

## Notify-only captures

`single_line` is not a capture in the buffering sense. The matching line is turned into a notice — concept name, source pane — and nothing else. No output is held, no pane is offered content, and the terminal never freezes. Notices are bounded at 64 per pane, oldest dropped, and forwarded to the event socket so a subscriber learns the trigger fired without receiving any of the text.

## Edge cases worth knowing

Concepts are not matched against alternate-screen output at all. While a capture is active, bytes printed in the 750 ms after a resize are dropped rather than buffered: they are the child repainting a screen the grid never received, and buffering them would put a duplicate prompt into the routed block. Lines longer than 16 KiB are never matched, though the grid and history still receive them. No second capture starts while one is active, so a command whose output happens to match another trigger does not nest.
