# CLI

`gpty` is the command-line client for a running gPTY workspace: one subcommand per action, one connection per invocation, no session to maintain. It is one of the three doors onto the [[control-api|Control API]] — the other two being the raw [[ipc|JSON-RPC socket]] and the [[mcp|MCP server]].

## What the CLI is for

The CLI is what a shell script, a Makefile, a coding agent inside a pane, or a human in a terminal uses to touch the workspace. It turns flags into a single JSON-RPC request, prints the result, and exits. That design keeps it composable: you can put it in a pipeline, call it from any language, and rely on the exit code.

Two behaviors follow from "no session":

| Behavior | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Stateless | Each invocation connects, sends one request, reads one response, exits |
| Client-side validation | Pane types and argument shapes are rejected before any round-trip, with "did you mean?" suggestions |

The second point matters for automation: a typo in a pane type fails immediately with a useful message instead of a socket timeout or a remote error.

## Subcommands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `new-pane` | Open a pane. `-t/--pane-type` (terminal, code_viewer, file_tree, inspector, reasoning, cli_view, wiki, media), `-c/--command`, `--arg` (repeatable, `cli_view` argv), `-s/--split`, `-f/--focus`, `--tags` |
| `list-panes` | Every pane with id, label, type, and grid position |
| `kill-pane` | Close a pane by id, or `"active"` for the focused one |
| `focus-pane` | Focus a pane by id |
| `inject` | Send text to a terminal pane by id |
| `pane-read` | Screen plus scrollback text (`--lines` 1–2000) |
| `pane-status` | Status of one pane, or of every pane when no id is given |
| `pane-run` | Run a command in a new terminal pane (`--command`) |
| `pane-wait` | Wait for output matching a regex (`--pattern`, `--timeout-ms` 100–60000) |
| `state` | Declare the current pane's agent state (`idle`, `working`, `needs-attention`, `completed`, `failed`) |
| `broadcast` | Inject text into every pane carrying one of `--tags` |
| `vault` | `search <vault> <pattern>` (`--limit` 1–500), `read <vault> <path>`, `weight <vault> <src> <target> --weight N` / `--clear` |
| `concept` | `list`, `toggle <name>` |
| `schema` | Print JSON Schema for all commands; `--format mcp` for the MCP tool manifest |
| `mcp` | Run as an MCP server over stdio |
| `daemon` | `start`, `stop`, `status` |
| `layout` | `save <name>`, `load <name>`, `list` |
| `plugin` | `install <owner>/<repo>[@ref]`, `list`, `enable`/`disable <id>`, `uninstall <id>`, `logs <id>`, `run <id> <action>`, `validate <path>` |
| `version` | Version information |

`observer` is a deprecated alias for `inspector`: `new-pane` translates it and prints a warning; manifests refuse it outright. `pane-run` deliberately does not reuse `inject`: it spawns a fresh terminal pane, which is what you want when the command should have its own scrollback and exit status rather than typing into someone else's shell.

`vault weight` is the one `vault` verb that writes anything, and the only thing it writes is gPTY's own declared-weight store (`user://link_weights.json`) — never a note, never the index. It also needs a running GUI, because that store belongs to the workspace. `search` and `read` do not need one.

## Global flags

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--skill` | Print the bundled agent skill (the instructions shipped for agents inside a pane) and exit |
| `--json` | Machine-readable output; failures keep exit code 1 and print the JSON-RPC error envelope |
| `--socket <path>` | Override the IPC socket path |
| `--timeout <ms>` | Connection timeout in milliseconds (default 5000) |
| `--no-daemon` | Never auto-spawn the GUI, even for the two commands that otherwise would |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | Verbose output on stderr |

`--json` is the switch to reach for in automation. Without it, results are printed for a human; with it, every command answers with the JSON document the socket returned. A failure is still exit code 1, and the envelope's `error.data.code` is the stable discriminator — `not_found`, `bad_path`, `outside_vault` and friends — so a script can branch on the failure kind instead of parsing a message.

## Examples

Open a pane and give it work:

```bash
gpty new-pane --pane-type terminal --command "cargo test" --focus
```

Run a command in a fresh pane, then check on it:

```bash
gpty pane-run --command "cargo test"
gpty pane-status
```

Wait for a pattern, then read the result — the two calls compose into "run, wait, capture":

```bash
gpty pane-wait T1 --pattern "tests passed" --timeout-ms 30000
gpty pane-read T1 --lines 200
```

Search a vault and read a hit:

```bash
gpty vault search ~/notes "ownership" --limit 20
gpty vault read ~/notes notes/idea.md
```

Tell the workspace what the pane you are running in is doing:

```bash
gpty state working
```

`state` is different from everything else in the table. It takes no target: it reads the credentials gPTY injected into the current pane (`GPTY_TERMINAL_SESSION_ID`, `GPTY_EVENT_CAPABILITY`, `GPTY_EVENT_SOCKET`, `GPTY_EVENT_PROTOCOL=1`), submits over the event socket, and is display only. It never triggers concepts, actions, or layout changes, and it is not an MCP tool because an MCP client is not inside a pane.

## Statelessness and auto-spawn

The rule is narrow on purpose: the CLI starts the GUI only for `new-pane` and `layout load`. Both are requests whose entire meaning is "make a workspace appear" — refusing them because nothing is open would be pedantic. A query (`list-panes`, `pane-read`, `version`, `vault search`) never opens a window: a monitor that polls every second should not be able to litter the desktop with GUIs.

`--no-daemon` disables even the two, so a CI job or a script that must not touch the user's session can guarantee it. With `--no-daemon` and no running GUI, the command fails rather than silently starting a second workspace.

When the CLI does spawn a GUI, it does so as a separate OS process — the CLI binary never links Godot. It finds the GUI through the `GPTY_GUI` environment variable (validated before use) or beside its own executable (`gpty-gui`, `gpty-editor`), then polls the socket until it answers.

## Schema and skill output

# Concepts

A concept is a saved rule that watches what a terminal prints and, when a pattern appears, hands the output that follows to another pane. It is configuration, not code: a concept captures and routes display content, and does nothing else.

## The mental model

Every concept has three parts:

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| Trigger | A regular expression tested against each visible line of terminal output |
| Conditions | Extra regular expressions that must all match the same line; they can only narrow a match |
| Action | The pane type that should receive the captured output |

The classic example is `cat`. Type `cat README.md` in a shell pane, and the `cat_command` concept matches the command line. The output that follows is buffered, and when the capture's stop condition fires the block is routed to the first code viewer pane — which is usually easier to read, scroll, and copy from than the terminal.

A concept can carry several actions, but only the first destination's target is used when matching: a concept routes to one pane kind.

## The two capture modes

`capture_mode` decides what happens after the trigger matches.

| Mode | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `until_stop` | Buffers the output that follows the trigger and routes the block to a receiver pane. This is the default, and what a missing or unknown mode means. |
| `single_line` | Notify-only. The match is published as an event; nothing is captured, routed, or shown. The output stays in the terminal. |

`single_line` exists for orchestrators that want to know a pattern appeared without stealing the output from the person reading it. Notify-only concepts never see the matched line's text leave the terminal — the published event carries the concept name and source pane, not the content.

`until_stop` needs stop conditions: a timeout in milliseconds (the shipped rules use 300 ms for `cat`, 2,000 ms for `cargo check`) and, optionally, "stop when the user types". How the buffering actually works is the subject of [[capture|Capture]].

## Why a concept cannot execute anything

The trigger runs against terminal output, which is untrusted: any program you run can print text that looks like a command. A concept that could act would therefore be an execution primitive driven by whatever a program happened to print — and it would fire in whichever pane matched, including a root shell or an SSH session. A downloaded `concepts.json` would be arbitrary command execution with an attacker-chosen trigger.

So the feature was reduced to data. An action names a pane type and nothing else. Parsers ignore a legacy `cmd` key rather than rejecting the file, which keeps old definitions loadable without keeping the capability.

## Matching and caps

Each line is first checked against one combined regex set built from every enabled trigger. A line that matches nothing — the common case — stops there and never enters the per-concept loop. When the gate hits, concepts are tried in order, and a capturing concept outranks a notify-only one if both match: otherwise a broad notify-only rule listed first would silently consume every line.

Constraints, enforced when definitions are parsed:

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Concepts | 128 |
| Trigger length | 1,024 bytes |
| Conditions | 8 per concept |
| Actions | 32 per concept |
| Stop timeout | 1–600,000 ms |
| Line length for matching | 16 KiB |

Matching is skipped for alternate-screen output (a full-screen TUI repainting itself is presentation, not shell output) and for 750 ms after a resize, when the child redraws the screen.

## The shipped set

Four concepts ship, merged with the user's file and any installed plugin's concepts:

| Name | Trigger | Enabled | Receives |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cat_command` | `cat <file>` at a prompt | yes | code viewer |
| `git_diff` | `git diff` | no | code viewer |
| `git_log` | `git log` | no | inspector |
| `cargo_check` | `cargo check`, `cargo test`, `cargo build` | no | inspector |

The last two target the Inspector, which is opt-in for captures (`accept_concept_captures`) because captured output would otherwise leave the terminal and be sent to the Inspector's backend. With the opt-in off, those rules have no receiver.

## Where definitions live

Your definitions are `user://concepts.json`. The shipped defaults are read from the app bundle and merged beneath your file; installed plugins contribute concepts between the shipped set and yours. Only enabled concepts are pushed into the engine, and disabling everything pushes an empty set — the engine really stops matching, rather than continuing with the previous list.

## Authoring

Settings has a **Concepts** tab. It shows each concept as a row with an enable toggle, the name and trigger, and buttons to edit or delete it; **Add Concept** opens the same form. The form covers the trigger, target, mode, stop timeout, stop-on-input, and conditions; its timeout field offers 50–5,000 ms, while a hand-edited definition may carry up to 600,000 ms.

**Open Visual Editor** is the primary authoring surface: rules are built as a node graph of trigger → conditions → action. The graph's own block in `concepts.json` holds canvas positions, unfinished drafts, and the order rules are tried in. It never holds content, so the `concepts` array stays the single source of truth, and a hand-edited graph cannot invent a trigger or an action. Plugin-shipped rules appear in the list with their plugin and revision as provenance.

The same control surface exists over the API:

```bash
gpty concept list
gpty concept toggle cat_command
```

`toggle` flips a concept's enabled flag by name. Both are queries against a running GUI; the CLI does not auto-spawn one for them.

# Contributing

gPTY is a Rust engine behind a Godot frontend. Contributing means cloning the repo, building the GDExtension, running the same checks CI runs, and landing a change through a hook-enforced commit format. This note is the short path; the authoritative rules live in `AGENTS.md` and `docs/content/docs/agents/`.

## Repository layout

The split follows the process boundary: everything that touches a PTY, a grid, or a parser is Rust; everything that draws is GDScript.

| Path | What lives there |
|---|---|
| `crates/gpty-core` | PTY spawn, ANSI/vte parsing, terminal grid, concepts, history, vault index |
| `crates/gpty-ipc` | JSON-RPC protocol, socket transport, client, server |
| `crates/gpty-gdext` | The Godot extension: FFI surface, IPC bridge, event socket, vault API |
| `crates/gpty-cli` | The `gpty` binary: workspace control, MCP server, plugin tooling |
| `crates/gpty-ai` | Inspector backends (no tools) |
| `crates/gpty-media` | Pinned FFmpeg media backend |
| `godot/` | Scenes, GDScript, the tiling workspace (`workspace.gd`), pane bodies |
| `extensions/` | First-party agent extensions (the OMP events forwarder) |
| `docs/content/docs/` | Agent guides, release notes, roadmap pages |
| `docs/content/wiki/` | This wiki vault |
| `scripts/` | Build, CI, hook, and media-dependency scripts |

The entry point is `godot/scenes/main.tscn` → `workspace.gd`, a root `Control` node. Rust code never touches a node; GDScript never touches a PTY directly. [[architecture|Architecture]] explains the seam.

## Build and run

Prerequisites are Rust 1.85 or newer (edition 2024) and Godot 4.7 with GDExtension support.

```bash
./scripts/media-deps                 # builds the pinned FFmpeg, once per checkout
source dist/ffmpeg/<platform>-<arch>/env.sh

cargo build -p gpty-gdext
cd godot && godot -e                 # open the editor
```

After a rebuild, restart the editor so it remaps the extension library. To launch the app directly:

```bash
godot --path godot
godot --path godot --headless
```

A one-shot standalone build is the script's job — it detects the host, builds release, stages the binary, exports into `dist/`, and bundles the media runtime:

```bash
./scripts/build
```

That requires export templates matching the editor version exactly; a 4.7.2 editor needs 4.7.2 templates, and a symlinked older directory silently exports with the wrong engine.

For day-to-day control of a running GUI, build the CLI and use it — it is the fastest way to see whether a bridge change works:

```bash
cargo run --bin gpty -- version
cargo run --bin gpty -- new-pane --pane-type terminal
cargo run --bin gpty -- list-panes
```

If a `cargo install`ed `gpty` shadows the checkout, reinstall it after a version bump; a stale binary fails opaquely in clap before any IPC.

## Tests and gates

One script is the contract:

```bash
./scripts/ci-check          # fmt, workflow lint, clippy, Rust tests, GUT, audit
./scripts/ci-check --fast   # fmt, workflow lint, clippy only
```

Narrower loops while iterating:

```bash
cargo test --workspace
cargo test -p gpty-core
cargo check
./scripts/gut-check                 # GDScript tests; fails if the run aborted
./scripts/lint-workflows            # workflow YAML + permissions block
(cd extensions/gpty-omp-events && node --test)
```

Two details worth knowing. GUT exits 0 even when a run aborts, which is why `scripts/gut-check` exists and why it is the command to trust. And `godot --headless --path godot --import` must run once before the first headless test, or the project has no imported resources and every scene load fails.

Tests are written `Given / When / Then` with expected output stated. Behaviour changes come with a test that would fail without them; a fix that only moves a symptom is not done.

## Hooks

Install the repository's git hooks once per clone:

```bash
./scripts/install-hooks
```

| Hook | Runs |
|---|---|
| `pre-commit` | Formatting, workflow lint, clippy |
| `commit-msg` | Conventional Commits check |
| `pre-push` | The full CI suite |

The hooks are symlinks into `githooks/`, so they update with the repo. Running `./scripts/ci-check` by hand before committing is equivalent and faster to iterate on.

## Commits

Format is Conventional Commits: `type(scope): summary`. Types follow the usual set (`feat`, `fix`, `chore`, `docs`, `test`, `refactor`, `ci`), and the scope names the area you touched:

| Scope | Area |
|---|---|
| `core` | `gpty-core` engine |
| `ipc` | Protocol, sockets, transport |
| `gdext` | The Godot extension and FFI |
| `cli` | The `gpty` binary and plugin tooling |
| `settings`, `terminal`, `layout`, `workspace`, `sidebar`, `ui` | GDScript frontend areas |
| `profiles`, `concepts`, `icons` | Feature verticals |
| `ai`, `inspector` | Inspector and reasoning backends |
| `ci` | Workflows, scripts, hooks |

One commit per coherent change. If a diff spans a refactor and a behaviour change, split it: the reviewer and `git bisect` both benefit.

## Where documentation goes

Three separate places, with different jobs:

| Location | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `docs/content/docs/agents/` | Developer guides: Rust, GDScript, security, testing, pitfalls, plugin manifest |
| `docs/content/docs/roadmap/` and `ROADMAP.md` | One page per release chain; the root file links them |
| `docs/content/docs/changelog/` | One page per release; `CHANGELOG.md` links them |
| `docs/content/wiki/` | This vault — durable explanation for a reader |

A behaviour change updates the page that describes it. A new feature that a user can reach gets a release-changelog entry; a new capability an agent can call updates the skill text under `skills/` and the schema it prints.

The wiki vault is source, not generated: after editing a note under `docs/content/wiki/`, run `./scripts/build-wiki` to refresh `godot/knowledge.json`. The CI gate fails when the bundle is stale, and release builds use the committed bundle.

## Your first change

Read `AGENTS.md` first, then the guide for the layer you are touching — `security.md` before anything near IPC, PTYs, plugins, or the filesystem. Build the extension, open the editor, install hooks. Make the smallest change that demonstrates the behaviour, run `./scripts/ci-check --fast` while iterating and the full `./scripts/ci-check` before pushing, write a Conventional Commit, and open the PR. If the change has a security dimension, the [[security-model|Security Model]] lists the threat boundaries it must not weaken.

# Control API

gPTY exposes one method set through three doors: a JSON-RPC socket, the `gpty` CLI, and an MCP server. The methods describe panes, layouts, concepts, and vaults; the doors differ in transport and in who is expected to use them.

The API is a control surface, not an orchestration layer. It can create a pane, type into it, read its output, wait for a pattern, and report status. It cannot decide what an agent should do next, and nothing in the API starts an agent for you.

## The three doors

| Door | Transport | Who uses it | Starts a GUI? |
|---|---|---|---|
| IPC | Newline-delimited JSON-RPC 2.0 over a Unix socket or named pipe | Programs that speak the protocol directly | No |
| CLI | The `gpty` binary, one request per invocation | Shells, scripts, agents inside a pane | Only `new-pane` and `layout load` |
| MCP | JSON-RPC over stdio, one tool per method | Agent harnesses outside gPTY | Never; `daemon-start` is explicit |

All three reach the same handlers in the running GUI. The CLI is a stateless client: it connects, sends one request, reads the answer, and exits. The MCP server is the same client underneath, wrapped in a tool interface.

## The methods

| Method | Params | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| `newPane` | `type`, `command?`, `split?`, `title?`, `focus?`, `tags?` | `{pane_id, label, type}` |
| `listPanes` | — | `{panes: [{id, label, type, title, col, row, tags, …}], count}` |
| `killPane` | `pane_id` | `{success}` |
| `focusPane` | `pane_id` | `{success}` |
| `inject` | `pane_id`, `text` | `{success}` |
| `paneRead` | `pane_id`, `lines?` (1–2000) | `{text}` — screen plus scrollback |
| `paneStatus` | `pane_id?` | One status document, or `{panes: [...]}` for every pane |
| `paneRun` | `command` | `{pane_id, label, type}` |
| `paneWait` | `pane_id`, `pattern`, `timeout_ms?` (100–60000) | `{matched, line?}` or `{matched: false, timed_out}` |
| `broadcast` | `tags`, `text` | `{success, count}` |
| `layoutSave` | `name` | `{success, name}` |
| `layoutLoad` | `name` | `{success}` |
| `layoutList` | — | `{layouts: [string]}` |
| `conceptList` | — | `{concepts: [{name, enabled, trigger, actions, …}]}` |
| `conceptToggle` | `name` | `{success, name}` |
| `vaultSearch` | `vault_path`, `pattern`, `limit?` (1–500) | `{results: [{path, title, snippet}], total, truncated}` |
| `vaultRead` | `vault_path`, `path` | `{path, text, truncated, crlf, mtime, size}` |
| `vaultWeight` | `vault_path`, `src`, `target`, `weight?` | The declared weight, or a clear |
| `version` | — | `{version, protocol}` |
| `shutdown` | — | `{success}` |

The `layout*` methods are named for the arrangement they restore, but in this build they save, load, and list **profiles**: `layoutSave` captures the active workspace as a reusable profile, and `layoutLoad` replaces the active workspace with that profile's tiles. See [[profile]] for the trust rules that apply to loading one, and [[layout]] for the arrangement itself.

The MCP door adds tools that are client-side rather than IPC methods: `daemon-start`, `daemon-stop`, `daemon-status`, and the layout/concept wrappers. It exposes 22 tools in total. Two CLI verbs are deliberately not tools: `state` (it reads the credentials of the pane it runs in) and the plugin verbs (install/enable/remove changes what code runs as you, so a human does it).

## Pane identity and status

A pane is addressed by its attachment ID (`T1`, `C1`, `W1`, …) or by `"active"` for the focused pane. A status document carries:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `pid` | The child process, or null once it is gone |
| `running` | A live terminal task with no exit code |
| `exit_code` | The child's exit code, when one was recorded |
| `exit_reason` | `exited`, `task_ended`, or null while running |
| `idle_ms` | Time since the last output |
| `agent_state`, `agent_state_tier` | The display-only badge and which tier supplied it |

`paneRun` opens a new terminal pane through the configured shell; it does not reuse an existing pane. `paneWait` is a regex match against recent output, not a promise about future output: it is held server-side until the pattern appears or the deadline passes. `paneRead` is a snapshot, so a caller that needs a stream should poll or subscribe to events instead.

## Design rules

- **The GUI owns state.** There is no daemon that mirrors the workspace and can disagree with it. If no GUI is running, only the commands that can satisfy a fresh workspace may start one.
- **One definition.** The CLI, MCP schemas, and IPC method list are generated from the same clap definitions; a tool cannot drift from `gpty --help` without failing a test.
- **Validation at the edge.** Request size is capped at 64 KiB, the server accepts at most 16 connections, and each handler has a budget. The CLI validates pane types before connecting, with suggestions.
- **No ambient authority.** The socket is owner-only and peer-checked on Unix. An optional shared secret keeps other users out, but it is not a boundary against a program inside a pane, which is a child of the GUI.

The separate event socket is not part of this API: it carries events and cannot create panes, inject input, or shut down the app. See [[omp-events]].

## Which door to use

- **Inside a pane, in a shell:** the CLI. `GPTY_ENV=1` confirms you are in a managed pane, and `GPTY_PANE_ID` names it.
- **Outside gPTY, in an agent harness:** MCP. It is stdio, declares its tools, and never opens a window implicitly.
- **From another program:** the JSON-RPC socket directly. It is the smallest contract and the one the other two are built on.

# History

History is the durable copy of what a terminal pane printed. The grid in memory is what you see; the history store is what survives closing the pane, closing the app, and rebooting the machine.

## Why persist scrollback

A terminal's scrollback normally dies with the process. gPTY keeps it because a pane is part of a saved layout: restoring a workspace should restore the shell, and a shell with an empty screen loses the reason you arranged the panes that way. It also makes the pane searchable across sessions — the failing test output from an hour ago is still there after a restart.

The store is keyed by a pane's stable `attachment_id`. A pane created without one gets no persistent store, because a per-run session id would only write rows that orphan at the next launch. When a pane is restored, the newest `history_lines` rows are loaded back into its scrollback.

## The store

History lives in one SQLite database, `user://history.db`, with an FTS5 full-text index beside the plain rows. FTS5 is the same engine the Wiki pane uses for note search; the difference is the tokenizer. Terminal lines use the default tokenizer so paths, flags, and identifiers stay searchable; the wiki uses stemming because prose is prose.

Writers never touch SQLite on the terminal path:

| Stage | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Terminal task | Queues each committed output line |
| Per-pane writer | Commits queued lines in batches on an interval, one writer per pane |
| Exit | The pane flushes on teardown so the last lines are in the database |

An insert costs roughly 30 µs, mostly the FTS index, so committing inline would stall output and hold the grid lock the renderer needs. The trade-off is that a search can miss the last few lines printed before the flush — the queue is drained, not instant.

Two caps bound a pane's store: a row cap from Settings (default 10,000 lines, adjustable from 100 to 100,000) and a derived byte cap of 1 KiB per row. The byte cap only binds when lines are unusually long: 10,000 rows of maximum-length 16 KiB lines would otherwise be 160 MB.

## Searching

`Ctrl+Shift+F` opens the search bar in the active terminal. Results are newest-first; the UI asks for 100 hits, and the API clamps the request to 1–500. History search is per pane — it searches that terminal's store, not every pane's.

The search box takes free text as a person types it, not an FTS5 query. Raw input would make ordinary searches fail: `main.rs` is a syntax error in FTS5, `error: x` reads as a column filter, an unclosed quote fails. Input is therefore sanitized into word-only terms, quoted and joined by a space, which FTS5 treats as AND. Punctuation is searchable because it becomes a separator; searching for `main.rs` finds `main.rs`.

A query that could not run at all reports an error, distinct from "no match", so an empty result is honest.

## What it costs on disk

Scrollback is plaintext. The point of a history store is that you can read it after the process is gone, and search it by content, so it is not encrypted.

Settings shows an **On disk** figure for the store, computed from the database file and its `-wal` and `-shm` siblings. That number is why the control is "history lines" rather than "megabytes": the row cap plus the per-row byte cap determine the bound, but the actual size depends on how long the lines actually were.

The database and its siblings are created owner-only (mode 0600), and the same rule covers the other JSON stores next to it. That protects against other accounts on a shared machine. It does not protect against anything running as you: any process of yours can read the file, the same way it can read a shell history file.

## Limits and edge cases

The store is per pane and per user; search does not cross panes. A pane whose task dies abruptly — a `SIGKILL`, a forced daemon stop — loses whatever was still queued. Search is line-based: a multi-line match is not a thing, so a query matches one stored line at a time.

# IPC

gPTY's inter-process control channel: a newline-delimited JSON-RPC 2.0 conversation over a local socket, where the GUI owns all workspace state and every client is a stateless caller. It is the transport under the [[control-api|Control API]]; the same method set also has a [[cli|command-line]] face and an [[mcp|MCP]] face.

## Why a socket exists at all

The workspace — panes, their PTYs, layouts, concepts, the wiki index — lives in one Godot process. Anything else that wants to act on it (a shell script, a coding agent in another pane, an editor plugin, a test harness) is a separate process. There is no safe way for another process to reach into the GUI's memory, so the GUI listens. Clients connect, send one request, read one answer, and leave.

## One state owner, many stateless clients

The GUI is the single writer. A CLI invocation does not cache pane lists, hold a connection, or remember a session: it connects, sends exactly one request, reads exactly one response, exits. Two `gpty list-panes` calls a second apart are unrelated events — no login, no reconnect logic, no client-side model to go stale.

The corollary is that the GUI must be running for a request to be answered. The CLI can start it on demand for two commands (`new-pane` and `layout load`); queries never spawn a window, and `--no-daemon` refuses even the two that would. The MCP server never spawns one at all.

## The request path

The socket thread is async and the scene tree is single-threaded, so a request is never handled on the socket thread. It is queued, and GDScript picks it up on the next frame:

```text
client ──▶ socket / named pipe ──▶ IpcServer (tokio task)
                                    │ queues the request
                                    ▼
                    GDScript _process() → drain_ipc_requests()
                    → workspace handler mutates the scene
                    → respond_ipc() completes the pending oneshot
                                    │
client ◀──────── response ──────────┘
```

`drain_ipc_requests()` hands back `{id, method, params, timeout_ms}`, where `timeout_ms` is what remains of the request's budget — a dialog that needs a human arms its own timer from it and cannot outlive the request. Deferred methods such as `paneWait` are held server-side: the connection stays open until the pattern matches or the deadline passes.

A method call is asynchronous from the GUI's point of view, and a long call does not block the frame loop — but it does occupy one connection slot.

## The wire

All traffic is newline-delimited JSON-RPC 2.0: one JSON object per line, both directions. A request:

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"newPane","params":{"type":"terminal","command":"/bin/bash","focus":true}}
```

The answer:

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{"pane_id":"T1","label":"T1","type":"terminal"}}
```

An error uses the standard envelope:

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"error":{"code":-32601,"message":"Unknown method: badMethod"}}
```

The client wrappers reshape them into command flags and tool arguments.

## Where the socket lives

| Platform | Path | Override |
|---|---|---|
| Linux | `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/gpty.sock`, then `/run/user/<uid>/gpty.sock`, then `/tmp/gpty-<uid>.sock` | `GPTY_SOCKET` |
| macOS | `$TMPDIR/gpty.sock`, then `/tmp/gpty-<uid>.sock` | `GPTY_SOCKET` |
| Windows | `\\.\pipe\gpty` | `GPTY_SOCKET` |

The fallbacks cover sessions with no runtime directory (a cron job, a stripped login); both sides derive the same list, so the client finds the bound endpoint.

## Control methods

| Method | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `newPane` | Create a pane; `type`, optional `command`, `split`, `title`, `focus`, `tags` |
| `listPanes` | Every pane with id, label, type, title, cell position, tags |
| `killPane` | Close a pane by id, or `"active"` for the focused one |
| `focusPane` | Focus a pane by id or `"active"` |
| `inject` | Write text to a terminal pane's PTY input, verbatim |
| `paneRead` | Plain text of a pane's screen plus scrollback (`lines` 1–2000) |
| `paneStatus` | Status document for one pane, or every pane when no id is given |
| `paneRun` | Run a command in a **new** terminal pane through the configured shell |
| `paneWait` | Hold the response until recent output matches a Rust regex (100–60000 ms) |
| `broadcast` | Inject text into every pane carrying one of the given tags |
| `layoutSave` | Save the active workspace's tiles as a named profile |
| `layoutLoad` | Activate a profile, replacing the active workspace's panes |
| `layoutList` | Names of the visible profiles |
| `conceptList` | Concept name, enabled flag, trigger, actions |
| `conceptToggle` | Enable or disable a concept by name |
| `vaultSearch` | FTS5 search over a Markdown vault (limit 1–500) |
| `vaultRead` | One note's text, with its size and mtime stamp |
| `vaultWeight` | Write or clear one declared link weight (display only) |
| `version` | GUI version and IPC protocol version |
| `shutdown` | Ask the GUI to exit |

`paneStatus` carries `pid`, `running`, `exit_code`, `exit_reason`, `idle_ms`, `agent_state`, and `agent_state_tier`; `exit_reason` is `exited`, `task_ended`, or null while running. With no pane it returns every tile, non-terminals carrying `status: null` so the list is complete rather than silently shorter.

## Why some methods are answered natively

`version` and `shutdown` are settled inside Rust — they describe or end the process, not the scene, and routing them through a frame would make them slower and less reliable. `vaultSearch` and `vaultRead` are answered natively too: a vault is a directory of files, not workspace state, and the walk plus the SQLite query run on the blocking pool instead of the GUI thread, so a large vault never stalls a frame.

`vaultWeight` is the exception that proves the rule. Its store is Godot's `user://link_weights.json`, so the write is routed to GDScript like every other stateful method — the split is by ownership.

## Security rules

The channel can create panes, inject keystrokes, and shut the workspace down, so it is hardened against other local users:

| Rule | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Socket placement | 0600 socket inside a per-user directory |
| Peer identity | Unix servers verify the connecting process shares the server's effective UID |
| One instance | A live endpoint is never replaced; only a crash leftover is rebound |
| Optional secret | `GPTY_SECRET` set on the GUI and clients; missing or mismatched yields `-32001` |
| Request size | Lines over 64 KiB are refused with `-32600` |
| `params` shape | Named-only: a JSON object, or absent (`null` reads as absent). Anything else answers `-32602` before dispatch |
| Connections | At most 16 concurrent; 30 s I/O bounds on read and write |
| Handler budget | 30 s default, 75 s for `paneWait`, 305 s for `pluginInstall`; overrun answers `-32000` |

`GPTY_SECRET` keeps *other users* out. It is not a boundary against a program inside a pane: that program is a child of the GUI, inherits its environment, and can read the secret back.

Named-only `params` is a batch rule as much as a protocol one. Every method takes its arguments by name, and a positional value used to reach a typed handler in the GUI's drain, where the resulting call error aborted the rest of that frame's batch — the requests already dequeued behind it were never answered. The server now refuses the shape before queueing it, and the drain's own guard answers the same code if one arrives another way.

## The second socket

Observability travels on a separate listener, `gpty-events.sock` (`\\.\pipe\gpty-events` on Windows), sitting beside the control socket. It is not an MCP tool, cannot create panes, inject input, or shut anything down, and does not honor `GPTY_SOCKET` or `GPTY_SECRET`. It serves three methods: `ompEvent` (capability-gated submission), `subscribe` (read-only, max 64 subscriptions), and `eventsPoll` (drain a subscription). Event types include pane spawn/kill, concept matches, declared agent state, and the OMP agent set — see [[omp-events|OMP Events]]. Keeping it separate means a program that only needs to report events never holds a handle that can drive the workspace.

# Keyboard Shortcuts

Most of gPTY's actions are reachable from the keyboard. Shortcuts fall into two scopes: those a terminal pane interprets, and those the workspace handles globally.

## Terminal pane

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| `Ctrl+Shift+C` | Copy the terminal selection |
| `Ctrl+Shift+V` | Paste the clipboard into the terminal |
| `Ctrl+Shift+F` | Toggle the scrollback search bar |
| `PageUp` | Scroll back one screenful |
| `PageDown` | Scroll forward one screenful |
| `Ctrl+V` | Sent to the shell as `^V` — deliberately not paste |

These are handled by the focused terminal before the workspace sees them. `Ctrl+Shift+F` opens a search bar over the pane; Escape closes it. Plain `Ctrl+F` is deliberately **not** intercepted, because full-screen programs like `vim` and `less` use it to page forward, so it reaches the PTY like any other key.

`Ctrl+Shift+C` copies only. With nothing selected it still consumes the chord and does nothing — it never falls through to a workspace shortcut, and it never clears the search bar or triggers an action. After a copy the selection is cleared.

`Ctrl+Shift+V` pastes. When the program running in the terminal has enabled bracketed paste, gPTY wraps the text the way the terminal protocol expects, so a shell or editor can tell a paste from typing. Either way the text is filtered first: control characters other than tab and newline are removed, escape included, so a clipboard that carries a paste terminator or an interrupt cannot end the bracket early or act as a keypress. Newlines and tabs survive, so a multi-line paste stays a multi-line paste.

`Ctrl+V` is the deliberate exception. It is passed through to the shell as a literal `^V` instead of pasting, because programs use it: readline's quoted-insert and vim's visual-block mode both rely on receiving it. Paste is `Ctrl+Shift+V` for this reason, not by convention.

`PageUp` and `PageDown` move the viewport through scrollback one screen at a time, without sending anything to the program. Typing, or pressing Enter, returns the view to the live prompt.

## Workspace and panes

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| `Ctrl+Shift+N` | New terminal pane |
| `Ctrl+Shift+D` | New code viewer pane |
| `Ctrl+Shift+T` | New file tree pane |
| `Ctrl+Shift+O` | New inspector pane |
| `Ctrl+Shift+W` | Close the focused pane |
| `Ctrl+Shift+R` | Close all panes in the workspace |
| `Ctrl+Shift+B` | Toggle the sidebar |
| `Ctrl+Shift+P` | Open the command palette |
| `F11` or `Ctrl+Shift+M` | Toggle fullscreen |
| `Alt+←` `Alt+→` `Alt+↑` `Alt+↓` | Move focus to the adjacent pane |
| `Ctrl+PageDown` | Next workspace |
| `Ctrl+PageUp` | Previous workspace |
| `Escape` | Close the palette, a search bar, or a settings popup |

New panes use the normal split rule: the largest tile halves along its longer axis, and the spawn is refused when both halves would be smaller than the 6-unit minimum. The four pane-type shortcuts are the only ones gPTY binds directly; Reasoning, CLI View, Wiki, and Media panes are spawned from the sidebar's Add Pane grid, the command palette, or the control API.

Closing a pane is guarded. If a command is still running, gPTY asks once before stopping it, and a pane holding unsaved work — a wiki note, for example — can cancel the close. `Ctrl+Shift+W` targets the focused pane; if focus is on a read-only pane, the workspace remembers the last terminal you clicked, so the shortcut still has a sensible target.

`Alt` plus an arrow moves focus to the nearest pane in that direction, judged by pane centers. It only works while a pane holds keyboard focus, which is the normal state after clicking into a pane. The workspace claims the chord before the terminal's key handling, so the arrow does not become a shell escape sequence; every other `Alt` combination still reaches the program.

Fullscreen is the same action on both bindings: `F11` and `Ctrl+Shift+M`. The sidebar's collapse state is independent of fullscreen, and `Ctrl+Shift+B` works in either mode.

## Command palette

`Ctrl+Shift+P` opens a small input with a filtered list. Typing matches anywhere in a command name, so `new` lists every pane type, `close` lists the close actions, and `load` lists the reload action. Enter runs the first match; clicking a row runs it too.

The commands are one `new <type>` entry for each of the eight pane types, then `close active`, `spawn 16 terminals`, `settings`, `close all`, `save`, and `load`. `save` writes the current workspace set, and `load` reloads the saved set from disk after asking every pane to close. See [[layout]].

## Wiki editor

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| `Ctrl+S` | Save the open note |

The wiki pane's editor saves explicitly: the Save button or `Ctrl+S` writes the note. There is no autosave; edits mark the note dirty, and leaving a dirty note raises Save / Discard / Cancel. A recovery copy is kept outside the vault between saves, so a crash does not cost the buffer, but it is offered back rather than applied automatically.

## Where shortcuts come from

Workspace shortcuts are registered once at startup, with fixed bindings. Pane-type spawn shortcuts are registered from the pane registry, so the tooltip on a sidebar button always names the same chord that actually works. Terminal chords are handled inside the terminal pane's keyboard path rather than through the global action map, which is why `Ctrl+V` and `Ctrl+F` can pass through to programs while `Ctrl+Shift+V` and `Ctrl+Shift+F` do not.

# Layout

A layout is the arrangement of panes inside one workspace: which rectangle each pane occupies, which pane sits in it, and the settings saved with that tile. It is geometry plus per-tile state, not a running session.

## The grid

Panes are placed on a tiling grid of 60 abstract units in each direction (`PaneTypes.GRID`). Every tile carries four integers — `col`, `row`, `cspan`, `rspan` — giving its top-left corner and its width and height in those units. The smallest allowed tile is 6 units (`MIN_TILE`), a tenth of the grid, which is roughly 100 px on a 1000 px pane.

Units are shares, not pixels: the grid stretches to fill the pane area, so a unit is about 17 px on a 1000 px pane and more on a wide monitor. When a tile is read from disk its geometry is clamped — corners inside the grid, spans at least 1 and at most 60, and never past the far edge. Stored terminal grid sizes are clamped separately (1–500 rows, 1–2000 columns).

## How panes get geometry

The first pane in an empty workspace fills the entire grid. Spawning another pane splits the largest tile in half along its longer axis; if either half would fall below `MIN_TILE`, the spawn is refused and gPTY warns that the grid is full. Panes never overlap, and no tile is ever automatically stacked on another.

Closing a pane frees its rectangle. An exact neighbour that matches the shape absorbs it; otherwise a group of tiles along exactly one side grows into the gap. A hand-edited or pinwheel arrangement with no such neighbour keeps the gap rather than stacking panes — except a lone survivor, which becomes the whole grid again.

Minimizing a pane hides its body but keeps its tile, so the arrangement is unchanged and the space stays reserved.

## Resizing by dragging

Each pane has thin edge strips on its borders. Dragging a strip moves the divider line that the edge sits on, and every tile touching that line moves with it — on both sides and along its whole length — so the result does not depend on which side of the divider you happened to grab. The drag previews in pixels while it runs and snaps to whole grid units when released, which keeps the model integral and the divider responsive. A tile never shrinks below `MIN_TILE`, and an edge on the window border does not start a drag because there is nothing on its far side.

The sidebar's swap-position action exchanges two tiles' stored geometry without touching what runs inside them.

## What a layout stores

Each tile saves its geometry plus the pane's layout state: type, pane name, attachment id, tags, font size, and whatever that pane type adds — a terminal's command, shell arguments, grid dimensions and cursor look; a wiki pane's vault path, view mode, open note and whether the graph was showing; a media pane's file; and so on.

A layout deliberately does **not** store:

- Running processes, exit state, or scrollback — history lives in a separate database and survives panes.
- Unsaved editor text. A dirty wiki buffer is not part of the layout; a recovery copy outside the vault covers a crash.
- Per-pane environment. That is user-owned, keyed by attachment id, and lives in its own store (see [[settings]]).
- Window size, position, sidebar width, or focus. Those belong to the application, not the arrangement.

Restoring a layout therefore starts fresh programs in the same shapes, not the same sessions.

## Saving and restoring

Automatic persistence and named saving are two different mechanisms.

The **workspace set** is auto-saved to `user://workspaces.json` whenever you switch or close a workspace, and on exit. Each entry holds a name, an optional default directory, and its layout array plus the `grid_unit` it was written in, so a file from an older build converts to the same shares. On startup the set is restored and the previously active workspace is re-selected. A legacy `user://layout.json` is imported once when the store is empty, which is why the older file name still appears in the code.

A **named layout** is saved on demand:

```bash
gpty layout save "My Split"
gpty layout load "My Split"
gpty layout list
```

The command palette's `save` and `load` entries do the same for the workspace set (save writes it, load reloads it from disk), and the control API exposes `layout-save`, `layout-load`, and `layout-list`. In this build a named layout is stored as a profile: saving captures the active workspace's tiles under a name, and loading replaces the active workspace with them. See [[profile]] for where those live and how activation behaves.

Restoring is subject to Workspace Trust when a tile names a different program or passes arguments compared with your configured shell; a saved tile's environment is always stripped. See [[workspace-trust]].

## Layout, workspace, profile

| Term | What it is | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Layout | The arrangement and per-tile settings | Inside one workspace |
| Workspace | A tab that owns one layout | One entry in the tab set |
| Profile | A reusable named tile set | Saved separately, activated into a workspace |
| Pane | One unit placed by a layout | The thing you type into |

A layout is not a workspace and not a profile: the workspace owns it, and a profile is a template you copy into a workspace.

# MCP

`gpty mcp` is a Model Context Protocol server over stdio: an AI harness that speaks MCP gets gPTY's workspace operations as tools, without writing socket code or shelling out. It is the third door onto the [[control-api|Control API]] — the same methods the [[cli|CLI]] exposes — reshaped into the tool-calling convention MCP defines.

## What the server is

The process reads newline-delimited JSON-RPC from stdin and writes answers to stdout. It implements the MCP handshake (`initialize`, answering protocol version `2024-11-05` with `serverInfo` naming `gpty`), discovery (`tools/list`), and dispatch (`tools/call`). Each `tools/call` is translated into one request on the [[ipc|control socket]]; the server holds a single client connection and forwards the result as tool output.

A stdio server is the right shape here because an MCP harness already owns the process: it spawns `gpty mcp`, keeps the pipes, and never needs a port, a URL, or a discovery file. There is nothing to secure on the network because there is no network.

Configure it the way your harness documents a stdio server: command `gpty`, argument `mcp`. The repo's root `mcp.json` is exactly that:

```json
{"mcpServers":{"gpty":{"command":"gpty","args":["mcp"]}}}
```

## The tool set

Twenty-two tools are published, mirroring CLI actions and kebab-cased:

| Area | Tools |
|---|---|
| Panes | `new-pane`, `list-panes`, `kill-pane`, `focus-pane`, `inject`, `pane-read`, `pane-status`, `pane-run`, `pane-wait` |
| Fan-out | `broadcast` |
| Layout | `layout-save`, `layout-load`, `layout-list` |
| Daemon | `daemon-start`, `daemon-stop`, `daemon-status` |
| Concepts | `concept-list`, `concept-toggle` |
| Vault | `vault-search`, `vault-read`, `vault-weight` |
| Misc | `version` |

Two CLI commands are deliberately **not** tools. `state` declares the agent state of the pane the command runs in and reaches the event socket, not the control socket — an MCP client has no pane, so advertising it would publish a tool that cannot dispatch. `plugin` installs and manages plugins: install waits on a human reading a review dialog, and the admin verbs touch local state rather than the workspace API. Both exclusions are enforced by a test, not a comment.

The heavy hitters for an agent are `pane-wait` and `pane-read`. Together they turn a terminal into a synchronous function call: run a command, wait for the line that means done, read the output. `pane-run` returns as soon as the pane exists, so the exit code is not the answer — `pane-status` is.

## The name gate

`tools/call` validates the requested tool name against `schema::mcp_tool_names()` before dispatch. This is not ceremony. Tool names are kebab-case and IPC methods are camel-case, so dispatch maps one to the other mechanically — and a mechanical mapping turns *any* string into a method name. Without the gate, a client that guesses `shutdown` — or any method that exists on the socket but was never published as a tool — would reach it. The allowed-name list is computed once at startup from the CLI definitions, so the gate and the advertised tool list cannot disagree.

The consequence for an MCP author is simple: if a tool is not in `tools/list`, calling it fails, even if the underlying control method exists.

## Where the schemas come from

Tool descriptions and argument schemas are generated from the clap command definitions in `crates/gpty-cli/src/commands/schema.rs`. Each subcommand becomes a tool, its arguments become JSON Schema properties with enums pulled from clap's possible values, and required-argument marking follows the clap definition.

Two transformations happen on the way. Nested subcommand groups are flattened: `daemon start` becomes `daemon-start`, `layout save` becomes `layout-save`. The concept and vault verbs are already flat. And the self-referential commands are skipped — `mcp` (the server describing itself as a tool makes no sense) and `schema` (an admin/discovery command, not a workspace action). Because both the schema and `--help` read the same definitions, `gpty schema --format mcp` is the authority whenever documentation and binary disagree.

## No auto-spawn

The [[cli|CLI]] starts a GUI on demand for `new-pane` and `layout load`. The MCP server never does: no tool call may open a window behind the user's back. When a call finds no GUI, the answer says so and names `daemon-start`, which is the one explicit bootstrap.

That asymmetry is deliberate. A CLI invocation is a deliberate act by a human or a script that named the command; an MCP client is a model calling tools in a loop, and it should not be able to fill the desktop with workspaces as a side effect of a retry. `daemon-start` exists so that "start the GUI" is a decision the model can make and the user can audit as a distinct tool call.

## MCP or CLI?

Both reach the same methods, so the choice is about where the caller lives.

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| A harness outside gPTY (an editor, a chat UI, a service) | MCP |
| A shell script, Makefile, or CI job | CLI |
| An agent running **inside** a gPTY pane | CLI, via the skill |
| Blocking on output until a pattern appears | Either; `pane-wait` in both |
| Declaring the current pane's state | CLI only (`state`) |
| Installing or validating a plugin | CLI only (`plugin`) |

The reason an in-pane agent uses the CLI is credentials and identity: the CLI reads `GPTY_*` from the pane's environment, so it knows which pane it is in and can declare state. An MCP server is a separate process spawned by the harness; it does not inherit the pane's injected identity in any meaningful way. The bundled skill, printed by `gpty --skill`, assumes the CLI for exactly this reason — see [[agent-workflow|Agent Workflow]].

# OMP Events

OMP Events is gPTY's observability channel: a second local socket that carries semantic events about agent sessions, turns, and tools. It is separate from workspace control on purpose — a terminal capability may append events, and nothing else.

## Why a second socket

The control socket is authority: create a pane, inject input, kill a pane, read a pane. An agent extension that only wants to say "a turn started" should not hold that. So the event channel is a different listener with a different method set and its own credential:

| | Control socket | Event socket |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Drive the workspace | Report what an agent is doing |
| Callers | CLI, MCP, scripts | A pane's program, subscribers |
| Credential | Same-UID peer, optional secret | Per-PTY event capability |
| Endpoint | `gpty.sock` / `\\.\pipe\gpty` | `gpty-events.sock` / `\\.\pipe\gpty-events` |

The event listener does not honour `GPTY_SOCKET` or `GPTY_SECRET`. It runs on the same transport server as the control socket, but registers exactly three methods.

## Methods

| Method | Gate | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `ompEvent` | Per-PTY capability, protocol version, bounded payload | Submit one event |
| `subscribe` | None (read-only) | Reserve a poll cursor; at most 64 live subscriptions |
| `eventsPoll` | Subscription id | Drain queued events; default 64, clamped to 256 |

There is no push transport in this protocol version: subscribers poll. A subscription that stops polling is released after 120 seconds and its queued events with it, so an abandoned client cannot exhaust the 64 slots.

## The credential

Every PTY is started with four variables:

| Variable | Value |
|---|---|
| `GPTY_TERMINAL_SESSION_ID` | Ephemeral session id for this PTY |
| `GPTY_EVENT_CAPABILITY` | Unguessable per-PTY secret |
| `GPTY_EVENT_SOCKET` | Absolute event socket path |
| `GPTY_EVENT_PROTOCOL` | `1` |

A submission names the terminal session and presents the capability, which is compared in constant time. The capability is not reused across panes and is unregistered when the pane goes away. Setting only some of the four variables does nothing.

## Vocabulary

Wire names are the adapter's; the trust boundary translates them into an adapter-neutral vocabulary, so Reasoning and agent state consume one contract:

| Wire event | Generic name | Carries |
|---|---|---|
| `omp.session.bound` | `session.bound` | Session identity reason |
| `omp.session.shutdown` | `session.shutdown` | Timestamp |
| `omp.agent.started` | `agent.started` | Timestamp |
| `omp.agent.settled` | `agent.settled` | Timestamp |
| `omp.turn.started` | `turn.started` | Turn index, times |
| `omp.turn.finished` | `turn.finished` | Turn index, time |
| `omp.tool.started` | `tool.call` | Tool name, call id |
| `omp.tool.finished` | `tool.finished` | Call id, error flag |
| `omp.reasoning.delta` | `thinking.delta` | Reasoning text, ≤8 KiB |
| `gpty.state.declared` | `state.declared` | One of the five agent states |

The socket also carries gPTY's own workspace events: pane spawn, pane kill, and concept matches. Plugin manifests subscribe to those by the names `pane.spawned`, `pane.killed`, and `concept.matched`; a notify-only concept produces a concept match with no content attached.

## What is forwarded, and what is not

The extension is a separately installable component and its payload is untrusted, so translation is a field allowlist, not a passthrough. Each allowed field has a type and a cap — identifiers up to 128 bytes, a session reason up to 64 bytes, thinking text up to 8 KiB — and anything not listed is dropped, including fields a future extension version invents. A declaration naming an unknown state is rejected rather than silently ignored, and an oversized reasoning delta is rejected rather than truncated.

Prompts, answer text, tool arguments and results, provider objects, session file paths, environment variables, and credentials are never forwarded. The event channel is metadata about a workspace, not a copy of the conversation.

## The bundled extension

`@gpty/omp-events` is the OMP extension that speaks this protocol. It is not loaded automatically; the user links it:

```bash
omp plugin link /absolute/path/to/gpty/extensions/gpty-omp-events
```

It is dormant unless all four variables are present, registers no tools or commands, and forwards from OMP's extension event hooks. Reasoning deltas are coalesced for up to 16 ms and sent as events of at most 8 KiB of UTF-8, split on code-point boundaries rather than truncated, which keeps a token-rate stream under the queue budget. The transport is one code path on both platforms: `net.connect(path)` opens a Unix domain socket for a socket path and a named pipe for a pipe path, with validation differing per platform.

## What consumes it

The Reasoning pane projects the event stream into its view; it needs the extension and the event socket to receive anything. Tier 1 agent state also reads these events: agent start becomes `working`, settled becomes `completed`, a failed tool call becomes `needs-attention`, and an explicit declaration passes its value through. See [[agent-state]] for the merge rules.

## What the channel cannot do

It cannot create panes, inject input, read pane output, change settings, or shut gPTY down. There is no method for any of it. Reading the fan-out is open to same-UID processes — the channel is not confidential from your own user — while submitting is gated by the per-PTY capability.

# Plugins

A gPTY plugin is a Git repository containing a `gpty-plugin.toml` manifest that adds profiles, concepts, link handlers, actions, and event bindings to a workspace. Plugins are installed explicitly, reviewed by a human in the GUI, and then run with your authority — they are the guest at the outer edge of the [[gpty|gPTY]] trust boundary.

## What a plugin contributes

A plugin is data plus commands, not a library loaded into the process. There is no plugin ABI, no in-process callback surface, and no way to replace a pane type. What it can do is narrower:

| Section | What it adds |
|---|---|
| `[[profiles]]` | Named tile sets that appear in the profile list — a workspace layout to open |
| `[[concepts]]` | Regex triggers that capture terminal output into a pane |
| `[[actions]]` | Named commands a user (or `gpty plugin run`) can invoke |
| `[[events]]` | Declared event subscriptions, shown in the review; gPTY does not dispatch them, and the plugin reads the event socket itself |
| `[[link_handlers]]` | Declared URL-scheme handlers, validated and shown in the review; no current runtime opens a link through one |

Every one is a declaration: install validates the file; the GUI decides when a profile opens or an action runs. Profiles and concepts are the two sections the runtime actually consumes; actions are invoked manually with `gpty plugin run`.

## The manifest

The schema lives in `crates/gpty-cli/src/plugin_manifest.rs`. Top-level keys:

| Key | Rules |
|---|---|
| `id` | `owner/name`, parts `[a-z0-9-]`, 1–63 characters each |
| `name` | 1–64 characters |
| `version`, `min_gpty_version` | Semver `X.Y.Z`, no pre-release |
| `platforms` | Subset of `linux`, `macos`, `windows`; default all |
| `build`, `startup` | argv arrays, declared and displayed but not executed by any current item |

The array-of-table sections each have a cap: `[[actions]]` ≤64 (`name`, `command`, optional `args`), `[[events]]` ≤64 (`name`, `type`), `[[link_handlers]]` ≤16 (`scheme`, `command` argv), `[[concepts]]` ≤128, `[[profiles]]` ≤64 with ≤64 tiles each.

Three rules make the manifest safe to read:

- **Nothing executes at parse or validation time.** `build`, `startup`, and link-handler commands are argv arrays, never shell strings, capped at 32 entries and 4096 characters; an action's `command` is a published tool name and its `args` become flags.
- **Every concept is engine-accepted.** Each `[[concepts]]` entry round-trips through the real concept engine (`concepts_from_json`). An entry the engine would silently drop — a PCRE2 lookbehind, say, when the engine speaks Rust `regex` — rejects the manifest instead of vanishing.
- **Tiles mirror the GUI's sanitizer.** Pane type must be one of the eight real types, grid geometry must fit the 60-unit grid, rows and cols within 500 and 2000. The sanitizer clamps legacy files; the validator rejects, because a manifest is authored content and an out-of-range value is an authoring error.

Unknown keys in manifest sections are rejected. The schema is closed: a typo fails at validate time instead of surfacing later as a missing feature.

## Install, review, pin

```bash
gpty plugin install godot-pty/gpty-omp
gpty plugin install godot-pty/gpty-lazygit@v1.2.0
```

Install clones `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>` — git driven by argv, never a shell — into a staging directory under the data directory. It accepts any advertised git ref: tag, branch, or commit SHA. A bare install means the default branch's latest.

Before anything lands it gates the manifest: the `id` must equal the install target, the current platform must be declared, and `min_gpty_version` must not exceed the CLI. Then, because the plugin's actions will run as you, it sends a summary over the `pluginInstall` IPC method for a human to accept in the GUI. The review dialog shows the requested ref beside the resolved revision and prints the distinct programs a profile's tiles would run. No GUI answering — declined, disconnected, `--no-daemon` — means nothing installs.

Content moves to `data_dir()/plugins/<id>`, runtime directories are created under `state_dir()/plugins/<id>/{config,state,logs}`, and a record lands in `state_dir()/plugins.json` with the resolved SHA and the manifest's profiles and concepts. **The store pins the SHA**, not the tag: a moved tag is a new revision and triggers a re-review. The GUI never parses TOML: the validator stays the single gate, and a broken record degrades one entry at a time.

Every `plugin` command reads the running GUI's version before it does anything else — bounded, best-effort, silent when no GUI answers. The store is shared state, so a CLI older than the GUI beside it rejects record keys it does not know and reports `plugins.json` as corrupt; that is what a stale `gpty` on `PATH` looks like. The warning names both versions and the fix: reinstall the CLI, or use the one shipped beside the GUI.

## The trust model

The review dialog is not a formality. A plugin's actions run as the user, through the same API a person at the CLI uses, so installing one is granting a third party the ability to create panes, inject keystrokes, and read your vault through your own account. That is why install always asks, why `pluginInstall` is deliberately not an MCP tool — a client cannot answer a dialog — and why the review names the programs the profiles would run.

The blast radius is bounded by published surfaces, not by sandboxing:

- **Actions may only name published tools.** `[[actions]].command` is validated against the same list `schema::mcp_tool_names()` derives — the 22 MCP tools. A manifest cannot name anything else on the socket.
- **Event types are a closed vocabulary.** `pane.spawned`, `pane.killed`, `concept.matched`, `state.declared`, plus the generic OMP set (`session.bound`, `agent.started`, `turn.started`, `tool.call`, `thinking.delta`). Adding one is a deliberate change in lockstep with the emitting side.
- **Concepts capture and route display content only**; they never execute. Plugin concepts are the same engine objects a hand-written concept is.
- **Profiles are consented at the pinned revision, down to their spawn plans.** Opening a tile that would spawn a different program or argv is already a [[workspace-trust|Workspace Trust]] decision; plugin profiles go through the same gate, and the install approval records the exact plans the review listed — a profile whose tiles change under the same revision asks again.

What none of this prevents is a plugin running arbitrary code in the panes it spawns, with a concept of its own choosing. The [[security-model|Security Model]] treats plugins as untrusted guests for that reason: they are gated at install and at the API surface, not contained at runtime.

## Managing installed plugins

| Verb | Effect |
|---|---|
| `gpty plugin list` | Installed records, their revision, and enabled state |
| `gpty plugin enable <id>` / `disable <id>` | Flip the record; a running GUI updates its profile list, or reads the store on next launch |
| `gpty plugin uninstall <id>` | Remove the record and directories; the GUI drops its profiles |
| `gpty plugin logs <id>` | Read the plugin's captured action output |
| `gpty plugin run <id> <action>` | Spawn the action's CLI command through `GPTY_BIN_PATH` and print its output |
| `gpty plugin validate <path>` | Run the shipped install validator offline |


## The authoring loop

`gpty plugin validate` is the whole local loop: it runs the same parser and gates the install uses, on a plugin directory or its manifest, with no GUI and no network. `--json` prints `{"ok": …}` and exits 1 on rejection, which is what a plugin repo's CI runs. Each first-party plugin repo — one per tool, each a single manifest — validates its own checkout and keeps a one-line assertion that its `id` equals the repo name, because that equality is the install gate's contract and the validator cannot see the repo.

The plugin verbs are CLI-only: `install` waits on a human, and the admin verbs touch local state rather than the workspace API, so none of them are MCP tools.

# Profile

A profile is a named, reusable set of tiles. Activating one replaces the panes of the active workspace with a copy of that set; the profile itself stays unchanged for the next activation.

## What is in a profile

A profile holds a list of tiles, each with the same geometry a layout uses — `col`, `row`, `cspan`, `rspan` on the 60-unit grid — plus the settings for the pane that goes there. Because it is a template rather than a live workspace, it stores no processes, no scrollback, and no environment: a profile that once contained a terminal's `shell_env` is stripped on restore, with a notice, because environment is user-owned and lives in its own store (see [[settings]]).

Activating a profile resets the active workspace and rebuilds its panes from the profile's tiles. That is why a profile behaves like restoring a layout, and why it can trip the same Workspace Trust gate described in [[workspace-trust]].

## Where profiles come from

There are three sources, shown in one list in the sidebar's Profiles section.

**Built in.** gPTY ships exactly one built-in profile, **Agent Workspace**: a wide terminal on the left with an Inspector and a Reasoning pane stacked on the right. Its terminal, Inspector, and Reasoning tiles carry stable attachment ids (`omp-terminal`, `omp-inspector`, `omp-reasoning`) so the Inspector and Reasoning panes can be wired to that terminal. The built-in is read from `res://profiles.default.json`, which ships with the application and is never written.

**Installed with a plugin.** The single-pane tool presets — Herdr, Lazygit, Neovim, Claude, and OMP — arrive from their own plugin repositories, one profile per tool, each restoring a full-window terminal that runs that tool. None of them installs the OMP event extension or launches `omp` for you; you do that inside the terminal. Plugin profiles are re-read from the installed-plugin store, are never written into the user profile file, and disappear with the plugin. Their sidebar rows show where they came from (`owner/repo@revision`) and offer no rename or delete, because the plugin owns them.

**Saved by you.** The `+` button in the Profiles header captures the active workspace's current tiles as a new profile. The dialog asks for a name and lets you edit each pane's command before saving, which is how you turn a working arrangement into a repeatable one. User profiles live in `user://profiles.json`.

Name collisions are resolved with a ` (n)` suffix rather than overwriting: built-in and user names keep the bare name and a colliding plugin profile yields, while among plugin profiles the first one wins. Double-clicking a user profile row renames it; its delete button removes it. Deleting or renaming a profile also clears or updates the accent on any workspace that had activated it.

## Activating a profile

Clicking a profile row activates it. If the active workspace has panes, gPTY asks first, because activation replaces the current layout. Each pane still gets its own close guard, so unsaved work — a wiki note with edits, for example — can cancel the whole activation.

Before anything is torn down, the trust check runs. A profile whose tiles would start a different program or pass extra arguments compared with your configured shell raises a Workspace Trust dialog naming the program and arguments. Approvals are remembered narrowly:

| Profile source | What an approval covers |
|---|---|
| Built-in | That profile name at the current app version, and the spawn plans recorded with it; a new release asks again, and so does different content under the same name |
| Plugin | That plugin id at the exact installed revision, and the spawn plans the install review listed; a new revision asks again, and so does different content under the same revision |
| Saved by you | Ask every time, unless every untrusted spawn plan was already approved through a shipped profile |

Where a profile came from is recorded by gPTY when it loads it, not read from the file. A hand-written `profiles.json` entry cannot claim to be a built-in or to belong to an installed plugin: those fields are stripped on load, so the entry is your profile and goes through the same plan check as any other. An approval also covers only the plans it recorded, which is why a profile whose tiles changed under an approved name or revision asks again.

A saved-by-you profile never writes a consent record, so it is a fresh decision each activation. The dialog's Cancel activates nothing and leaves the workspace as it was.

The activated profile's name is remembered by the workspace that activated it, and its row is accented while that workspace is active. Resetting the workspace's panes (`Ctrl+Shift+R` or Close All) clears that state, because an empty layout is no longer that profile.

## Automation

The control API's layout commands operate on profiles:

```bash
gpty layout save "Review"
gpty layout load "Review"
gpty layout list
```

`layout save` captures the active workspace under the given name, creating a user profile; `layout load` activates a profile by name; `layout list` prints every visible profile name. The same methods are available as the `layout-save`, `layout-load`, and `layout-list` MCP tools.

A caller cannot answer a dialog, so these paths are stricter than the sidebar. Loading a profile that would spawn an unapproved program or argument list is refused with an explanation instead of prompting, and loading is refused when a pane in the active workspace holds unsaved changes. A running process is not a reason to refuse — naming the profile is taken as consent to stop what it replaces. Loading also starts the GUI when needed, unlike queries.

## Profile, layout, workspace

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Profile | A named template of tiles, reusable across workspaces |
| Layout | The arrangement currently inside one workspace |
| Workspace | The tab that owns a layout and a directory |
| Pane | One unit placed by either |

Saving a profile copies the current layout; activating one copies the profile's layout back into a workspace. Neither operation changes the other: editing the workspace afterwards does not edit the profile, and there is no implicit "update profile" action — save a new profile instead.
