# Security Model

The security model is a short list of what gPTY trusts, what it does not, and which control stands at each boundary. It is a threat model, not a promise of isolation: a pane is a shell running as you, and the app says so rather than sandboxing it.

## What is trusted

Your own user account. gPTY trusts same-UID processes by design — a process running as you can already read your files and attach to your terminals, so "another program of mine can drive my workspace" is not treated as a vulnerability. `GPTY_SECRET` raises the bar for *other users* on a shared machine. On Linux and Windows it also keeps the secret out of a pane program's reach (see below), which makes the socket gate real for panes when a secret is set — a credential, not isolation. It never changes the trust class.

Untrusted by default: everything printed in a pane, every saved file (layouts, profiles, workspaces, concepts, notes, scrollback), remote responses such as release metadata, and other users on the machine.

## Boundaries

| Boundary | What crosses it | Primary control |
|---|---|---|
| Control socket | Workspace commands: panes, input, layouts, queries | Owner-only socket in a private directory, peer UID check, one-instance ownership, size and connection caps |
| Event socket | Agent metadata and declarations | Per-PTY capability for submission; field allowlist; bounded queues |
| Pane programs | Whatever a shell can do, as you | Environment scrub, argv instead of shell strings, executable validation, Workspace Trust |
| Plugins | Code you chose to install, running as you | Human review, pinned revisions, validated manifest, published tool surface |
| Untrusted files | Tile settings, paths, vault and media locations | Validation, clamping, path gates, trust prompts |
| Rendered content | Markdown, captures, decoded media | Escaping, scheme checks, codec and container allowlists |

## The control socket

This is the highest-value target: it can type into any pane and read any pane. Its hardening is layered.

- **Location.** The socket lives in a per-user directory — the runtime directory when one exists, otherwise a private state directory created owner-only. Only when no private directory can be used does it fall back to a predictable `/tmp/gpty-<uid>.sock`; that path is a denial-of-service target for another user but never a spoof, because ownership and mode are validated before use.
- **Permissions and peers.** Mode 0600, and the connecting process must run as the same user. The peer check fails closed on a lookup error on Linux, macOS, the BSDs, Solaris, and Windows.
- **One owner.** The server probes an existing socket before replacing it and refuses when another server answers, so a second instance cannot take over a live endpoint, while a stale file left by a crash is replaced after the probe finds nobody listening.
- **Bounds.** Requests cap at 64 KiB, at most 16 connections are served at once, `params` must be a JSON object — a positional or scalar value answers `-32602` before it is queued, so one bad request cannot take the frame's batch with it — and I/O has time bounds so a stalled client cannot hold the GUI.
- **Optional secret.** `GPTY_SECRET` is compared in constant time when set. Clients also validate the socket path and the GUI binary before connecting or spawning.

The protocol itself is documented in [[ipc|IPC]]; the point here is that none of these guards make the socket safe against a process running as you.

## The event socket

The second listener registers exactly three methods and nothing else. Submitting an event requires the per-PTY capability; payloads pass a field allowlist, so a future extension field is dropped rather than forwarded. Reading the fan-out is open to same-UID processes: the channel is non-confidential from your own user. Its methods cannot create panes, inject input, read output, or stop gPTY.

## Pane programs

Every pane is a child of the GUI running with your permissions — there is no sandbox, and the app never claims one. What is controlled is the path *into* a child:

- Environment is sanitized at one choke point. Dynamic-loader keys (`LD_*`, `DYLD_*`), startup-evaluation keys a shell or tool would execute (`PROMPT_COMMAND`, `BASH_ENV`, `ENV`, `NODE_OPTIONS`, `PERL5OPT`, `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`, and similar), the event-channel credentials, and the pane markers are removed from untrusted environment sources.
- Spawns take a program and an argv array. Nothing in the spawn path evaluates a shell string, and absolute programs restored from files must be regular files owned by you or root and not group- or other-writable.
- Concepts cannot execute anything, and the parser interprets exactly one escape sequence — the state declaration that paints a badge. There is no clipboard access via escape sequences.
- Output cannot grow the GUI without a bound. A program can open an escape string and never close it, which both stops the stream being interpreted and accumulates its payload; one shared guard in front of both parsers closes a string that passes 64 KiB, so what a pane's output can make the GUI hold is finite — a grid fed 256 MiB of unclosed OSC payload stayed flat at 6.2 MB. The mechanism, and why only OSC needs counting, is in [[ansi-escape-sequences]].
- Restored tiles and profiles pass the [[workspace-trust|Workspace Trust]] gate before they run.

## Keeping the secret out of a pane's reach

A pane's shell is a child of the GUI and runs as you, so no file permission separates them: whether the shell can read the GUI's environment is decided by the kernel. The GUI and the CLI therefore call `gpty_core::hardening::harden_process()` once at startup, and on Linux that clears the process's *dumpable* bit (`PR_SET_DUMPABLE 0`).

| | Linux | macOS | Windows |
|---|---|---|---|
| How a same-user process reads another process's environment | `/proc/<pid>/environ` | sysctl `KERN_PROCARGS2` (`ps -E`, `pgrep`) | `ReadProcessMemory`, after `OpenProcess` into the PEB |
| What decides same-user access | the target's dumpable bit | the target's user id | the target's process DACL |
| Hardened by gPTY | yes | no | yes |
| Effect on `GPTY_SECRET` | a pane cannot recover it | still readable | a pane cannot recover it |

On Linux a non-dumpable process also loses `/proc/<pid>/maps`, `/proc/<pid>/mem`, and same-user `ptrace` attachment. Measured 2026-10-29 with `GPTY_SECRET` set: before, a program in a pane read the GUI's environment and recovered the secret; after, that file is owned by root, the read fails with `EACCES`, `/proc/<gui>/maps` fails too — and a child of the pane shell can still read the shell's environment. That last part is what makes the trade acceptable: a pane's shell is a separate `exec`ed program, and `exec` restores dumpability, so the GUI is hidden while the user's own code stays debuggable.

### Why the macOS analogue does not carry over

`ptrace(PT_DENY_ATTACH)` denies *tracing*: a debugger cannot attach to the process. It has no effect on `KERN_PROCARGS2`, which is how `ps -E` and `pgrep` return argv and the environment block to any same-UID reader. So on macOS the environment stays readable and `GPTY_SECRET` remains protection against other users only. Unsetting the variable after reading it does not help: `KERN_PROCARGS2` — like Linux's `/proc/<pid>/environ` — reads the initial environment block a process was started with, not the `environ` pointer array that `setenv`/`unsetenv` edits.

### The Windows equivalent

Windows exposes the environment only by reading process memory. gPTY therefore gives the process a DACL that withholds `PROCESS_VM_READ`, `PROCESS_VM_WRITE`, `PROCESS_VM_OPERATION` and `PROCESS_CREATE_THREAD` from the owner — so `ReadProcessMemory` into the PEB is refused, and so is code injection — while keeping `PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION` (the mask the control socket's peer check opens a client with), `PROCESS_TERMINATE` (Task Manager can still end a hung GUI), `SYNCHRONIZE` and `READ_CONTROL`. It is one ACE, for the process owner: `SYSTEM` gets no blanket entry, because it holds `SeDebugPrivilege` and a full grant would re-grant everything when the app itself runs as SYSTEM. A process that enables that privilege overrides any process DACL; that is an elevated debugger, not a pane.

### Cost and limits

A non-dumpable process on Linux produces no core dump and cannot be attached to by a same-user debugger or profiler; a hardened Windows process cannot be opened for memory reads by the same user. `GPTY_ALLOW_DEBUG=1` (also `true`, `yes`, `on`) opts out for a developer who needs one; an empty value or `0` does not.

The barrier is not absolute on either platform. `exec` resets the dumpable bit (and the DACL is installed from `main`/init), so the marking lands a moment after a client starts and a process polling the platform's access check can catch a short-lived client's secret. And a shell rc file that exports `GPTY_SECRET` puts it back into every pane that reads that file, because the PTY strip happens before the shell starts.

## Plugins

Plugins are arbitrary code running as you; that is the trust model, stated plainly in [[plugins|Plugins]]. Install clones into a staging directory with git invoked by argv, validates the manifest against the engine's own vocabularies and caps, and requires a human review in the GUI; the store pins the revision, so a moved tag re-prompts. A manifest's actions can only name the published MCP tool surface, and its commands are argv arrays rather than shell strings.

## Untrusted files and rendered content

Saved tiles are validated before they are trusted: the pane type must be known, grid geometry is clamped, arguments are capped, and viewer paths must be absolute. Media paths must be absolute local regular files — no URLs, no device nodes — and the decoder is built without network protocols. Markdown renders to escaped text: raw HTML is not interpreted, images become alt text, only `http`, `https`, and `mailto` links become metadata, and a link opens only after an explicit confirmation. Captured output handed to the Inspector is fenced so that content cannot close the fence and become instructions.

## Known limitations

These are the ones that matter, and they are documented rather than implied.

- **A program in a pane can drive every other pane, unless a secret is set on Linux or Windows.** Panes are children of the GUI, so they pass the control socket's same-user gate, and the default socket path is derivable from the inherited runtime directory. With `GPTY_SECRET` set, the hardened GUI and CLI keep the secret out of a pane program's reach — a credential, not pane isolation. The default install sets no secret; macOS still exposes the environment to same-user processes; and the startup window and rc-file re-export described above still apply. When it is reachable, the reach is the whole surface: inject, pane-run, broadcast, new-pane, kill-pane, and pane-read. Workspaces do not isolate panes from each other. Per-pane permission and a "sensitive workspace" that no client can reach are tracked, not implemented.
- **A pane inherits your environment** other than the stripped keys — `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, cloud credential pointers, proxy settings, and `DISPLAY` all reach every pane, including a GUI auto-spawned by the CLI.
- **Scrollback is plaintext.** The store and its SQLite siblings are owner-only, but anything printed in a pane — tokens included — is on disk like a shell history file.
- **Media decoding is in-process C.** The pinned FFmpeg build is minimal and allowlisted, but it is not a sandbox.
- **Peer verification has gaps.** A few Unix targets have no peer-credential API wired up and fail open, leaving file permissions as the only gate. The shared-`/tmp` fallback allows pre-creation denial of service.
- **Release artifacts are unsigned**, though they carry build provenance and checksums.
- **Concept matching cost is lines × enabled concepts per burst**, which remains a denial-of-service item under load.

# Settings

Settings is the global panel for how gPTY looks and behaves. It has six tabs — System, Terminal, Appearance, Reasoning, Concepts, and About — and writes to `user://settings.json`.

## Opening, applying, resetting

Open it from the sidebar's Settings button or the command palette entry `settings`. Changes apply while you make them: the panel debounces edits for a fraction of a second, saves the settings file, and live panes re-read the values, so font size, colors, scrollback length, and FPS limits take effect without restarting.

Each tab ends with its own **Reset tab to defaults** button. The reset is scoped to that tab — resetting Appearance does not touch your shell command, and resetting Terminal does not restore the default colors.

Per-pane settings are a separate popup reached from a sidebar pane row or a pane's titlebar. They are described below; the tabs here are global.

## System

| Setting | Default | Values |
|---|---|---|
| Max FPS | Unlimited (`0`) | 60, 120, 144, 165, 240, Native (`-1`, follows the monitor), Unlimited |
| Window Mode | OS | OS, Windowed, Windowless |
| Check for updates on startup | On | On / Off |

`Native` asks the display server for its refresh rate and caps there; `Unlimited` removes the cap entirely. Window Mode is the same value as the sidebar's window-mode dropdown: `OS` keeps the operating system's window frame and hides gPTY's own titlebar, `Windowed` is a borderless window that draws gPTY's titlebar, and `Windowless` is fullscreen with that titlebar. The update check is a startup query only; it installs nothing on its own.

## Terminal

| Setting | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|
| Cursor shape | Block | Block, Underline, Beam |
| Cursor blink | On | On / Off |
| Blink speed | 0.5 s | 0.1–2.0 s, step 0.1 |
| Beam width | 2 px | 1–8 px |
| Underline height | 3 px | 1–8 px |
| Default size | 24 rows × 80 cols | rows 10–100, cols 40–200 |
| Scroll lines | 3 | 1–10 per wheel step |
| History lines | 10,000 | 100–100,000, step 100 |
| Shell | Platform default | Any command line |
| Environment | Empty | `KEY=value`, one per line |

These are the defaults for **new** terminals: a pane that already exists keeps the grid dimensions it was spawned with, though cursor and color changes are applied live. The default size is the initial terminal grid, not the pane's pixel size.

History lines caps how much scrollback each pane writes to the history database, which is also the text `Ctrl+Shift+F` searches. The tab shows an **On disk** readout for the history store; it is a snapshot taken when the panel opens, because the true size depends on how long the retained lines were, not just how many.

The shell field is the program a new terminal runs. On Linux and macOS it defaults to `/bin/bash`; on Windows to `%COMSPEC%`, falling back to `cmd.exe`. The environment box is the global environment for terminals, one `KEY=value` per line; it is separate from per-pane environment.

## Appearance

| Setting | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Font | `DejaVuSansMono.ttf` | Any `.ttf` |
| Font size | 14 px | 8–32 px |
| Color scheme | None | Optional `.txt`, `.json`, or `.csv` scheme file |
| Show titlebar | On | Per-pane title bars |

Below those, seven color pickers control the chrome: wrapper background, title-bar background, wrapper border, sidebar background, focus border, selection, and the scrollback indicator. The scheme file supplies the terminal's own palette; clearing it returns terminals to the built-in palette, which is applied live.

## Reasoning

| Setting | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|
| Max turns | 16 | 1–64 |
| Max turn bytes | 65,536 | 4,096–1,048,576, step 4,096 |

These bound the Reasoning pane's retained session: how many turns it keeps and how much text one turn may carry before it is cut. Lowering them trims what the pane keeps in memory.

## Concepts

This tab lists the concept rules that are active for the terminal engine, with a button to open the visual graph editor and a button to add a rule. Each row can be enabled or disabled and deleted. Concepts are covered in [[concepts]]; nothing here executes commands — rules capture and route display content.

## About

Version, the IPC protocol version gPTY speaks, and the repository address. The protocol number is useful when a CLI and a GUI from different builds disagree about the wire format.

## Global settings versus per-pane settings

| Scope | Where | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| Global | Settings panel, `user://settings.json` | Fonts, colors, terminal defaults, shell program, global environment, FPS, window mode |
| Per pane | Pane Settings popup, saved with the tile | Name, attachment id, font size, environment override, and type-specific view options |
| Workspace | Sidebar folder button, `user://workspaces.json` | Default directory inherited by new terminals |
| File-supplied | Layout or profile tile | Pane type, geometry, and a spawn plan (program and arguments) |
| Trust | Workspace Trust dialog, `user://trusted.json` | Approval memory for file-supplied spawn plans |

The Pane Settings popup is type-aware. For a terminal it edits the pane's name, public attachment id, font size, environment lines, cursor shape, blink and blink speed, cursor color, beam width, underline height, grid rows and columns, scroll lines, default foreground and background colors, font file, and color scheme. It does **not** edit the shell program, its arguments, tags, or a working directory — those come from the creation call, a layout tile, or a profile, and a file-supplied program or argument list is exactly what Workspace Trust gates. Clearing the environment box removes that pane's override, so it inherits the global environment again.

Per-pane environment is the one setting only you can supply. It is stored in `user://pane_env.json`, keyed by the pane's attachment id, and only the pane settings UI writes it. A saved layout or profile that carries environment has it stripped on restore with a notice; the file is never allowed to become spawn-time authority. Renaming a pane's attachment id moves its environment entry to the new key.

Two related files are not part of settings: `user://trusted.json` holds Workspace Trust approvals, and `user://workspaces.json` and `user://profiles.json` hold the arrangements. See [[workspace-trust]], [[workspace]], and [[profile]].

# Sidebar

The sidebar is the 180 px panel on the left of the window. It gives one place to switch window mode, spawn panes, change workspace, activate a profile, and operate on the pane you are looking at.

## Shape and collapse

The panel has a header with the gPTY title and a collapse arrow, then four sections in this order: window mode, workspaces, profiles, and panes. Between the window-mode row and the sections sit the Add Pane grid and three actions — Search, Settings, and Close All.

Collapsing shrinks the sidebar to a 20 px strip with a single expand button; the pane grid widens to take the space. `Ctrl+Shift+B` toggles it, and the arrow in the header or the expand button does the same. The collapsed state is not saved, so each run starts expanded.

The workspace and profile lists show at most five rows at full height and gain an inner scrollbar beyond that, so a long list cannot push the rest of the panel off-screen; the pane list takes the remaining height and scrolls. Row labels are clipped with an ellipsis rather than stretching the 180 px panel and clipping their neighbours.

## Window mode

The top dropdown switches how gPTY presents its window: `OS`, `Windowed`, or `Windowless`. This is the same setting as Window Mode in the Settings panel's System tab; changing either updates the other. `OS` keeps the operating system's window frame and hides gPTY's own titlebar, `Windowed` is a borderless window that draws gPTY's titlebar, and `Windowless` is fullscreen with that titlebar. The fullscreen shortcut toggles between the last two (see [[keyboard-shortcuts]]).

## Add Pane and the actions

`Add Pane` is a two-row grid of eight buttons, one per pane type: Terminal, Code Viewer, File Tree, Inspector, Reasoning, CLI View, Wiki, and Media. Tooltips name the type and, where one exists, its shortcut. Clicking a button spawns that pane into the active workspace using the same split rule as every other spawn: the largest tile halves along its longer axis, and the spawn is refused if the halves would fall below the 6-unit minimum. The new pane becomes active, and a terminal takes the keyboard.

Below it:

- **Search** opens the scrollback search bar on the active terminal (or the workspace's first terminal when a non-terminal is focused). Same as `Ctrl+Shift+F`.
- **Settings** opens the global settings panel described in [[settings]].
- **Close All** closes every pane in the active workspace. It asks before stopping running commands or discarding unsaved work; a Cancel leaves everything in place. Same as `Ctrl+Shift+R`.

## Workspaces

This section answers "which tab am I in". Its header has a `+` button that creates a workspace (up to eight), and each row has three parts:

- The **name** switches to that workspace on a click and begins an inline rename on a double-click. Enter or clicking away commits; Escape restores the old name. Names are trimmed to 32 characters and default to `Workspace`.
- The **folder button** opens a directory picker for that workspace's default directory. A set directory colours the button and appears in the tooltip; `Use default` clears it. New terminals spawned there inherit it, including terminals created by profile activation, but running shells are never moved. There is no per-pane directory setting.
- The **close button** appears only when more than one workspace exists. Closing asks the workspace's panes first and cannot close the last tab.

The active workspace is accented. Because the sidebar only ever shows the active workspace's panes, workspace rows are how you move between arrangements; see [[workspace]] for what a workspace owns.

## Profiles

Profiles are reusable tile sets. Clicking a row activates that profile into the active workspace, replacing its panes after a confirmation when the workspace is not empty. A profile row is accented while the active workspace was built from it, until the layout is reset or another profile is activated.

The header's `+` saves the current arrangement as a new profile; the dialog asks for a name and lets you edit each pane's command. A user profile can be renamed by double-clicking its row and deleted with its trash button. Built-in and plugin-provided profiles have no rename or delete: the built-in ships with the application and plugin profiles follow their plugin. A plugin row's tooltip names the plugin and revision it came from, and the section ends with a `More layouts →` row that opens the plugin registry in your browser. [[profile]] covers the sources, storage, and the trust check activation runs.

## Panes

The Panes section mirrors the active workspace's grid, one row per tile in tile order. It is a second way to reach each pane, and it stays useful when a pane is hidden by minimize.

A row has a label button (`T1`, `C1`, `F1`, and so on — the type's prefix plus a running number) followed by five icon buttons:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| Label | Focuses that pane; the row is accented when it is active |
| Minimize / Restore | Hides or shows the pane body; its grid tile and reserved space stay |
| Swap position | Opens a list of the other tiles and exchanges this pane's geometry with the chosen one |
| Change pane type | Opens a list of the eight pane types and rebuilds this tile as the chosen type |
| Pane settings | Opens the type-aware settings popup for that pane |
| Close | Closes that pane, after the running-work and unsaved-work questions |

The label is also the pane's public identity: `T3` is what the CLI and MCP tools accept when you target a pane. Changing the type destroys the old pane body, so it asks the same questions as closing one. Minimizing a terminal keeps its process running; the tile does not change, so restoring it puts it back exactly where it was.

## What the sidebar is not

It is not a settings panel and not a layout editor. Global look-and-feel lives in [[settings]], pane geometry is changed by dragging dividers or using swap position, and the arrangement itself is saved with the workspace. The sidebar shows the state; the workspace owns it.

# Workspace Trust

Workspace Trust is the consent dialog that stands between a saved file and a process. Restoring a layout, activating a profile — including one an installed plugin ships — can start programs; the dialog asks before a file decides something you did not.

## What a restore can run

A terminal tile's spawn is a program plus an argument array — never a shell string. Both come from the tile's saved settings:

| Key | Precedence |
|---|---|
| `command` | First choice |
| `shell` | Second choice |
| the tile's legacy `shell` | Last resort |
| `shell_args` | Appended arguments |

A tile is **untrusted** when its program differs from your current default shell command, or when it carries any non-empty `shell_args`. Both matter: a `shell`-only check once missed a tile that shipped `command` or an argv payload like `["-c", "…"]`. A tile that matches your defaults needs no prompt — restoring it starts what you would have started anyway.

The same keys gate `cli_view`, whose pane runs its argv directly. Installed plugin profiles go through the same gate, because their tiles are saved content too.

## When the dialog appears

The prompt appears when a restore would spawn a different program or extra arguments, on the paths where a user is present to answer:

- restoring the saved workspace set at startup, or reloading it with the palette's load action;
- activating a profile from the sidebar.

On the workspace path the dialog describes every affected workspace. Cancelling does not run the file's programs: the affected workspaces are rebuilt with their panes dropped, so the app opens without the untrusted spawns.

Over IPC, `layoutLoad` **refuses** an untrusted profile instead of prompting. A caller cannot answer a dialog, so naming a profile is not consent to what the file asks for. It loads only when the consent record already covers the content.

## The consent key

Consent is per spawn plan, not per file. The key is the exact program and argv joined in order, with a unit separator between parts — the same derivation the trust predicate uses, so the thing shown in the dialog, the thing stored, and the thing checked can never drift. A file that changes one argument is a new decision.

The dialog shows the plan rather than a summary sentence: which pane type, which program, which arguments. Values are escaped and length-capped because they are attacker-controlled file content, and newlines in particular would forge an extra dialog line.

## Who records consent

| Content | Approval recorded as | Invalidated by |
|---|---|---|
| Builtin profile | Profile name + app version + every tile's spawn plan | A new gPTY version, or tiles that changed under it |
| Installed plugin | Plugin id + pinned revision + the spawn plans the review listed | A new revision, or tiles that changed under it |
| User-authored profile | Nothing | — (asks each time) |

Only the trust dialogs' confirm paths write records. A user-authored profile never records consent, so approving one does not make the next activation silent. A builtin ships with the app, so its approval is tied to the version that shipped it: a new release re-prompts by construction. A plugin is approved at the revision the install pinned, so a moved tag or new commit re-prompts, and the plans the review listed are recorded with it so a different profile set at the same pin re-prompts too. The profile dialog can extend an already-approved revision's plans after showing the tiles, but only the install review approves a revision.

Provenance is gPTY's, not the file's. Every profile is stamped with where it was loaded from — the shipped defaults, the installed-plugin store, or your own `profiles.json` — and identity fields are stripped out of user entries on load. A hand-written entry that says `"builtin": true`, or carries an installed plugin's id and approved revision, is still your profile: its tiles go through the plan gate like any other, so it cannot borrow someone else's approval.

The store is `user://trusted.json`, with two namespaces: `builtins` mapping a name to a version and a list of plan keys, and `plugins` mapping an id to a revision and the plan keys the review listed. It is hand-editable, so it is read like any other untrusted file: typed reads, shape checks, and caps on entries, name and version lengths, plan counts, and key length. A record written before plugin plans existed (an id mapped straight to a revision) still approves that revision and covers no plans, so such a plugin's profiles ask once more. A bad entry costs itself, not the file.

That also describes revocation: remove the entry — or delete the file — and the next launch reads a store with no record, so the next restore asks again. The store is a memory of approvals, not a lock.

## Why environment is not a file decision

Environment reaches a child as authority, not configuration. A saved tile's `shell_env` is dropped on restore with a notice naming what was dropped; it never reaches a spawn, so there is no env clause in the trust predicate and nothing to show in the dialog.

Per-pane environment is yours: it lives in `user://pane_env.json`, keyed by the pane's stable id, written only by the pane settings UI, and applied at spawn over your global environment. A file cannot supply it. The environment a pane still inherits is the GUI's own — that is a real boundary and is covered in [[security-model|Security Model]].

## Limits

The gate is about **what runs**, not about what a program then does. After you approve, gPTY runs what the file asks for, with your permissions, in a shell that can drive the rest of the workspace. The dialog exists so that decision is explicit, not so it is harmless. Approvals are also per machine and per user; copying `trusted.json` to another machine carries your decisions with it.

# Workspace

A workspace is a tab that holds its own layout. Switching tabs changes which panes you see and type into; the other workspaces keep their panes alive in the background.

## What a workspace is

Every window has at least one workspace and at most eight. Each one owns a grid, a set of tiles, and a default working directory. Panes are not shared between workspaces: a terminal in one tab is a different process from a terminal in another, and closing a workspace closes the panes it contains.

The sidebar lists them in its Workspaces section, with the active one accented. Clicking a row switches to it; double-clicking the name edits it in place (Enter or clicking away commits, Escape cancels). The add button creates one, and the close button appears only when more than one exists, because the last workspace cannot be closed.

Rows show the workspace's name and, when one is set, its directory; hovering explains the directory. The profile accent is per workspace — activating a profile in one workspace does not light that row while another workspace is active.

## Creating, switching, closing

A new workspace starts blank: gPTY does not auto-spawn a terminal, so you decide what fills it. It inherits the current workspace's default directory, the way a new terminal tab usually starts where you are, and you can point it elsewhere afterwards.

Switching keeps every pane in the previous workspace running. Only the visible grid is processed, so hidden terminals do not redraw, but their shells and programs continue. The workspace set is saved to disk on each switch, so a crash loses at most the current tab's latest change.

Closing a workspace asks its panes first — a running command raises one confirmation for the whole set, and a pane with unsaved work (such as a wiki note) can cancel the close. When it proceeds, the workspace's panes are torn down and its grid freed. Closing a non-active workspace does not change which tab you are looking at.

Switching also has shortcuts: `Ctrl+PageDown` moves to the next workspace and `Ctrl+PageUp` to the previous one, clamped at the ends.

## The default directory

Each workspace can carry a default directory, chosen through the folder button on its sidebar row. The picker offers `Use default` to clear it. A cleared or never-set directory means new terminals start wherever gPTY itself starts, which is the older behavior.

The directory applies to terminals spawned **after** the change — including terminals created by activating a profile — and never moves a shell that is already running, so it cannot disturb work in progress. A directory is accepted only as an absolute path; gPTY warns and keeps the old value when the path is relative, missing, or carries control characters. Panes like the file tree and wiki pane may open where the workspace points, but the terminal is the setting's main surface.

Because a profile is a layout template rather than a workspace, the directory is stored on the workspace instance, not on the profile. Activating the same profile in two workspaces can therefore produce terminals in two different directories.

## Persistence

The whole set lives in `user://workspaces.json` under `version`, `active`, and `workspaces`. Each workspace entry stores its sanitized name (at most 32 characters, defaulting to `Workspace`), its `cwd`, and its layout array. The layout is the tile geometry described in [[layout]]; the workspace is the container around it.

On startup gPTY loads the store, clamps the active index into range, and rebuilds every workspace. If the store is missing or empty, a legacy `user://layout.json` is imported as a single workspace named `Workspace 1`; that migration exists so older installs keep their arrangement.

If a saved tile would start a different program or pass extra arguments compared with your configured shell, the restore pauses at a Workspace Trust dialog listing what the file asks to run. Cancel rebuilds the workspaces with their panes emptied but their names and directories kept. Approvals are remembered per exact spawn plan, so an arrangement you already approved does not ask again. See [[workspace-trust]].

## Workspace, layout, profile

| Term | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| Workspace | Which tab am I in, and where do its terminals start? |
| Layout | What panes are arranged how inside this tab? |
| Profile | Which reusable tile set can I copy into a tab? |
| Pane | Which single unit am I typing into? |

A workspace is not a layout: the layout is a detail inside it. Nor is it a profile: a profile can be activated into any workspace and replaces that workspace's panes, while the workspace keeps its name and directory. Saving the current arrangement under a name creates a profile, not a second workspace.

# Pane

A pane is the visible unit of a gPTY workspace. It has two layers — a **tile** that owns geometry and chrome, and a **body** that owns content — and the body is what most people mean when they say "pane".

Panes are the reason the app is not just a terminal window: every body is a first-class UI surface, and every body is addressable through the same public API.

## The two layers

A tile is a cell in the tiling grid. It knows its `col`, `row`, `cspan`, and `rspan` in the 60-unit layout grid, draws the titlebar around the body, and carries the minimize, position, type, settings, and close controls. `terminal_manager.gd` owns tile lifecycle: spawn, split, swap, drag, and close.

A body is a Godot `Control` that extends `PaneBody`. It paints the content, handles its own keyboard and mouse input, and implements the settings UI for its type. The body is created from the registry in `PaneTypes.ALL`; the type key is also what the Rust side understands, so the Python-like seam between GDScript and Rust is one vocabulary rather than two.

| Layer | Owns | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Tile | Geometry, titlebar, focus border, close/minimize, settings button | a terminal and a wiki pane can have the same tile |
| Body | Content, input, per-type settings, status document | `terminal_pane.gd`, `wiki_pane.gd`, `media_pane.gd` |

When a layout is saved, it stores both: the tile's geometry and the body's sanitized settings. A profile does the same for a set of tiles.

## The eight pane types

| Type key | Body | Open with | Use it for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `terminal` | [[terminal-pane]] | `Ctrl+Shift+N`, sidebar, palette, API | A shell, a TUI, an agent CLI |
| `code_viewer` | [[code-viewer]] | `Ctrl+Shift+D`, palette, file tree, API | Reading a file without leaving gPTY |
| `file_tree` | [[file-tree]] | `Ctrl+Shift+T`, palette, API | Browsing a directory and opening files |
| `inspector` | [[inspector]] | `Ctrl+Shift+O`, palette, API | Private, read-only Q&A about what you see |
| `reasoning` | [[reasoning]] | Palette, profile, API | Watching an agent's lifecycle events |
| `cli_view` | [[cli-view]] | Palette, API, plugin profile | Streaming a command's stdout without a PTY |
| `wiki` | [[wiki-pane]] | Palette, API, profile | Browsing and editing a Markdown vault |
| `media` | [[media-pane]] | Palette, API, file tree | Playing a local audio or video file |

The registry also supplies the display name, icon, label prefix, and creation shortcut. `inspector` and `reasoning` split what an older build called Observer; a saved Observer tile is migrated on load, not rejected.

## Opening a pane

Every door ends at the same spawn path, so validation and trust behave the same way regardless of how the pane was requested:

- The sidebar's `+` control and its pane rows.
- The command palette (`Ctrl+Shift+P`, then `new <type>`).
- The CLI: `gpty new-pane --pane-type wiki`, or MCP `new-pane`.
- A workspace layout, a profile, or a plugin-provided profile.
- Another pane, when it routes a file: the file tree opens supported files in a viewer or media pane.

A pane never spawns another pane directly. A body that needs one emits `request_pane`, and the workspace — the only spawner — answers. That is what keeps layout and trust policy in one place.

## Identity

Each pane has a display label and an attachment ID.

- The label is a prefix plus a number: `T1` for terminal, `C1` for code viewer, `F1` file tree, `I1` inspector, `R1` reasoning, `V1` CLI view, `W1` wiki, `M1` media.
- The attachment ID is the stable identifier the control API uses. It follows `[a-z][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}`, defaults to a generated `pane-xxxxxxxx`, and can be set in **Pane Settings**. The API accepts `"active"` where a pane is expected, meaning the focused pane.
- Tags are lowercase identifiers attached at creation (`gpty new-pane --tags ci,backend`) and used by `broadcast` to address several panes at once. They follow the same pattern and are not edited in Pane Settings.
- A terminal also receives `GPTY_ENV=1`, `GPTY_PANE_ID`, and the event-socket credentials in its environment, which is how a program inside the pane can address the workspace.

Duplicate attachment IDs are regenerated at spawn. They would otherwise make `inject`, `pane-read`, `pane-status`, `pane-wait`, `kill-pane`, and `focus-pane` silently act on the wrong pane.

## What a pane can be asked to do

The control API addresses panes, not windows. See [[control-api]] for the full method table.

| Question | Method |
|---|---|
| What panes exist? | `listPanes` |
| Focus or close one? | `focusPane`, `killPane` |
| Type into a terminal? | `inject` |
| Read what it shows? | `paneRead` (screen plus scrollback, 1–2000 lines) |
| Is its process still running? | `paneStatus` |
| Run a command and watch it? | `paneRun`, then `paneWait` |
| Talk to every tagged pane at once? | `broadcast` |

`paneRun` opens a **new** terminal pane; it does not reuse the target's shell. `paneRead` is a snapshot, not a stream. `paneWait` matches a Rust regular expression against recent output and holds the request open until the pattern matches or the deadline passes.

## Routed content

Some panes accept content routed by a concept. The receiver set is explicit: `code_viewer` and `inspector` declare `receives_content`, and every other type does not. A concept action names one of those types; if no receiver is open, the captured bytes replay into the terminal that produced them instead of vanishing.

Concepts are display-only. They can choose which pane shows captured output; they cannot write into a shell. See [[concepts]] and [[capture]].

## Pane settings

The **Pane Settings** popup is type-aware. For a terminal it edits the name, attachment ID, font size, environment, cursor shape and blink, grid rows and columns, scroll lines, default foreground and background, font file, and color scheme. The wiki pane adds its vault path and view mode; the media pane adds its volume and loop state.

Two things it does **not** edit: the shell program and argv, and tags. A pane's program comes from its tile settings in a profile or layout, or from the creation call (`gpty new-pane -c ... --arg ...`); tags come from creation. The working directory is a workspace-level default inherited by new terminals, not a per-pane field.

Per-pane environment is the exception that is user-owned: it is edited in Pane Settings, stored in `user://pane_env.json` keyed by attachment ID, and never adopted from a layout or profile file. A file that carries `shell_env` has it stripped on restore with a notice.

## Closing and restoring

Closing a pane asks when a command is still running in it; a terminal with a foreground job is not removed by a single click. A wiki pane with unsaved text uses the same leave guard as its Back button. Closing every pane in a workspace is **Close All** in the sidebar (also `Ctrl+Shift+R`), and it asks once for the workspace.

Tiles are restored from the workspace's saved layout on startup, and a layout or profile that would spawn a different program or argv goes through [[workspace-trust]] first. A pane whose configured program is the child (a full-screen tool) reports that state through the same status document as any other terminal.

# CLI View Pane

A CLI view pane runs one program with an argument vector and shows its merged output as plain text lines. It is the "plugin UI v1" pane: a third-party command gets a home inside gPTY without being handed a terminal, a shell, or any Godot surface.

## What it is

The body is `CliViewPane` (`godot/scenes/panes/cli_view_pane.gd`); the registered type key is `cli_view` and its label prefix is `V`. The process itself belongs to the Rust extension class `GptyCliView` and the core `gpty_core::cli` module — the script is only the view, plus the Stop and Restart buttons.

The distinction from a [[terminal-pane|Terminal Pane]] is deliberate and structural: there is no PTY and no grid. A CLI view runs a line producer, so lines are the whole contract. The command is always `program` plus `args`, never a shell string, so a saved tile cannot smuggle in shell syntax and a plugin manifest cannot turn a display pane into a shell.

## When to use it

Use it for a tool that prints a report and exits, or streams log-ish output: a build watcher, a formatter in check mode, a status command, a plugin's front end. It is the pane a plugin action opens when the plugin's job is "show me this CLI's output".

Do not use it for anything interactive. There is no input path at all — the child's stdin is `/dev/null` — so a program that prompts will read end-of-file rather than your answer. For prompts, full-screen output, colours and cursor movement, use a terminal pane.

## How to open it

| Method | Action |
|---|---|
| Sidebar | the CLI view button |
| Palette | `new cli view` |
| CLI | `gpty new-pane -t cli_view -c <program> --arg <value>` |
| MCP | the `new-pane` tool with `type: "cli_view"`, `command`, `args` |
| Layout/profile | a saved tile restores `command` and `shell_args` |

The pane has no keyboard shortcut. A pane created without a command stays idle and says so; set the program in Pane Settings and press Restart. Applying settings never restarts the child by itself — the panel re-applies on every keystroke, and relaunching a tool per keystroke is not a preview — so a changed plan shows "Command changed — Restart to apply".

## What it shows and how it is driven

stdout and stderr are merged into one queue of complete lines; two reader threads feed it, and the pane drains the whole queue once per frame. A header row carries the status text and the two buttons:

| Control | Effect |
|---|---|
| Status | `Idle`, `Running (pid N)`, `Exited (code)`, `Stopped`, or the start error |
| Restart | starts the program, replacing a live child |
| Stop | kills the child and its process group |

The status label is written on transitions only. A restart keeps the existing output — this is a log view, and the next run continues it rather than erasing what the previous one printed. The view follows the bottom only while you are already at the bottom, so scrolling up to read an earlier line is not yanked back down by the next one.

Backpressure is the design, not a side effect. The Rust queue holds up to 512 complete lines; when it is full the readers stop reading, the pipes fill, and the child's write blocks. Nothing is dropped while the process runs. A line with no newline is split at 16 KiB so a byte dump cannot grow the buffer without a ceiling, and the GUI keeps the newest 4,000 lines it has drained, re-rendering only when it trims.

`paneRead` works on this pane: its answer is the drained text, not the status label. `paneStatus` returns the process document with `program`, `args`, `pid`, `running`, `exit_code` and `exit_reason`.

## Settings that matter

| Setting | What it changes |
|---|---|
| Name | the pane's title |
| Font size | 8–32 px |
| Program | the executable to run: a bare name is resolved through `PATH`, an absolute path must pass the executable gate |
| Arguments | the argv, shown space-joined |

The arguments field renders the argv joined by spaces, which cannot represent an argument containing a space. The pane therefore keeps the original argv and only re-parses the field when you actually edit it, so changing the font size cannot fragment an argument that contains whitespace.

## What it does not do

It does not use a shell: `>` redirection, `&&`, globs and quotes are not interpreted, so `-c "a && b"` reaches the program as one argument. It does not emulate a terminal: no grid, no alternate screen, no colour interpretation. It does not accept input, and it does not merge the child into the pane's process — closing the pane stops the child and its process group, which is the only thing that kills it.

It also does not hand the child the workspace credentials. The spawn strips the inherited control-socket keys (`GPTY_SECRET`, `GPTY_SOCKET` and the rest of the stripped set) from the child environment, because a tile is not a reason to hand a third-party CLI the ability to control the workspace. An absolute program is additionally held to the terminal's executable rule — regular file, owned by you or root, not group- or other-writable — while a bare name is resolved through `PATH`, as shipped profiles do.

## Limits and edge cases

One child at a time, one command per pane. Output is retained up to 4,000 lines in the view; older lines are dropped from the pane even though the child's own backpressure already bounded what was in flight. Starting a command that is not found or fails the executable gate reports the error in the status row instead of leaving the pane silent. Because the command is pane state, restoring a tile that names a program is a spawn plan and passes through Workspace Trust on restore.

# Code Viewer Pane

A code viewer pane shows a file's text read-only, with basic syntax colouring, and renders Markdown as formatted prose. It is the pane the file tree opens supported files into, and the pane concepts route command output to.

## What it is

The body is `CodeViewerPane` (`godot/scenes/panes/code_viewer.gd`). It holds two widgets behind one toolbar: a read-only `CodeEdit` for source, and the shared sanitized `MarkdownView` for rendered prose. The registered type key is `code_viewer`, its label prefix is `C`, and it is one of the two pane types that accept routed concept content.

The pane is a viewer, not an editor. There is no save path and no writable state: the file's bytes are read once on open, and the only way to see a newer version is the toolbar's **Reload** button. That is a deliberate trade — the pane's scroll position, selection and rendered/source mode belong to its document, so it is stable while you read.

## When to use it

Use it to read source, config, logs, diffs, or documentation without leaving gPTY. It is also what `cat`-style captures and `git diff` output land in when a concept routes to a code viewer, which makes it the usual place to inspect what a command produced.

For a directory listing use [[file-tree|File Tree]]; for a vault of Markdown notes with editing, links and search, use the [[wiki-pane|Wiki Pane]].

## How to open it

| Method | Action |
|---|---|
| Shortcut | `Ctrl+Shift+D` |
| Sidebar | the code viewer button |
| Palette | `new code viewer` |
| CLI | `gpty new-pane -t code_viewer` |
| MCP | the `new-pane` tool with `type: "code_viewer"` |
| From a pane | activating a supported file in the file tree |
| A concept | any enabled concept whose action targets the code viewer (`cat_command` and `git_diff` ship this way) |

A pane opened from the CLI or API starts empty; the file it should display is pane state, set through Pane Settings or a saved layout tile. A file tree request for a path this workspace already shows in a viewer focuses that pane instead of opening a second copy, because a duplicate would split the scroll and mode state across two panes.

Panes do not spawn panes directly: the file tree emits a request and the workspace decides whether to create a pane or focus an existing one.

## What it shows and how it is driven

The file is read through one shared gate: the path must be absolute, must be a regular file (Godot's regular-file check rejects directories, devices and FIFOs before the GUI thread blocks on an open), and at most 1 MiB is read. A read that hits the cap still displays, with a truncation notice — appended to the text in source view, and shown as a banner above the body in rendered view.

Syntax colouring is deliberately shallow: comment delimiters are registered for `gd`/`py` (`#`) and `rs`/`c`/`cpp`/`h`/`hpp` (`//`), so those files edit and read with sensible comments highlighted; the pane does not ship a full grammar per language.

Markdown gets a second mode. When the language resolves to `md` or `markdown` — from the `language` setting or the file extension — a toolbar toggle appears:

| Stored `view_mode` | What you see |
|---|---|
| `auto` (the default) | Markdown rendered; everything else as source |
| `rendered` | Markdown rendered |
| `source` | the raw Markdown text |

The toggle reads **View source** while rendered and **Render Markdown** while in source. Rendering goes through the same sanitized pipeline the wiki uses: raw HTML and BBCode are escaped, images reduce to alt text, and only `http`/`https`/`mailto` links are kept as links. Nothing in a Markdown file can execute.

When a concept delivers a capture, `receive_content` replaces the pane's text and clears its `file_path` — the pane now shows the capture, not a file, so a later request to open a file must not focus a viewer that no longer displays it. The captured text is the whole document; the only cap that applies is the renderer's own, and it reports itself.

## Settings that matter

| Setting | Values |
|---|---|
| Name | the pane's title |
| Font size | 8–32 px |
| File | absolute path of the file to show |
| Language | `(auto)`, `md`, `gd`, `py`, `rs`, `c`, `cpp`, `h`, `js`, `ts` |
| View | `Auto`, `Source`, `Rendered` |

`Auto` means "render if this is Markdown, otherwise source". Language is only used to decide Markdown-ness and is not a highlighter selection beyond the comment delimiters above.

## What it does not do

It does not edit or save files. It does not open arbitrary binaries: from the file tree, only extensions in the closed `ViewableFiles` table (source, config/data, docs/prose extensions plus a handful of extensionless names such as `Makefile` and `Dockerfile`) are routed here, and anything else keeps the confirm-then-system-handler path. It does not watch the file for changes — Reload is explicit, which also means a file that was moved or replaced by a directory clears the pane instead of showing stale text as if it were current. It does not render images or play media; that is the [[media-pane|Media Pane]].

## Limits and edge cases

Reads are capped at 1 MiB and happen on the GUI thread, so a pathologically large file costs the first MiB, not the whole file. The truncation notice is how you know. A capture arriving while a file is open replaces the document permanently — reopening the file is a new pane request. Saved layouts record `file_path`, `language` and `view_mode`, so a viewer reopens on the same file in the same mode.

# File Tree Pane

A file tree pane browses a directory and opens what you activate into the right in-app pane: text into the [[code-viewer|Code Viewer]], media into the [[media-pane|Media Pane]], everything else through the system's default handler after a confirmation.

## What it is

The body is `FileTreePane` (`godot/scenes/panes/file_tree.gd`), a thin wrapper around one Godot `Tree`. The registered type key is `file_tree` and its label prefix is `F`. It is a browser, not a file manager: it lists a single root and its subdirectories, and it hands paths to other panes.

Its main job is to keep you inside gPTY. Activating a source file does not launch an editor; activating a video does not launch a desktop player. The tree decides by two closed tables — `ViewableFiles` for text and `MediaFiles` for media — so the same extension always goes to the same place.

## When to use it

Use it when you want to look around the workspace directory, open a specific file in a viewer, or pull a recording into the media pane. Use the [[terminal-pane|Terminal Pane]] for `ls`, `git status` and anything that changes files; this pane cannot.

## How to open it

| Method | Action |
|---|---|
| Shortcut | `Ctrl+Shift+T` |
| Sidebar | the file tree button |
| Palette | `new file tree` |
| CLI | `gpty new-pane -t file_tree` |
| MCP | the `new-pane` tool with `type: "file_tree"` |
| Layout/profile | a saved tile with `type: "file_tree"` restores its root and open mode |

A fresh pane starts at `/`. The CLI and the `new-pane` tool have no root parameter — the root is pane state, set in Pane Settings or carried by a saved layout tile. The workspace's directory setting does not retarget an existing tree.

## What it shows and how it is driven

The tree shows the root's direct entries and grows on demand: activating a directory lists its children the first time and then expands or collapses it. Nothing below the root is read until you ask for it, so pointing a tree at a large directory costs one listing.

Entries whose names begin with `.` are skipped at every level, so `.git`, `.env` and editor state directories never appear. Only one directory's worth of names is held per expanded node; there is no search box and no filter.

Activating a file goes through one of three routes:

| File kind | Route |
|---|---|
| extension in `ViewableFiles` | a `code_viewer` pane request with `file_path` |
| extension in `MediaFiles` | a `media` pane request with `file_path` |
| anything else | a confirmation dialog, then the system handler with a `file://` URI |

The open mode is per tree, not global. **Viewer pane** is the default and enables the first two routes; **System application** keeps the confirm-then-open path even for files the viewer could show. A file the tables do not name always stays on the system path, because the in-app route is an allowlist rather than content sniffing — a downloaded `script.desktop` is never "viewed" as text, and it is never opened without you seeing its exact path first.

Directories and files are both validated at activation: a path that is no longer a regular file produces a warning toast instead of a handler call, and a non-absolute path is refused outright. Panes do not spawn panes; the tree emits a request and the workspace creates the viewer or media pane (or focuses the one already showing that path).

## Settings that matter

| Setting | What it changes |
|---|---|
| Name | the pane's title |
| Font size | 8–32 px |
| Root path | absolute directory to list; changing it clears and re-lists |
| Open files | `Viewer pane` or `System application` |

The root is validated at use — an empty, relative or missing path simply lists nothing. A saved layout records `root_path` and `open_in`; an unknown `open_in` value from a file falls back to the default rather than leaving the pane with neither route authoritative.

## What it does not do

It does not rename, delete, move, copy or create files. It does not show hidden entries, so there is no toggle to reveal them. It does not recurse eagerly or index the tree for search. It does not open a file into an existing viewer pointed at another file — a second view is a deliberate layout choice, made by opening another viewer pane.

## Limits and edge cases

Only absolute paths are ever opened, and only regular files reach a handler; this is why a FIFO or device node that appears in a listing produces a refusal rather than hanging the GUI thread. The system route constructs the `file://` URI itself and shows the exact path in a confirmation, which is the guard against a filename that looks like another scheme. Because listing is lazy, a directory that changes after it was expanded is not refreshed — children stay as first read. Re-applying the root path in Pane Settings rebuilds the tree from disk.

# Inspector Pane

An Inspector pane is a private, read-only question-and-answer session: you ask, a model answers, and the exchange stays in that pane. It is not the agent running in your terminal, and it does not follow that conversation.

## What it is

The body is `InspectorPane` (`godot/scenes/panes/inspector_pane.gd`); the registered type key is `inspector` and its label prefix is `I`. It owns exactly one in-memory session through the `gpty-ai` crate, which speaks to a backend and hands envelopes back to GDScript for display.

The point is the fence around it. The session is opened tool-free, so an answer cannot run a command, edit a file, or reach the workspace through a tool. It is also private: it is a different process with its own prompt history from the omp session in a terminal pane, even when both use the same model. The default `omp` backend is launched as `omp --mode rpc --no-session --no-tools --no-extensions --no-skills --no-rules`, which is the flag set that makes "no tools, no workspace rules, no stored session" true rather than aspirational.

## When to use it

Use it to ask about something you are looking at without derailing the terminal agent: paste an error, ask what a flag does, get a short explanation. Because it is read-only and tool-free, it is also the safe place to ask about untrusted text — the answer can describe a suspicious file but cannot act on it.

Use the [[reasoning|Reasoning Pane]] if you want to *watch* what the terminal agent is thinking. Use the terminal if you want an agent that can actually do work.

## How to open it

| Method | Action |
|---|---|
| Shortcut | `Ctrl+Shift+O` |
| Sidebar | the inspector button |
| Palette | `new inspector` |
| CLI | `gpty new-pane -t inspector` |
| MCP | the `new-pane` tool with `type: "inspector"` |
| Profile | the shipped **Agent Workspace** includes one |

Saved layouts that predate the split of the old observer pane are migrated: an `observer` tile with the answer stream becomes an inspector tile. A pane opened through the CLI or API starts with the default backend; everything else is pane settings.

## What it shows and how it is driven

The pane is a single column: a status line, an optional thinking area, the answer, and a prompt field. Type a question and press Enter.

While a turn runs, the status reads `Inspecting via <backend>…`. Reasoning text, when the backend emits it, streams into a separate area above the answer so the two do not interleave; the answer itself renders as Markdown through the shared sanitized view. Cancelling a turn stops it; closing the pane ends the session.

Backends:

| Backend | What runs |
|---|---|
| `omp` | one long-lived, tool-free omp RPC process per session — the default |
| `cli` | a subprocess NDJSON bridge: your adapter command is started per prompt, argv only, never through a shell |
| `mock` | a deterministic local pass-through, used by tests and offline work |

The CLI bridge contract is one JSON request line in for a prompt and JSON event lines out (`thinking`, `delta`, `done`, `error`, `status`). Adapters translate a tool's documented hooks; nothing scrapes a TUI and nothing counts tokens.

A capture routed from a terminal concept can reach the pane only when you enable **Accept terminal concept captures**. That gate is off by default and is the whole security story of the feature: a capture is terminal output, and delivering it means that text leaves the pane and goes to a model. With the gate on, captures queue in the pane; **Auto-run** decides whether a capture starts a turn immediately, and **Run on last capture** replays the most recent one by hand. Auto-run is off by default and never survives a restore: a capture that arrives on a freshly restored pane waits for you.

## Settings that matter

| Setting | What it changes |
|---|---|
| Name, Attachment ID | title and stable id |
| Font size | 8–32 px |
| Backend | `omp`, `cli`, `mock` |
| Model | optional model passed to the backend |
| Command | the `cli` backend's adapter argv (whitespace-split, no shell) |
| Auto-run | whether a capture starts a turn immediately (per session, off by default) |
| Accept terminal concept captures | the opt-in gate for routed output (per session) |
| System prompt | replaces the default inspector prompt (per session) |

The three rows that decide what a capture becomes — Auto-run, Accept terminal concept captures and System prompt — are per-session state, not part of the layout. A restored pane starts with captures and auto-run off and no prompt, and a profile, layout or workspace file cannot set any of them: only the pane panel can, and a file that names them has those keys ignored with a notice. A prompt you type is therefore a session note, so keep anything you want to reuse somewhere outside gPTY for now.

Changing the backend, model, system prompt or CLI command closes the session, so the next prompt opens one under the new configuration.

## What it does not do

It does not attach to the OMP conversation hosted in a terminal, and it does not read terminal output on its own — a terminal session can be busy for an hour and this pane will not show a word of it. It does not use tools, skills, extensions or workspace rules, and it does not write anything to disk. Its session is in-memory: closing the pane ends it, and there is no transcript to reopen.

## Limits and edge cases

One session per pane, so a second Inspector is a second conversation with its own history. The `omp` backend needs `omp` on `PATH`; a stale extension build reports that the bridge is missing and asks for a rebuild rather than failing silently. The thinking area is not a log — it is the current turn's reasoning. Captures are gated per pane, so enabling the opt-in on one Inspector does not enable it on another, and a restore turns it back off. Because captures leave the pane, treat that toggle as a data-sharing decision, not a display preference.

# Media Pane

A media pane plays one local audio or video file: video as a letterboxed surface, audio through a generated stream, with its own play, pause, seek and loop controls.

## What it is

The body is `MediaPane` (`godot/scenes/panes/media_pane.gd`); the registered type key is `media` and its label prefix is `M`. It is the eighth pane type and the only one that decodes anything: video frames arrive as textures, audio as samples, both from the pinned FFmpeg backend in the `gpty-media` crate.

A media pane is a path carrier. It holds an absolute local file path, and the path is validated at the moment it is used, not when it was stored. Nothing about a path is trusted: it may have come from a saved layout or a profile, which are files.

## When to use it

Use it to check a screen recording, watch a reference clip, or listen to a voice memo without leaving the workspace. Use the [[file-tree|File Tree]] to reach the file — activating a supported media file there opens this pane — or point the pane at a path yourself.

For still images there is no image pane; the file tree hands them to the system handler after confirmation. This pane plays containers with audio and/or video streams, not pictures.

## How to open it

| Method | Action |
|---|---|
| Sidebar | the media button |
| Palette | `new media` |
| CLI | `gpty new-pane -t media` |
| MCP | the `new-pane` tool with `type: "media"` |
| From a pane | activating a supported media file in the file tree |
| Layout/profile | a saved tile restores its file and transport settings |

A fresh pane opens empty and shows a placeholder asking for a path in Pane Settings. The file is pane state, so the CLI and API cannot name it; the file tree route passes it in the pane request. Opening the same file that an existing media pane already holds focuses that pane instead of starting a second decode — two panes on one file would double both the sound and the work.

## What it shows and how it is driven

Video is drawn into a texture with aspect-preserving fit, so a clip narrower or wider than the pane is letterboxed rather than stretched. Presentation is clocked against audio playback position when there is audio, and against a monotonic start clock otherwise, so a decoder that runs faster than real time does not play the file several times too fast.

Audio is decoded to interleaved 32-bit float and pushed into Godot's audio generator at 48 kHz stereo by default. Video and audio share one session; only the streams the pane will actually drain are opened, because an unconsumed queue is backpressure and would stall the other stream.

The transport bar appears under the content:

| Control | Effect |
|---|---|
| Play / Pause | toggles playback at the current position |
| Seek slider | drag to seek; the seek is acknowledged by the backend before playback continues |
| Time label | position and duration (`0:00 / 0:00`) |
| Loop | replays from the start at end of stream; stored with the tile |

`paneStatus` reports the pane through the shared status document: `kind` (`video` or `audio`), `file`, backend `state`, `position_us`, `duration_us`, `paused`, `loop`, `volume_db` and `muted`. A pane with no file (or no backend) reports `null` rather than disappearing from the pane list.

## Formats

The pane's table is closed. Anything outside it is refused with a message that names the supported set.

| Kind | Extensions |
|---|---|
| Video | `.mp4` `.m4v` `.mov` `.mkv` `.webm` `.avi` `.ts` `.m2ts` `.ogv` |
| Audio | `.ogg` `.oga` `.opus` `.mp3` `.wav` `.flac` `.m4a` `.aac` |

The backend decodes H.264, H.265, VP8/VP9, AV1 and Theora video. The list is an allowlist, not a sniff: the extension decides, so the same file always takes the same route and an unknown extension never reaches a decoder.

## Settings that matter

| Setting | What it changes |
|---|---|
| Name | the pane's title |
| Font size | the placeholder and status text |
| File | absolute path of the media to play |
| Volume | −40 dB to +6 dB, in 0.5 dB steps |
| Mute | silences output without changing the volume value |

Volume, mute, loop and the file path are saved with the tile. The panel re-applies its whole dictionary on every keystroke, so only a path that actually changed restarts the decode; editing the name does not interrupt the clip.

## What it does not do

It does not open remote media. A path containing `://` is refused as a remote URL, and `res://` and `user://` are refused as project schemes rather than local files. The FFmpeg build compiles no network protocols, so even a crafted stream is not a network client. It never loads a path through `ResourceLoader`, which is what would otherwise let a `.gd` or `.tscn` renamed to a media extension be loaded as code.

It also does not play playlists, burn in subtitles, or provide frame stepping; the transport is the four controls above.

## Limits and edge cases

The path is refused if it is empty, a `res://`/`user://` project scheme, or any URL containing `://`; otherwise it must be absolute, carry a known extension, and name a regular file, so a FIFO or device node cannot reach a decoder. The pane holds one session and one file. Long file names are ellipsized in the placeholder at 120 characters — the settings row still shows the full path. Closing the pane stops the decode; there is no background playback without a pane.

# Reasoning Pane

A reasoning pane is a passive window onto an agent's lifecycle: it shows the reasoning an OMP session reports, turn by turn, without running the agent or reading the terminal's screen.

## What it is

The body is `ReasoningPane` (`godot/scenes/panes/reasoning_pane.gd`); the registered type key is `reasoning` and its label prefix is `R`. It listens to semantic events from one terminal in its own workspace, identified by that terminal's stable `attachment_id` (the default source is `omp-terminal`), and projects them into a scroll of foldable turns. Delivery is workspace-scoped: the dispatcher resolves the emitting PTY by its session id and hands the event only to receivers in that terminal's workspace, so activating the same profile in two workspaces keeps each Reasoning pane on its own terminal.

The important word is *reported*. The pane never starts an agent, never sends it a prompt, and never scrapes the TUI. It only displays events the agent publishes through gPTY's event socket. When nothing publishes, the pane is a status line explaining what to link.

## When to use it

Use it next to a terminal running omp to watch what the agent is doing between tool calls — the reasoning stream, the turn boundaries, whether a session has settled. Use the [[inspector|Inspector Pane]] when you want to ask your own questions privately. Use the terminal itself when you want to interact with the agent.

Both panes are in the shipped **Agent Workspace** profile alongside a terminal, which is the arrangement they were designed for: one terminal as the work surface, one Inspector for side questions, one Reasoning for the running commentary.

## How to open it

| Method | Action |
|---|---|
| Sidebar | the reasoning button |
| Palette | `new reasoning` |
| CLI | `gpty new-pane -t reasoning` |
| MCP | the `new-pane` tool with `type: "reasoning"` |
| Profile | the shipped **Agent Workspace** |

The pane has no keyboard shortcut of its own. It has no chat field: everything it shows arrives from the event stream, so `new reasoning` followed by linking the extension is the whole setup.

## Setting it up

The pane needs two things a fresh install does not have by default: the bundled OMP extension and the event socket it forwards to. The pane's idle status spells out the steps:

```bash
omp plugin link <gpty>/extensions/gpty-omp-events
```

Then restart omp in the terminal it should observe. Inside that terminal, `echo $GPTY_EVENT_PROTOCOL` should print `1` — the variable is set per PTY when the shell spawns, along with the event socket path and a per-terminal capability that gates who may publish.

The event listener is a second socket beside the control socket: `gpty-events.sock` on Unix and `\\.\pipe\gpty-events` on Windows. The implementation is platform-neutral, and the extension and listener are exercised on Windows by the project's smoke job, so the pane is not Unix-only.

## What it shows and how it is driven

A status line sits above a scrolling list of turns. Each turn is a fold you can collapse, titled `Turn N · <state>`, with the reasoning rendered as Markdown through the shared sanitized view.

The event vocabulary it consumes is small and semantic:

| Event | Effect on the pane |
|---|---|
| `session.bound` | binds the pane to an OMP session id |
| `agent.started` | starts a new turn and sets the status to `Reasoning…` |
| `thinking.delta` | appends reasoning text to the live turn |
| `agent.settled` | closes the turn; status becomes `Done` or `No reasoning emitted` |
| `session.shutdown` | freezes the live turn and marks the session ended |

The view follows the bottom while you are at the bottom, and stops following when you scroll up to read an earlier turn; scrolling back down re-arms it. This is a display state, not a mode you toggle.

A turn record is the pane's own source of truth: it holds the turn index, the status, and the accumulated text up to the configured cap. Records live in RAM for the current OMP session; the pane does not write a transcript.

## Settings that matter

| Setting | What it changes |
|---|---|
| Source attachment ID | which terminal's events this pane shows; it must match that terminal's Attachment ID, not its display name |
| Settings → Reasoning → max turns | how many turns are kept; default 16, clamped 1–64 per pane |
| Settings → Reasoning → bytes per turn | how much reasoning one turn retains; default 65,536 bytes, clamped 4,096–1,048,576 |

The two global caps are read when a pane is created, so a change applies to panes opened afterward. Changing the source attachment id clears the pane's turns and rebinds: the events of a different terminal are a different conversation. Renaming the *terminal* in Pane Settings is not that — the link follows the new id and the pane keeps its turns, and only companions in the renamed terminal's own workspace move: a pane in another workspace keeps the id you typed.

## What it does not do

It does not run an agent, send prompts, or accept input. It does not parse terminal output — if the extension is missing, the pane stays empty and says so rather than guessing from the screen. It does not receive routed concept captures; its body declines content. It does not persist turns, so closing the pane or restarting gPTY starts a fresh view of the next session.

## Limits and edge cases

The pane displays one source terminal at a time. Events from another terminal are ignored. A new OMP session rebinds the pane, and the session's `session.shutdown` marks the view as ended rather than silently freezing. The turn and byte caps bound memory, and the oldest turns are dropped first. If the view looks slow rather than empty, `GPTY_REASONING_DEBUG=1` prints a once-per-second line with the input rate, render rate and the event server's drop counters — enough to tell a slow model from a stalled GUI.
