# Terminal Pane

A terminal pane is a real shell process attached to a pseudo-terminal (PTY), drawn onto the pane's surface one character cell at a time. It is the pane every workspace starts with, and the one to use whenever a program expects a terminal rather than a pipe.

## What it is

The pane is only the screen and the input path. The shell, the PTY, the ANSI parser and the character grid all live in the Rust engine; `godot/scenes/terminal/terminal_pane.gd` is the body that asks the engine for changed cells and paints them in `_draw()`. That split is why the pane can spend its time on selection, search and scrolling while the child process keeps running at full speed.

The grid is what makes a terminal a terminal: a fixed rectangle of cells, each with a character and a colour, rather than a stream of lines. Programs move a cursor around that rectangle with escape sequences, and a full-screen application — a text editor, a pager, an agent TUI — can take it over entirely and restore the previous screen when it exits.

## When to use it

Use a terminal pane for anything interactive: a shell prompt, a build you want to watch, a REPL, `git`, an editor, or an agent CLI such as omp that expects a TTY. It is also the pane that produces the output concepts match and the pane that reports agent state.

If a program only prints a report and never prompts, a [[cli-view|CLI View]] pane is the lighter choice: it runs argv with no PTY, merges the output, and bounds what it keeps.

## How to open it

| Method | Action |
|---|---|
| Shortcut | `Ctrl+Shift+N` |
| Sidebar | The terminal button in the new-pane row |
| Palette | `new terminal` (`Ctrl+Shift+P` opens the palette) |
| CLI | `gpty new-pane -t terminal`, or just `gpty new-pane` |
| MCP | the `new-pane` tool with `type: "terminal"` |
| Layout/profile | every shipped profile contains at least one, and restore recreates them |
| API | `paneRun` opens a *new* terminal pane and runs a command through the configured shell |

Panes are never spawned by other panes. Every route above asks the workspace, which is the only spawner: it attaches the new tile to the grid, gives it a label (`T1`, `T2`, …) and a stable `attachment_id`, and activates it.

## What it shows and how it is driven

The body paints the grid, the cursor (block, underline or beam, with configurable blink speed and colour), the selection highlight, and the scrollback indicator. Keyboard input goes to the child; mouse input is either used for local selection or reported to the child as terminal mouse events when the program has enabled mouse reporting.

Keys the pane recognises itself:

| Key | Effect |
|---|---|
| `Ctrl+Shift+C` | copy the selection |
| `Ctrl+Shift+V` | paste (bracketed paste when the child asked for it; control bytes are stripped either way) |
| `Ctrl+Shift+F` | toggle the scrollback search bar (regular expressions) |
| `PageUp` / `PageDown` | scroll the viewport |
| `Ctrl+V` | deliberately passed through to the child as `^V` |

Pasting treats the clipboard as untrusted input. Both modes drop control characters other than tab and newline - escape sequences included - before anything reaches the child: a clipboard holding `ESC[201~` would otherwise close a bracketed paste early and have the rest arrive as typing, and a pasted `^C` would interrupt. The bracketed mode then wraps the surviving text in `ESC[200~`/`ESC[201~`.

Wheel scrolling moves three lines by default. Output that scrolls past the viewport goes to the pane's scrollback, which is written to SQLite and restored when the pane comes back after a restart; the default depth is 10,000 lines and the global setting clamps it to 100–100,000.

`paneStatus` reports the process and the grid as a document with `pid`, `running`, `exit_code`, `exit_reason`, `idle_ms`, `agent_state` and `agent_state_tier`. The titlebar badge and the status document share one source: the tiered agent-state tracker, where capability-authenticated events outrank OSC declarations, which outrank heuristics. All three are display-only and never trigger an action.

## Settings that matter

Pane Settings for a terminal edits the presentation and the environment, not the spawn plan:

| Setting | What it changes |
|---|---|
| Name, Attachment ID | the title, and the stable id used by per-pane env, tags and companion panes |
| Font size, Font file, Color scheme | rendering |
| Environment | `KEY=value` lines, stored per pane in `user://pane_env.json` |
| Cursor shape, blink, speed, colour, beam width, underline height | rendering |
| Rows / Cols | the grid, 10–100 rows and 40–200 columns in the UI |
| Scroll lines | wheel step, 1–10 |
| Default FG / BG | the fallback colours behind a scheme |

The program and its arguments are not here. `shell_command` and `shell_args` come from a profile or from a saved layout tile. The call that creates a pane can set the program (`gpty new-pane -t terminal -c <program>`); `--arg` values are an argv for a [[cli-view|CLI View]] pane, not for a terminal. A file-supplied program or argv is what Workspace Trust exists for: restoring a tile that would run something other than your defaults asks you to approve the exact program and arguments, and a tile's `shell_env` is stripped on restore because environment belongs to you.

There is also no per-pane working directory. A pane inherits the directory of its workspace, which is the workspace row's folder button, and the workspace wins over any stored key.

## What it does not do

It does not edit files, render Markdown, or browse a directory — those are the [[code-viewer|Code Viewer]] and [[file-tree|File Tree]] panes. It does not mediate your keystrokes beyond its own shortcuts, which is why `Ctrl+V` reaches the child. It does not keep a process alive after the pane is closed: closing stops the pane's work, and the workspace asks first when a foreground job is running (on platforms that can report the foreground process group; a Windows ConPTY shell answers "live" while it lives, because the alternative is ending work silently).

## Limits and edge cases

Scrollback is per pane and is not a log file: the 10,000-line default is the depth, the store keeps it across restarts, and search runs over what was kept. The status document is sampled by a slow child poll, so a command that starts and finishes inside that window can read as idle. Full-screen applications work, including the alternate screen, but leaving the pane does not detach them — the child is a child of the GUI.

# Wiki Pane

A wiki pane browses a directory of Markdown notes as a vault: it lists the notes, searches them, renders one through the sanitized Markdown pipeline, edits it with a live preview, and draws the vault's link graph. You are reading one of its notes right now.

## What it is

The body is `WikiPane` (`godot/scenes/panes/wiki_pane.gd`); the registered type key is `wiki` and its label prefix is `W`. A vault is just a directory of `.md` files — the pane does not own a database format. The search index lives elsewhere, in gPTY's state directory, so a vault stays plain and portable.

The pane has two faces. The **list** shows the vault's notes, a search box and a **Graph** button. Opening a note switches to the **note view**: a source editor, a live rendered preview, a small toolbar with the view modes, and a links panel for what the note points at and what points back at it.

## When to use it

Use it for durable notes you want to keep next to the work: project context, decisions, runbooks, recipes. It is also a working example of the link model behind [[wikilinks]] and the [[link-graph]], since it is the only pane that implements both.

For reading a single arbitrary file, the [[code-viewer|Code Viewer]] is lighter and read-only. For writing code, use an editor in a terminal.

## How to open it

| Method | Action |
|---|---|
| Sidebar | the wiki button |
| Palette | `new wiki` |
| CLI | `gpty new-pane -t wiki` |
| MCP | the `new-pane` tool with `type: "wiki"` |
| Layout/profile | a saved tile restores its vault path, open note and whether the graph was showing |
| Built-in profile | **Knowledge Base** opens the app's bundled vault without a path |

The pane has no keyboard shortcut of its own. A new pane has no vault until one is set in Pane Settings (or supplied by a profile or layout); a hand-set path must be absolute and existing, and it is validated every time it is used rather than trusted once. The built-in **Knowledge Base** profile stores the `@knowledge` token instead of a machine path: the pane resolves it to the copy seeded from the app's bundle on first use, and a later release with changed notes seeds a new copy rather than overwriting local edits. The repository ships this wiki at `docs/content/wiki` — that directory is a good first vault in a checkout.

The same vault is reachable without a pane: the control surface exposes `vault-search`, `vault-read` and `vault-weight`, so an agent or a script can query notes and set link weights while you work. Those tools share the pane's index rules, so both agree on what a note is.

## What it shows and how it is driven

The list is built by one recursive walk: `.md` files only, hidden entries skipped at every level, at most 2,000 notes and 16 levels deep. Search runs against an SQLite FTS5 index with porter stemming (notes are prose, so `run` matches `running`), waits 0.15 s after a keystroke, and asks for up to 200 hits; the store itself accepts 1–500.

The note view has three modes, remembered per pane as `view_mode`:

| Mode | Layout |
|---|---|
| `edit` | source editor only |
| `split` | source and live preview (the default) |
| `preview` | rendered Markdown only |

Editing is explicit. A dirty marker appears while the buffer differs from disk; **Save** or `Ctrl+S` writes; there is no autosave. Closing or leaving a note with unsaved changes raises a Save / Discard / Cancel guard, and every path that can destroy the buffer runs through it. Saves are atomic and carry a stamp of the file's `mtime` and `size`, so a note changed by something else since it was loaded is not silently overwritten. An unsaved buffer also gets a recovery copy outside the vault, offered back the next time the note is opened — never applied on its own.

The note verbs are **New note** (default name `Untitled.md`; a bare name gains the extension inside the vault), **Rename** (which offers to rewrite references), and **Delete**. Paths follow the same vocabulary as the walk, and the Rust side refuses any path that would leave the vault.

In the preview, `[[wikilinks]]` render as internal links and are followed in place, through the same leave guard. Below the note, the links panel lists **Links to** (this note's outgoing mentions) and **Linked from** (backlinks), ordered with any declared weights taken into account.

**Graph** replaces the list with the vault's link structure: one node per indexed note plus one ghost per unresolved target, edges aggregated per ordered pair. The layout is deterministic; you can pan, zoom and drag nodes, and clicking a note opens it through the leave guard while clicking a ghost runs the same resolution a preview mention does. A right-click on an edge sets or clears a declared weight between 1 and 100. Weights are display-only and live in `user://link_weights.json`: they change thickness, layout stiffness and link order, never which edges exist or what a click can reach.

## Settings that matter

| Setting | What it changes |
|---|---|
| Name | the pane's title |
| Font size | 8–32 px in the editor and preview |
| Vault path | absolute directory to index and edit |
| Note view | `Edit`, `Split` or `Preview` |

## What it does not do

It does not index anything but `.md` files, and it does not show hidden files. It does not write outside the vault, and it does not store note content in the database: the index is derived and can be rebuilt. It does not treat front matter as metadata — a `---` block is text. It does not auto-save, auto-reload an outside edit, or silently apply a recovery copy.

## Limits and edge cases

A note body is capped at 1 MiB. A note that hits the cap while loading is shown read-only, because saving would replace the file with its visible prefix. The walk's 2,000-note and 16-level limits bound both the list and the index. The graph caps answers at 10,000 edges per class and 2,000 ghosts, and reports when a cap cut the answer. Graph geometry is session state — node positions are not saved — while declared weights and the open note are.

# Agent Workflow

An agent is useful in gPTY when it can open panes, run work in them, and read what came back. This note is the sequence for that, from both places an agent can stand: inside one pane of the grid, and outside the app entirely.

## Two positions, two doors

The same method set is reachable three ways — a JSON-RPC socket, the `gpty` CLI, and an MCP server. Which door you use depends less on taste than on where you are running.

| Position | Door | May start the GUI? |
|---|---|---|
| Inside a gPTY pane | `gpty` CLI over the control socket | yes, for `new-pane` and `layout load` only |
| Outside, as an MCP client | `gpty mcp`, JSON-RPC over stdio | never; `daemon-start` is the bootstrap |

Both speak to a single running workspace, so the GUI is the state. Nothing an agent does here creates a second window: a `new-pane` call lands as a tile beside the others.

## Inside a pane: confirm the guardrail first

A pane injects `GPTY_ENV`, `GPTY_PANE_ID` and the event-socket credentials into every program it spawns. An agent that was launched elsewhere has none of them.

1. Run `echo "$GPTY_ENV"`. If it does not print `1`, you are not inside a gPTY-managed pane — say so and stop rather than guessing at pane ids.
2. Run `gpty --skill` to print the bundled agent skill, and `gpty schema` for the full command set as JSON Schema. The schema needs no GUI and is generated from the same definitions as `--help`, so it wins when documentation and binary disagree.
3. Run `gpty list-panes` to see the current grid by stable id (`T1`, `C1`, `I1`, and so on) and display label.

## Recipe: split, run tests, wait, read

Prerequisites: a running GUI, and an agent whose `GPTY_ENV` is `1`.

1. Open a pane that runs the command immediately: `gpty new-pane -t terminal -c "cargo test" -f`. The call answers with the new pane's id, label and type — say `T2`.
2. Wait for the line that tells you it ended: `gpty pane-wait T2 --pattern "test result" --timeout-ms 60000`. The pattern is Rust regex syntax; the timeout is 100–60,000 ms and the wait is held server-side, so a dead pane does not hang your client past the bound.
3. Read the tail: `gpty pane-read T2 --lines 200`. This is the plain-text screen plus scrollback, up to 2,000 lines.
4. Check how it exited: `gpty pane-status T2` answers `pid`, `running`, `exit_code`, `exit_reason` and `idle_ms`.

What you should see: a new tile appears on the first step, the wait returns the matching line, the read shows the test output, and the status carries the exit code the shell reported.

If it does not work: a wait that matches nothing fails on its timeout rather than returning an empty success. `pane-read` is a snapshot, not a stream — call it again for new output, or use the wait between calls. And `pane-run --command "cargo test"` always opens a *new* pane; it does not reuse `T2`.

## Recipe: fan out with tags

Tags are how one message reaches many panes without listing ids.

1. Create panes carrying a tag: `gpty new-pane --tags ci`. Tags follow the attachment-id pattern (lowercase, up to 32 characters), and a pane holds up to 16.
2. Send the same text to every tagged pane: `gpty broadcast --tags ci --text "make test"`.

The text is written verbatim; the shell in each pane interprets it, so quoting and newlines are the shell's business, not the API's. Use this for "run the suite everywhere", not for structured commands you cannot afford to have half-executed in a pane that is mid-prompt.

## Declare what you are doing

`gpty state working` sets the badge on the pane the command runs in — one of `idle`, `working`, `needs-attention`, `completed`, `failed`. It takes no target: it reads the credentials the pane injected and submits over the event socket. It is display only and never triggers actions, captures or layout changes. There is deliberately no MCP tool for it, because an MCP client is not inside a pane.

## Outside a pane: the MCP door

1. Start the app if it is not running: `gpty daemon start`. From an MCP client, the equivalent is the `daemon-start` tool.
2. Launch the server: `gpty mcp`. It speaks JSON-RPC over stdio and exposes 22 tools covering the same operations — pane lifecycle, `inject`, `pane-read`, `pane-status`, `pane-run`, `pane-wait`, `broadcast`, layouts, concepts, the vault reads and weights, `daemon-*` and `version`.
3. Check health with `gpty daemon status`, and stop the app with `gpty daemon stop` when the harness is done.

MCP never auto-spawns a workspace. A tool call that finds no GUI answers with that fact and names `daemon-start`, which is the explicit bootstrap. This is a safety property: a background model server should not be able to open a desktop application as a side effect of a query.

## Guardrails worth keeping

- Installing, enabling or removing a plugin is a human decision: installation ends in a review dialog in the GUI, and a plugin's actions run with your user's privileges. If a task needs one, name it and why rather than doing it.
- A concept cannot execute anything. Its trigger is a regex over untrusted terminal output and its only effect is routing text to a pane that accepts content, so captured output is data, never a command.
- Nothing above is a stream. Every read is a snapshot of a pane, and `pane-wait` is the mechanism for "tell me when".

# Concept Recipes

A concept is a named regex over terminal output plus a decision about what to do with the matching lines. These are four working rules you can observe or build, with the parts that bite.

## The mental model

One rule is a chain: a trigger pattern matched against one line of terminal output, zero or more conditions that must also match that same line, and an action that names a receiving pane type. The trigger fires, the rule captures raw bytes until its timeout window ends or the next keystroke arrives, and the captured text is handed to a pane that accepts content.

Two properties matter more than the fields:

- A concept never executes anything. There is no command field and no write to a PTY. It can only capture display text and route it.
- Only two pane types accept routed content: the Code Viewer and the Inspector. The target picker is built from that list, so a rule cannot aim anywhere else.

`gpty concept list` prints every concept with its enabled state, and `gpty concept toggle <name>` is the API for flipping one. The visual editor lives in Settings → Concepts: a canvas where each rule is trigger → condition → action and the vertical order is priority.

## Before any recipe

Open the receiving pane first, or the capture has nowhere to land. A route with no receiver at the far end produces a toast naming the concept and the missing target type, and the text stays in the terminal. Also run `gpty concept list` once so you know the exact rule names.

## Recipe 1 — `cat` into the Code Viewer

The one rule that ships enabled.

1. Open a Code Viewer pane with `Ctrl+Shift+D`.
2. In a terminal pane, run `cat Cargo.toml`.
3. Watch the Code Viewer receive the file's text as a capture.

The trigger is `(?:^|[$#>]\s)\bcat\s+\S`, an `until_stop` capture with a 300 ms window that starts when the trigger matches, plus stop-on-input. In practice: the file prints in the terminal, the capture ends a third of a second later (or sooner if you type), and the viewer shows it as content you can scroll without the shell prompt mixed in. A file that takes longer than the window to print is cut, so raise the timeout for large files.

Expected result: the viewer fills with the file, and the terminal still has the original output.

If nothing arrives, check `gpty concept list` — the rule may be off — and check that a Code Viewer pane is actually open in this workspace.

## Recipe 2 — compiler errors into the Inspector

Off by default, and gated on the Inspector's own consent.

1. Open an Inspector pane with `Ctrl+Shift+O`.
2. In the Inspector's pane settings, enable `Accept terminal concept captures (opt-in)`. The Inspector does not follow the terminal conversation on its own; this is what allows captured output to leave the terminal pane.
3. Turn the rule on: `gpty concept toggle cargo_check`.
4. In a terminal, run `cargo check` in a project with an error.

The trigger is `(?:^|[$#>]\s)\bcargo\s+(?:check|test|build)\b` with a 2000 ms window — longer than `cat`'s, because a compile run is chatty and you do not want the capture cut in half.

Expected result: the Inspector receives the compiler output as context for a question you then ask it.

If it does not work: the Inspector is private and read-only by design, so a disabled opt-in means the capture is silently dropped at the receiver, not routed somewhere else. The Inspector also runs without tools, so it can explain an error but cannot fix the file for you.

## Recipe 3 — `git diff` into the Code Viewer

Off by default; the useful default for review work.

1. Open a Code Viewer pane.
2. Run `gpty concept toggle git_diff`.
3. Run `git diff` in a terminal pane.

Trigger `(?:^|[$#>]\s)\bgit\s+diff`, `until_stop`, 500 ms. The receiver gets the diff as plain text, ANSI escapes stripped; the viewer is the place to read it at full width instead of in an 80-column terminal.

Expected result: the diff appears in the viewer while the terminal keeps its copy.

If the capture is truncated, the diff took longer than the 500 ms window to print — a pager or a slow filesystem can do that. Raise the timeout in the editor rather than shortening the command.

## Recipe 4 — a notify-only rule

Some signals are worth announcing and not worth capturing. Add a rule in Settings → Concepts with Add Trigger, Add Condition (if you need one) and Add Action, set the action's mode to Notify only, then Save.

1. Open the concept editor and add a trigger with the pattern `\btest result: ok\b`, named `tests_done`.
2. Add an action node, set mode to Notify only, and connect the trigger's output to it.
3. Save.
4. Run your test suite in a terminal and subscribe to the event socket, or watch a tool that does; the pane shows no notice of its own.

The saved rule is one entry shaped like this — no target, no stop settings, because there is nothing to route and nothing to capture:

```json
{
  "name": "tests_done",
  "trigger": "\\btest result: ok\\b",
  "enabled": true,
  "capture_mode": "single_line"
}
```

Notify-only is the `single_line` capture mode: it publishes a notice naming the rule and its source pane, captures no bytes, and delivers nothing to a pane. The matched line is deliberately not published — the event carries metadata only.

Expected result: a `concept.matched` event when the line matches, carrying the rule name and source pane; nothing is captured, nothing appears in a receiver pane, and the matched line is not published. If the rule fires constantly, the pattern is too broad — `result: ok` alone would match a line that merely mentions it. Tighten it with an anchor or a condition rather than turning the rule off.

## When a recipe goes wrong

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| Toast about a missing pane | No open pane of the action's target type |
| Capture ends mid-output | Silence timeout reached during a pause |
| Rule never fires | Pattern dialect: Rust `regex`, no backreferences or lookaround |
| Rule fires on prose in a transcript | Trigger matches any line, not just the prompt line |

The prompt-anchored prefix `(?:^|[$#>]\s)` in the shipped rules is there for the last problem: it keeps a rule from firing on a line of documentation that happens to contain the word `git diff`, or on an agent's own narration of a command it is about to run.

# Vault Workflow

A vault is just a directory of Markdown files. This walks one from empty pane to a graph an agent can query: open it, write, link, read backlinks, search, curate, rename, recover, and hand it to an agent.

## Point the pane at a directory

1. Open a Wiki pane — `Ctrl+Shift+P` and search for the Wiki pane, or `gpty new-pane -t wiki`.
2. Open the pane's settings popup and fill in **Vault path** with an absolute directory. In this repository that is `/path/to/gpty/docs/content/wiki`.
3. Wait for the list to fill.

The pane walks the directory recursively for `.md` files, skipping hidden entries at every level, up to 2,000 notes. If it hits that cap, a footer says the listing stopped rather than pretending the vault is smaller than it is.

Expected result: the note list shows every note by vault-relative path. If it stays empty, the path is wrong, not absolute, or contains no Markdown — the pane does not search parent directories for you.

The index lives in gPTY's own state directory, never inside your vault, so pointing a pane at a git checkout writes nothing into it.

## Write a note and link it

1. Press **New note**. The pane creates `Untitled.md` at the vault root; a bare name you type instead gains the `.md` suffix. The directory must already exist inside the vault.
2. Write in the editor. The toolbar switches between **Edit** (source only), **Split** (source and live preview) and **Preview** (rendered only); Split is what makes the preview update as you type.
3. Link another note with a wikilink target such as `[[getting-started]]`, a labelled one such as `[[pane|the pane note]]`, or a heading one such as `[[vault#Titles and search]]`.
4. Save with **Save** or `Ctrl+S`. The dirty marker (`● Unsaved changes`) clears.

Expected result: the note appears in the list immediately, and the preview turns your wikilink into a link you can click.

If you try to leave — switch notes, close the pane — a guard offers Save, Discard or Cancel. There is no autosave: a note is on disk only after an explicit save.

## Read the links back

1. Click a rendered wikilink. The target opens in place, behind the same leave guard.
2. Open the note's link panel: **Links to** lists this note's mentions, **Backlinks** lists the notes that mention this one, and unresolved mentions show with their candidates so you can tell a missing note from a mis-typed target.
3. Press **Graph** to draw the vault. Nodes are indexed notes plus one ghost per unresolved target; edges aggregate mentions between a pair.
4. Click a node to open it, or click a ghost to create the note it names.

Expected result: the panel and the graph agree, because both read the same index rows. A long mention list ends with a footer like `… 3 more mention(s) not shown`, which is truncation in the panel, not in the index.

If a link looks dead, it is: a target resolves by exact case first, then by a unique case-insensitive match, and an ambiguous match is never silently picked. Backslashed or fenced occurrences are literal text and create no edge.

## Search

1. Type into the **Search notes** field. The list is replaced by hits as you type.
2. Read a hit to jump to the note.

Search is full-text over the vault, with stemming — `owning` finds `ownership` — and terms are ANDed, so more words narrow the result. To search the same vault from a shell or an agent:

```bash
gpty vault search /path/to/gpty/docs/content/wiki "vault"
```

The answer carries `results`, `total` and `truncated`. A `truncated: true` means the walk hit its note cap, so the answer is partial.

## Curate a link's weight

1. Right-click an edge in the graph to set a weight (1–100) or clear it, or from a shell: `gpty vault weight /path/to/gpty/docs/content/wiki wiki/vault.md wiki/wikilinks.md --weight 40`.
2. Press Relayout or reopen the graph to see the edge thicken and the pair settle closer together.

A declared weight is 1–100 and display-only: it overrides the measured mention count for edge thickness, layout stiffness and link-panel order. It never hides an edge, never gates navigation and never writes to the vault. The store is the running GUI's, so the command needs a live workspace and will not start one.

## Rename without breaking links

1. Open the note and press **Rename**.
2. Enter the new vault-relative path.
3. Accept the prompt that reports how many mentions in how many notes still name the old target.

Expected result: the file moves and the references are rewritten. If you decline, the rename still happens and those links simply stop resolving — which is what the prompt is warning about. Renames never follow a symlink out of the vault.

## Recover an unsaved buffer

1. If gPTY closes with a dirty buffer, the next time you open that note you are asked: *had unsaved changes when gpty last closed. Restore them?*
2. Choose Restore to load the buffer, or decline to read the file on disk.

Recovery copies are kept outside the vault, are never applied automatically, and are written on a throttle rather than on every keystroke. There is a second guard for the other direction: if the file changed on disk while you had it open, saving asks before overwriting your version.

## Expose the vault to an agent

1. Note the absolute vault path — an agent needs the same one you typed into the pane.
2. Give the agent read access with the two read-only commands:

```bash
gpty vault search /path/to/gpty/docs/content/wiki "link graph" --limit 20
gpty vault read /path/to/gpty/docs/content/wiki wiki/link-graph.md
```

Search re-indexes notes whose modification time or size changed before answering, so a note edited outside gPTY is visible to the next search without reopening the pane. `read` returns `path`, `text`, `truncated`, `crlf`, `mtime` and `size`.

Expected result: the search returns ranked hits with vault-relative paths, and read returns the note body.

Neither command writes to the vault, and a miss is an error with a stable code (`not_found`, `bad_path`) rather than an empty success. A read is capped at the same 1 MiB display limit as the editor, and `truncated` says so; a note larger than that opens read-only in the pane as well.

# Declared Link Weights

A declared weight is a number you author for one pair of notes, overriding the mention count the [[link-graph|link graph]] measured. It is curation, and it is display-only: it changes how strongly a relationship is drawn, never what the app does.

## Measured versus authored

The index counts mentions. That number is honest and often misleading: two notes can be deeply related and name each other once, while one note can name-drop another ten times and share nothing of substance. The measured count is also not yours to argue with — it is a fact about the text.

So there are two layers over the same edge. The measured one is the `count` in the index. The authored one is a declaration you make, from 1 to 100, for one directed pair `(src, target)`. When a declaration exists it is the edge's display weight; when it does not, the count is. Neither layer changes the count itself, and clearing a declaration simply returns the edge to what the text says.

## Where it lives, and who owns it

Declarations live in `user://link_weights.json`, keyed by vault, then source note, then target note:

```
{"vaults": {"/abs/vault": {"note.md": {"other.md": 10}}}}
```

That file is deliberately not `vaults.db`. The index is a derived cache that a schema bump may rebuild from scratch; authored work must survive a rebuild. The weights file is user-owned, hand-editable, and validated on load: the file is a boundary like every other store, so a malformed entry loses itself rather than the file, and paths and weights outside the vocabulary are dropped.

The store belongs to the running GUI. The graph canvas writes through it, and the CLI's write is routed to the GUI as well — a `gpty vault weight` call needs a running gPTY, and there is no independent copy of the file for a headless process to edit. [[cli|CLI]] describes the client's general posture.

## What a weight changes

A declared weight feeds exactly three things:

| Effect | Detail |
|---|---|
| edge thickness | logarithmic and clamped, so 100 is emphatic but not a wall |
| layout stiffness | the Relayout springs use the same logarithm |
| link-panel order | a declared pair sorts above measured ones in "Links to" / "Linked from" |

That last one matters more than it sounds. The link panel shows a bounded number of rows per section; ordering by declaration lets a curated relationship surface from past the cap, and the footer still counts everything the cap excluded.

## What it never does

A declaration is not consent, not navigation, and not data about the vault:

- It never hides an edge. Every edge the index found is still drawn.
- It never gates a click. A declared or undeclared edge opens the same note.
- It never writes to the vault. No note text changes.
- It never counts as a trust decision, a spawn permission, or an instruction to an agent.
- It never survives as a fact about the notes; delete the JSON and the graph is exactly the mentioned structure again.

The pause is worth stating plainly: the strongest thing a weight can do is make a line thicker and pull two nodes closer on a canvas you are looking at.

## Setting one

In the graph, right-click an edge and choose Set declared weight… then pick a number; the same menu clears it. A ghost edge is not offered, because a declaration names two notes. The prompt says what the value affects, so the display-only boundary is visible at the moment of authoring. Setting a weight re-applies the canvas immediately but does not reshuffle it; Relayout applies the new springs.

For an agent or a script:

```bash
gpty vault weight ~/notes wiki/vault.md wiki/wikilinks.md --weight 80
gpty vault weight ~/notes wiki/vault.md wiki/wikilinks.md --clear
```

The MCP tool is `vault-weight`, with the same parameters. A clear of an absent declaration succeeds, so "no declaration" can be stated idempotently. Note that the canvas's human control writes both directions of a drawn pair in one write, while the CLI writes one directed number — the file's shape stays directed, so an agent can express exactly one endpoint.

## Rename and prune

A declaration is keyed by vault-relative note paths, so a rename would strand every entry naming the old path. The pane re-keys both endpoints immediately after a successful rename: declarations on the note, pointing at it, or naming it on both sides move to the new path in one write, a stale row already stored under the destination loses to the moved one, and unrelated declarations are untouched. This runs before any question about rewriting references, because it does not depend on that answer.

Pruning is lazier by design. When the pane shows a *complete* graph, declarations whose endpoints are no longer notes in the vault are dropped, so the file does not accumulate names forever. A truncated graph does not prune: the edges it does not name are still real, and deleting their authored weights would be unrecoverable.

# Link Graph

The link graph is a canvas view of how the notes in a [[vault|vault]] name each other. It is generated from the same index the note list and search use, so it is a picture of the stored [[wikilinks|wikilinks]], not a second document you maintain.

## Nodes, ghosts, and edges

The graph is read from `vaults.db` each time you open it; nothing is stored and no note is re-parsed for the drawing.

| Element | What it is |
|---|---|
| node | one indexed note; its id is the vault-relative path and its label the indexed title |
| ghost | one node per distinct unresolved target, named `ghost:<target>` |
| edge | one ordered `(src, dst)` pair, with a count of occurrences |
| `truncated` | a cap cut the answer short |

Edges aggregate: two notes that mention each other several times do not produce a crowd of lines. The index answers one row per ordered pair with its mention count, resolved rows first and unresolved ones after, each ordered by count then name. The canvas then draws each note pair once, adding both directions, so a mutual pair is a single edge — with direction shown when Arrows is on. A ghost edge is an edge, not a separate class of anything: it is the same mention with nothing on the other end.

Caps bound what a drawing can reasonably be. A canvas past 10,000 edges in one class, or 2,000 ghosts, is a hairball and also a large answer to move across the bridge. `truncated` means a cap cut the answer, so the drawing is real but partial. The status line says it plainly: notes, links, missing targets, declared weights, and `truncated`.

## Why there is no graph file

There is no `.canvas`, no saved coordinates, and no second format. Open the graph and it queries the index; open it again after an edit and it queries again, because every mutation — a save, a create, a rename, a delete, a reference rewrite — re-indexes before returning. One source of truth means the graph cannot describe a vault that no longer exists.

The cost of that choice is that geometry is session state. Positions live in the canvas view only, so the arrangement is not shared, not committed, and not part of the vault. That is also what lets a drag survive a re-query: the view keeps the positions of nodes it already placed and only seeds new ones, so opening the graph again mid-session does not undo your arrangement. A fresh session starts from the deterministic layout.

## The layout is deterministic

The same nodes and edges always lay out the same way. A sunflower seed (no random source) places the nodes, then a relaxation pass runs a bounded number of iterations, with each pair's spring strength derived from its display weight through the same logarithm used for thickness — so a chatty note cannot dominate the arrangement any more than it can dominate the line widths. Node radius follows degree, edge thickness is logarithmic and clamped to 1–3 px, and labels are drawn for every node only while the graph is zoomed in enough and small enough to read (up to 120 nodes); the hovered and selected nodes always get one.

Relayout runs the deterministic pass again. It is also the moment a newly declared weight changes the arrangement: setting a weight re-applies the display values without reshuffling the canvas, and Relayout applies it to the springs.

## Using it

The Graph button on the notes list opens it and re-reads the index. The interface is small and stated on screen:

- drag the background to pan, wheel to zoom, drag a node to move it
- Fit frames the whole graph
- Arrows toggles direction drawing; a mutual pair is drawn double-headed
- Relayout restores the computed arrangement

Clicking a note node opens it, behind the same Save / Discard / Cancel ask that leaving a note always makes — a click can replace an unsaved buffer, so the graph cannot open over one. Clicking a ghost runs the same resolution a mention does: a missing target offers create-from-link, while an ambiguous stem reports its candidates and does nothing, because either choice would be a guess.

Right-clicking an edge offers to set or clear a declared weight. That control is described in [[declared-link-weights|Declared Link Weights]]; the graph itself only draws what the store answers.

## What it is not

The graph is not an editor, not a validator, and not a dependency map. It shows mention structure only: two notes that are deeply related but name each other once will sit far apart, which is exactly why a weight can be declared. It also cannot show what the index refused to resolve — a ghost is a target, not a note, and it disappears the moment a note resolves it.

# Note Editor

The note editor is the Wiki pane's writing half: a buffer beside a live preview, an explicit save, and a set of guards that exist because losing typed prose is worse than any inconvenience they cause. It edits notes that are already in the [[vault|vault]], and it creates, renames, and deletes them under the same path rules.

## Three modes, one buffer

Edit shows the source, Preview shows the rendered note, and Split shows both; Split is the default. The preview renders the *buffer*, not the file, so unsaved work is what you see as you type. Rendering settles rather than running per keystroke — a full render of a large note is real work, and queueing one per character would spend it on text nobody has paused to read. Switching modes and opening a note render immediately, because those are explicit acts.

The preview is the same sanitized Markdown pipeline used elsewhere: raw HTML and BBCode are escaped, images reduce to alt text, and only http, https, and mailto links become metadata. [[wikilinks|Wikilinks]] are the exception the wiki adds: the renderer reuses the index's own parser, so the mentions that become clickable are exactly the occurrences that became edges. A note read past the 1 MiB cap shows a truncation banner above the body, saying so rather than stopping silently.

## Saving is explicit

The Save button and `Ctrl+S` do the same thing: write the buffer to the file. There is no autosave to the vault. Unsaved changes show as a marker next to the note, and Save is disabled while there are none.

Leaving a dirty note asks first, with Save / Discard / Cancel. The same question guards more than Back: following a mention, opening a node from the graph, closing the pane (titlebar, sidebar, `Ctrl+Shift+W`), changing the pane type, resetting the workspace, activating a profile, closing a workspace, reloading layouts, and quitting the app all route through the pane's own close request. Cancel cancels the whole action, including a quit. An IPC `killPane` is the one path that cannot show a dialog: it refuses with "unsaved changes" while the buffer is dirty, rather than asking or discarding. The pane can therefore never be destroyed around a buffer it did not get an answer for.

## Recovery copies

Because the vault write only happens on an explicit save, a crash or an outside kill would take everything typed since. The editor therefore snapshots a dirty buffer as a *recovery copy* outside the vault, under `state_dir()/scratch`, with the directory created owner-only on first use. It is not a note write and never touches the vault.

The snapshot is throttled to at most once every 1.5 seconds while the buffer stays dirty. That is a throttle, not a per-keystroke debounce: a debounce that restarts on every keystroke never fires during a long typing run, which is precisely when the most work is at risk. At most about a second and a half of typing can be lost.

Reopening the same note — same vault, same path — offers the copy: Restore puts the buffer back, dirty, still carrying the stamp of the file revision it was typed against, so a later save still checks the file the user saw; Discard drops it. It is never applied on its own. The copy is dropped the moment the buffer reaches the file or the user discards it. Each write also prunes records whose vault is definitively gone, erring toward keeping a vault that is merely unreadable.

## Writing safely

A save is atomic: a hidden random sibling temp file is written, then renamed over the target, keeping the note's own mode. A reader either sees the old file or the new one.

A save also carries a stamp — the `(mtime, size)` the buffer was loaded from. If the file changed on disk since then, the write is refused with `changed_on_disk` and the pane offers an explicit overwrite instead of quietly discarding someone else's edit. Forcing the save accepts that. The pane's own saves refresh the stamp, so consecutive saves do not trip it.

Line endings are preserved: the editor works in LF, and a CRLF note is converted back on the way out, byte for byte for everything else. A CRLF note opens clean, because dirty is measured in the editor's own space.

The 1 MiB read cap makes a larger note read-only. The pane says why ("Read-only — larger than 1 MiB") rather than pretending the truncated prefix is the whole file.

## The note verbs

New note asks for a path, starting at `Untitled.md`; a name whose last component has no extension gains `.md`, and any other extension is left as typed so the vault can refuse it. Create claims the destination with `create_new`, so an existing note answers "exists" and is never replaced. The directory must already exist inside the vault — the editor never creates folders and never writes through a directory symlinked out of it. Paths follow the walk's vocabulary: relative, ordinary components, none hidden, ending in `.md`, at most 1,024 bytes, with `..` unrepresentable. Save is contained too: a symlink pointing at a sibling note is written through, one pointing out of the vault is refused.

Rename offers to update references after the move: "N mention(s) in M note(s) still name old — update them?" Nothing is written unless you answer Update, and the pass touches only occurrences that resolved to the old name, preserving aliases and fragments. Delete asks for confirmation, then acts on the vault entry: a symlinked note is unlinked as a link, its target untouched.

# Vault

A vault is an ordinary directory of Markdown notes that gPTY lists, searches, and edits. Nothing in the directory belongs to gPTY: the files are yours, and everything the app derives from them lives somewhere else.

## A directory, not a file format

Point the [[wiki-pane|Wiki pane]] at any absolute directory and gPTY treats the `.md` files inside it as notes. Subfolders are part of the vault, and other file types are simply not notes. There is no manifest to keep in sync, no database inside the vault, and no required front matter. A vault made in Obsidian opens as-is, and a vault made here opens in Obsidian.

That compatibility is deliberate. The index, the search table, and the link edges are all derived data; the notes alone are the source of truth. Copy the directory to another machine and the wiki is intact. Delete gPTY entirely and the folder still reads as plain Markdown.

## The index lives outside the vault

The note list, search hits, wikilink edges, and the [[link-graph|link graph]] all come from one SQLite store at `state_dir()/vaults.db`. `state_dir()` is gPTY's own private state directory, never the vault, which has three consequences worth knowing:

- Copying or syncing the vault moves your notes and nothing else. The index is rebuilt locally.
- Deleting the store loses nothing. The next index pass re-reads the files and recreates every derived row.
- The control socket and the CLI can reach the store without resolving Godot's `user://` paths, which is why an agent can search a vault with no pane open.

## What the walk calls a note

Every listing and every search starts with a walk of the directory. Its rules are fixed, and they are the same rules the pane's list, the editor, and the graph obey.

| Rule | Value |
|---|---|
| Hidden entries | skipped at every level (`.obsidian`, `.git`, `.trash`) |
| Extension | `.md` as the last path component |
| Order | sorted per directory, then by relative path |
| Notes per walk | 2,000, then `truncated` is set |
| Depth | 16 directory levels |
| Unreadable entry | skipped; the rest of the vault still lists |
| Path length | 1,024 bytes |
| Body read | 1 MiB, a torn UTF-8 tail dropped |

The walk is best-effort on purpose: a vault is user data, and one unreadable subdirectory does not hide the rest of it. A symlinked directory is walked like a directory, with the depth cap stopping a loop.

The count cap has a subtler rule attached. Notes are dropped from the index only when a walk was complete; a truncated walk can add and refresh notes but never concludes that anything vanished, because the files it did not reach are still real.

## Titles and search

A note's title is what the list and the search results show. gPTY takes the first heading past a closed YAML front matter block; if there is no heading, it uses the file stem. Titles are capped at 200 characters. An unterminated `---` is not front matter and is treated as ordinary text.

Search is SQLite FTS5 with the `porter unicode61` tokenizer over title and body. Porter stemming suits prose, where "saving", "saved", and "save" should find each other. What you type is not an FTS5 query: free text is first sanitised into quoted, ANDed terms, so an ordinary search such as `main.rs` works instead of being rejected by the query parser. Hits come back best-rank-first with a body snippet; the API accepts 1–500, and the pane's search box asks for 200.

Indexing is incremental. Only notes whose modification time or size changed are re-read, and saving a note re-indexes the vault before the call returns. An edit made outside gPTY — in an editor, in Obsidian, by another agent — is picked up by the next query because a search indexes changed notes first.

A note is read and stored at the same 1 MiB cap. That shared cut is not cosmetic: if the index stored more than the viewer shows, a search hit could match text you can never see. A larger note still opens, but read-only.

## Reaching a vault from outside the pane

The absolute vault path is the only handle needed. The CLI and the MCP server expose the same operations over the control socket:

```bash
gpty vault search ~/notes "atomic save" --limit 20
gpty vault read ~/notes wiki/vault.md
```

Search answers `{results, total, truncated}` and read answers the note document `{path, text, truncated, crlf, mtime, size}`. The MCP tools are `vault-search`, `vault-read`, and `vault-weight`; the two reads are answered natively by the Rust side off the GUI thread, because a vault is a directory rather than workspace state. Curating link weights is the exception — `gpty vault weight <vault> <src> <target> --weight N` goes to the running GUI, because the store belongs to it, as [[declared-link-weights|Declared Link Weights]] explains. The full method surface is in [[control-api|Control API]].

## Why plain files are the point

Every feature in this cluster is disposable on top of the files. [[wikilinks|Wikilinks]] are text spans in the notes; the edges they produce are index rows. The graph is a query. The weights are a separate user-owned JSON file. Remove gPTY and you have a folder of Markdown that any other tool can read — which is also why a note you do not touch is a note gPTY cannot break.

# Wikilinks

A wikilink is a note naming another note in double square brackets. It is the only cross-note link syntax in a [[vault|vault]], and it is stored as a real edge, so the same text that navigates the preview also draws the [[link-graph|link graph]] and answers backlinks.

## The three forms

```
[[target]]
[[target|alias]]
[[target#heading]]
```

The first is a plain link, and the target is its own label. The second keeps the same edge but displays the alias instead. The third keeps the same edge and lands on a heading inside the target.

Only the target forms the edge. An alias is display text and never part of the edge, and a fragment says where inside the resolved note to scroll, never which note to open. Both are re-read from the line for rendering, so the stored edge cannot disagree with what the preview shows.

A target is resolved one of two ways. If it contains `/`, it is a path relative to the vault root, with or without the `.md` extension (`notes/vault` and `notes/vault.md` both name the same file). Otherwise it is a file stem, so two notes in different folders can share a stem — and that is the source of the ambiguity rule below.

## How a target resolves

Resolution runs in two stages, and the second only happens when the first finds nothing:

| Stage | Rule |
|---|---|
| Exact | the path, or the exact stem, matched as written |
| Case-insensitive | a *unique* case-insensitive match on the same key |

More than one match at either stage is ambiguous. An ambiguous target is reported with its candidate paths and is never chosen — picking one would be a guess, and the next unrelated file could change the answer. The link panel shows it as `ambiguous:` with the candidates and does not make it clickable. A target nothing matches is "missing" and stays unresolved until a note appears that resolves it.

Resolution is the index's own rule, used by the preview, the link panel, and the graph alike, so following a mention and counting an edge can never disagree.

## One row per occurrence

Every occurrence is its own stored row, with the line it was written on. A note that says the same target three times has three rows; each is a mention you can navigate to, and the graph counts three. Backlinks are the same rows read in reverse: the notes that mention this one are a query over the same table, not a second authored thing, so a backlink cannot fall out of date relative to its outgoing mention.

The link panel under the open note shows both directions: "Links to" lists the note's mentions with line numbers, and "Linked from" lists the notes that name it. A resolved outgoing row opens its target in place, and a backlink row opens the linking note at the mention's line, derived from the nearest heading above it. Following a link goes through the same leave guard as leaving the note, so a dirty buffer is never replaced silently.

## What stays literal

A note has to be able to document this syntax without linking to anything. Four things are therefore never parsed as links:

- fenced code blocks (three or more backticks or tildes, closed by the same character at the same length or longer)
- inline code spans (a backtick run closed by a run of the same length)
- an opener escaped with a backslash
- a target longer than 1,024 bytes

That is why the examples in this note sit inside code spans and fences. Outside one, the same text is a live mention — and an unresolved one becomes a ghost node in the graph.

Parsing is capped at 512 occurrences per note. The cap exists to bound what one note can write: at the 2,000-note walk cap a single pathological note would otherwise add a million rows. A note that mentions a target fifty times is a list, not fifty distinct relationships, though each mention still counts until the cap.

## Following, creating, renaming

Following a mention is in-place navigation, not a history stack: the notes list is the way back. A heading fragment lands on that heading after the note renders — exact text first, then case-insensitive — with anchors read only from source outside front matter and fenced code, so a note documenting Markdown grows no anchors.

An unresolved target offers create-from-link: the pane asks for a path pre-filled with the missing name (and `.md` appended when the last path component has no extension) and creates exactly the note you confirm. An ambiguous stem gets no offer, because creating either candidate would be a guess.

Renaming a note offers a second, separate step: "N mention(s) in M note(s) still name old-name — update them?" The preview and the write use the vault as it stands after the move, so only occurrences that resolved to the old name are respelled. Mentions of a stem two notes shared were ambiguous, so they stay untouched. An alias and a `#fragment` survive, line endings and every other byte are preserved, and fenced code, code spans, and escaped openers are not link occurrences and are not edited. The renamed note itself joins the pass only when its editor buffer is clean, because a dirty buffer must never be written under.
